News.title: Shocking moment brave woman pins shark down then pulls hook out of dangerous mouth during family beach trip
News.content:
Next

THIS is the heroic moment a mother pulls a fishing hook out of a shark’s jaws in North Carolina.

Wild footage shows a mum at Cape Hatteras, North Carolina carefully removing a wire from the mouth of a beached shark using pliers.



She bravely pins down the animal between her legs and attempts to free it.

The shark wriggles around in discomfort as the she fearlessly grabs its mouth with her bare hands.



Video captures the beachgoer using pliers to pull the hook out of the it’s jaws.

She calms down the shark and helps it return to the water.



Bystanders watched in shock as the ordeal unfolded.

The courageous moment was captured on video by Olivia Talbot in Cape Hatteras on July 4.



Talbot said that the woman and her family were fishing in the area when the shark caught the bait and ran them about 200 yards down the beach.

A crowd then gathered to watch as the family pulled the shark to shore and tried to get the hook out of its mouth.

Talbot said: “To my knowledge, this specific shark is nearly classified as endangered, so she worked as quickly as possible to unhook it.”

“She released him quickly after.”

Shark fishing is legal in the state of Florida, but is strictly regulated by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission to protect apex predator populations.



Some species of sharks are legally required to be released back into the water, according to guidelines outlined by North Carolina Marine Fisheries.

The brave beachgoer was lucky to not be injured helping the shark, after a spate of shark attacks in America this summer.

On September 21, a great white shark was caught on camera tearing apart a helpless victim at Great Point Beach in Nantucket, Massachusetts,

Terrifying footage captured the surrounding water turn blood red, as the predator’s ripped apart the swimmer.

In August, a 71-year-old veteran lifeguard was yanked six feet beneath the waves in a terrifying suspected great white shark encounter.



The drama unfolded at Scarborough Beach State Park in Maine, where Greg Wilfert has worked as a lifeguard for more than five decades.

He said: “There’s no fish that’s going to do that.

“It has to be a big fish or a shark. It had to be the shark.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

John Schweizer, a 69-year-old dad from Connecticut, was dragged underwater by shark on July 24 off the coast of the Bahamas.

The devastating attack happened in front of his wife and sons while on a family adventure cruise for the parents’ 40th wedding anniversary.

News.title: Putin ‘willing to meet’ to end war in Ukraine, claims Donald Trump as tyrant unlikely to attend G20 summit in US
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin is “willing to meet” to end the war in Ukraine, Donald Trump claimed yesterday.

The US President said the Russian tyrant wanted to end the bloody conflict he began waging in 2022.



Addressing the United Nations in New York, he said: “We’ve had a meeting in Alaska already.

“I think he’d do another one.



“I don’t know about Miami. We have a big thing happening in Miami soon. But, no, he’ll meet.

“He’s willing to meet. He’d like to see the war ended.”



Mr Trump’s reference to Miami comes with the US hosting the G20 summit there this December, but Putin is unlikely to attend.

A historic summit between the US President and his Russian counterpart was held in Alaska last year, but failed to break the deadlock.

During a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky yesterday, Mr Trump predicted Ukraine would “make a deal”.

Mr Trump also criticised Britain’s former PM Sir Keir Starmer of being “too tough” on Putin.



New PM Andy Burnham has pledged to stand with Ukraine like his predecessor and chose Kyiv for his first overseas trip in office.

News.title: Burnham blasts Russia & vows ‘we will be unflinching’ in defending Britain in speech to UN General Assembly
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has blasted Russia for subjecting the UK to an “industrial-scale assault” and has vowed to take action.

The PM took to the stage at the United Nation General Assembly and told world leaders “we will be unflinching” in defending Britain.



In his maiden address in New York the PM slammed Russia as “repulsive” and said the country had preyed on people’s fear.

Speaking just after midnight on Wednesday UK time he added: “Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation.”



He continued: “We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events.

“The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive – but it is what they do.”

He pointed to attempts from Russia to meddle in European elections and said the Kremlin had spent £1.3m on manipulating information.

Mr Burnham continued: “They’ve used bots and fake websites, falsified articles, forged the branding and tried to stoke unrest after horrific events.”

In response to Russian interference he said “security starts at home” and revealed plans for a new National Centre for Information Defence.

The centre will look “to detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks – to support and defend our democracy”.



He said AI only stands to increase the threat and announced a new partnership with the US on AI defence to protect national infrastructure.

This will be part of a wider move to put AI “at the heart of the UK’s G20 presidency next year”.

He again called for global regulation on AI to ensure the technology is developed safely that needs to be dealt with similarly to the 2008 financial crisis.



Mr Burnham said the new centre will work to “to detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks – to support and defend our democracy”.

He announced a new AI defence partnership with the US to “protect our critical national infrastructure”.

While praising the opportunities for AI in the economy and in medicine he said the technology will be a “multiplier of risk”.



He said: “We will bring the right people together on the key issues: delivering on the potential of AI for good, and dealing with the risks.”

Mr Burnham added: “We will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness – and to ensure that AI development is safe.”

The UK will share its experience of dealing with disinformation with other allies, he said.

However, positioning the UK as a leader in creating a set of rules to prevent the spread of rogue AI could cause a rift between Mr Burnham and the US President.

The Prime Minister reiterated his wish for the UK to act as an “honest broker” to draw up “a single set of global principles and standards” for the development of frontier AI.



But his speech at the United Nations General Assembly came just hours after Mr Trump told the same event that he would resist attempts to rein in what he called “super intelligence”.

After a meeting with Donald Trump earlier, Mr Burnham insisted Britain was “America’s greatest ally” in his speech.

He also said Britain will also stand against threats to the rights of British territories such as the Falkland Islands.

Mr Burnham similarly earlier told Donald Trump Britain would “stand firm in the face of any threats” to the Falkland Islands.

He said that he told the US President that he would “defend” the territory during their meeting on Tuesday.



This comes after Mr Trump boasted he could “settle” any future conflict over the Falklands during a recent trip to Ireland.

Mr Trump said a war between the UK and Argentina would be a “potential disaster”.

The PM managed to escape relatively unscathed from his showdown with Donald Trump.

The President praised Mr Burnham as a “natural businessperson” and said he “gets it”.

He even told reporters he preferred Mr Burnham to Sir Keir Starmer and said relationships between the two countries were on the “up”.



Mr Trump added: “Based on my relations with your prime minister Andy. I think we’re doing very well.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But he took a slap from the US President over his continued support to give the Chagos Islands away to Mauritius.

Mr Trump said: “I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. They [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership.

News.title: Cop used AI to generate victim statement to ‘make a judge or reader weep’ and achieve the ‘highest sentence’
News.content:
'DEPLORABLE' Cop used AI to generate victim statement to ‘make a judge or reader weep’ and achieve the ‘highest sentence’







Next

A POLICE officer used AI to write a victim impact statement designed to “make a judge or reader weep”, a court heard.

The cop also told Microsoft Copilot they wanted to “achieve the highest sentence” for Jerome Gibson, who was convicted of crimes including domestic abuse last year.

The 23-year-old thug was jailed for 44 months after he admitted kicking down a door and threatening his partner with a knife, as well as GBH toward a police officer in a separate incident.

But he appealed the sentence, with lawyers arguing the AI-generated statement had helped influence the judge at Nottingham crown court.





The Court of Appeal in London rejected the claims yesterday.

Mr Justice Lavender deemed the cop’s usage of AI “deplorable” but noted that the text was entirely based on things the victim stated in her interview, with no machine “hallucinations”.

He said: “These facts were not AI-generated hallucinations but things F had stated in her interview.”

He added: “It does not appear that the use of AI, deplorable though it is, caused the appellant’s sentence to be any longer than it otherwise would have.”



Denis Barry, for the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “Everyone in court would agree that facts in criminal cases speak for themselves and they do not require exaggerated language in criminal proceedings.

“The conduct of the officer displays a use of evidence-gathering that is concerning.”

He added: “The officer has been removed from frontline duties.”

News.title: Like the Bayeux Tapestry, the latest mega-dinghy to cross the Channel was given a VIP escort… govt needs a deterrent
News.content:
Route ’66







Next

JUST two weeks ago, Britain and France celebrated a priceless symbol of our shared history.

The Bayeux Tapestry, brought across the Channel under massive police escort, went on display in a sell-out exhibition at the British Museum.



Yesterday another convoy set sail from a beach near the town that gave the 950-year-old relic its name. But this time it was not carrying a medieval masterpiece. It was packed with migrants.

Like the tapestry, the mega-dinghy was given a VIP escort by French ships before its occupants were transferred to lifeboats to land on the Kent coast.



It’s a bitter irony that the coastline immortalised by the 1066 conquest of England has become the launchpad for a new generation of Channel crossings.

Labour has just signed a £660million, three-year deal with France to increase the number of anti-migrant beach patrol officers to 1,000.

But people smugglers are still launching boats and are now looking beyond the Calais area. The only way the Government will halt the crossings is to develop a realistic deterrent.

Until then, the tragic reality of life’s rich tapestry will continue to unravel.

A terrible bet

BRITAIN’S ailing high streets are on life support after a series of tax hammer blows to pubs and betting shops.

Bookies have already been forced to close branches and shed hundreds of jobs. Despite this, further raids are expected in the Budget.



Betting shops are a major high street employer, providing 37,500 jobs.

But tax rises risk driving punters towards unregulated and illegal betting sites, while putting high street bookies and thousands of jobs in jeopardy.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch believes Labour is “cannibalising” business by trapping the economy in a “tax doom loop”. A further hike in betting tax would pile yet more pressure on the jobs market — and our high streets.

It’s a senseless gamble that risks making everyone a loser.

Bloc heads

AS if we didn’t have enough problems, some people think the answer is to surrender power back to the EU.



Lib Dem leader Ed Davey thinks taking Britain back into the single market would boost the economy.

Has he forgotten you have to pay to join, give up control of our borders and hand over trade policy to Brussels?

Meanwhile, Andy Burnham refuses to rule out rejoining the EU after the next election.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The dangers of a coalition of the Left should give the Tories and Reform plenty to think about.

If they don’t keep the “progressives” out, we’ll end up back in the EU.

News.title: Putin using fake movie casting calls to lure unwitting into fighting for him as ads promise ‘chance to change your life’
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin is using fake movie casting calls to lure unsuspecting Africans into fighting for Russia – with ads promising the opportunity to “change your life”.

The desperate tyrant is reportedly using social media to bait in low-paid workers around the world – promising much higher salaries and passports.



Russian military recruitment has relied on advertising and tracking from Meta and Google to reach potential troops around the globe, a Code for Africa report has found.

It claimed 89 websites, seven social media accounts and 39 messaging accounts were being used to reach the Kremlin’s targets.



Many of these false adverts for “work” in Russia appeared while unwitting users scrolled on Facebook or Google.

The shoddy ads promised things like construction jobs, security work or acting roles.

But when users clicked on these, they were led to disguised recruitment websites.

Several of these even used western logos such as the BBC, suggesting some sort of endorsement.



In one shocking ad, a “global casting call” for a new movie sought “African male actors”.

The poster, shared by a Facebook page in Germany, showed an AI-generated image of three Black men wearing military vests.

Another ad, sponsored by the account “IRC Russian Bear”, showed another Black soldier with Russian flags stitched to his khakis.

The job description promised £11,000 immediately upon signing the contract and a £2,200 monthly salary.



It also said: “A chance to change your life.”

The investigation also detailed how the depraved recruitment scheme relies heavily on Western technology.

The flagship recruitment site was hosted on a server in Amsterdam, while many websites across the network were built using AI from US or Swedish firms.

When recruits were tricked into handing over their details through application forms, software from an Austrian company collected their info before it was sent over to Moscow.

The report said: “Behind that Western layer sit ordinary Russian commercial hosts, and behind those a bulletproof-hosting tier built to survive complaints.



“The result is that a war sold to Africans, Asians and Belarusians is sold with the tools of the countries that publicly oppose it.”

The bombshell probe also found users were easily led to these sites by searching for things like “contract service” or “engineer contract for foreigners” in Russian.

There was also a glaring difference in how Google’s AI-generated search summaries presented the recruitment services depending on language.

Researchers found that European language showed warnings of risks much more prominently than other languages.

Ukraine estimates there are currently roughly 1,700 people from 36 African nations fighting for Russia.



The Sun reached out to Google and Meta for comment.

It comes amid speculation Putin is mulling a mass mobilisation of hundreds of thousands of soldiers in order to fuel his stalling war machine.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The dictator has already recruited tens of thousands of North Koreans, as well as South Americans, to fight in Ukraine.

News.title: Gran battling ‘Lego blockade’ after ‘childish’ council dumps concrete slabs in her garden
News.content:
BRICKING IT Gran battling ‘Lego blockade’ after ‘childish’ council dumps concrete slabs in her garden







Next

A GRAN is battling her local council after giant “Lego” blocks were dumped outside her home.

Helene Ball, 81, previously won £50,000 following a three-year-long legal fight over a metal fence which was erected across a gap in her garden wall.



But the gran-of-four is now gearing up for round two after 54 huge “Lego-style” blocks were placed outside her home.

Helene moved into her home on George Road in the picturesque village of Matlock, Derbyshire, nearly 60 years ago.



In April 2023, Derbyshire County Council ordered a six-foot high green fence to be installed in a gap in her garden wall which led to a council car park.

The barrier meant the retired school teacher found herself caged into her own home by “spiteful” council bosses eager to sell-off a car park to developers.





She claimed her right of way had been illegally blocked as the cut-through had offered her a shortcut to friends who live on nearby Cavendish Road.

Last month Helene won back her right of access following a tribunal, where she proved she had used the gate since the 1960s and the council were ordered to pay her legal fees of around £50,000.

Now 2ft-high bricks line the narrow road behind her property and the grass verge alongside her garden wall.

Helene, who has two grown-up children, said: “It’s just so petty of the council to do this after they lost the case but they have been spiteful from the start.

“The judge said I had a right of access by foot and by car to the rear of my house.



“However, the council have made it impossible to drive a car up the road and turn round, it’s ridiculous.”

She is now preparing for another legal battle in a bid to force the council to remove the blocks.

Her son David, 50, who has been carrying out legal work on behalf of his mum, said: “The council have not acted in the spirit of the law.



“Our legal team are investigating whether the council are interfering with access to my mum’s home.

“Basically my mum won her case but the council have made it impossible for her to use the access road which she has used since she moved in.

Derbyshire County Council admitted it had been “unreasonable” to erect the original green fence at the centre of the dispute.

A spokesperson said: “It would not be appropriate to comment further on matters that have been considered by the court other than that the council has a duty to safeguard its legal interests in public assets, including land that it owns and manages on behalf of residents.

“Where issues arise concerning council-owned land or access rights, the council has a responsibility to consider the matter carefully and, where appropriate, defend any action.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Its actions are always guided by its statutory duties.”

The council has until Friday to appeal Judge Robert Brown’s ruling on access to Helene’s home.

News.title: Plastic-lined ‘narco torture chamber’ found in Costa del Sol as blood-soaked escapee screams ‘they want to kill us’
News.content:
GRUESOME FIND Plastic-lined ‘narco torture chamber’ found in Costa del Sol as blood-soaked escapee screams ‘they want to kill us’







Next

A HORRIFYING torture chamber has been found in the Costa del Sol with hammers and pliers discovered next to a chair wrapped in plastic.

The twisted room at the holiday hotspot in Spain was only uncovered by cops on September 5 after a bloodied and naked man was able to escape.



Photos released by police show the gruesome room, which had plastic sheeting covering the floor and walls, and several torture tools.

They believe the plastic was used to cover up any traces of the horrific torture, as it was regularly collected and burned to remove all biological evidence.



Seven gang members were arrested in Estepona and imprisoned for torture, kidnapping, and other crimes.

Police also revealed that the two victims and seven criminals all had criminal records, with one of the victims and several of those arrested having previously served jail time.



Investigators have not confirmed why the men were being held captive, but they believe the torture was a drug-related settling of scores, likely to do with a failed job or money owed to the gang.

Police were initially tipped off at 1.05am by one of the victims’ girlfriends who feared for his life.



She said: “My partner has gone to a house to carry out shady business and told me that if I didn’t contact him in ten minutes I should call the police.”

After the distressing emergency call, police arrived at the property to conduct a search but no one answered.

As two officers climbed over the fence, a naked man drenched in blood ran out of the house shouting “they’ve kidnapped me and they’re going to kill me!”

He was later identified as the Moroccan man whose girlfriend had alerted the police.

Two of the assailants, wearing face coverings, attempted to escape police by jumping over the neighbours’ fence.



An officer fired a warning shot into the air after noticing one of the men was carrying what looked like a firearm.

They called for backup, and once inside, uncovered a horrific torture chamber with a second naked man, a Spanish national, tied to a chair and covered in blood.

During the raid, officers seized two AK-47 assault rifles and several pistols.

Speaking to EL ESPAÑOL, authorities said: “[This] is a gang dedicated to trafficking cocaine and hashish, whose activity also includes other crimes such as extortion.”

The National Police have confirmed that some of the seven arrested had records for robberies with violence, drug trafficking, and even had pending court summonses.



Spanish authorities are considering contacting Interpol to help track down the remaining gang members.

The Provincial Brigade of Judicial Police of Malaga said: “The activity of this organization of professional criminals had a presence on the Costa del Sol, in the Campo de Gibraltar and in the Levante area.”

The wild and terrifying case comes just a month after a similar incident in nearby Fuengirola.

Six men were jailed over the kidnap and torture of a young Dutch man in Fuengirola.

The victim, who was in his mid-twenties, had worked for an international cocaine-trafficking network operating between the Netherlands and Malaga.



He was suspected of helping to steal a drug shipment worth more than €3 million.

Three of the arrested men were sentenced to nine and a half years each for unlawful detention, organised crime membership, causing injury, and robbery with violence.

In March 2023, police arrested 15 people in Marbella for kidnapping and torturing four men.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

One of the victims nearly died after going into a diabetic coma.

The captors reportedly blamed the men for the theft of 1,500 kilos of hashish.

News.title: UK to fight Russian disinformation and push new global AI standards, Burnham says
News.content:
The UK will set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of hostile state attacks, including Russian disinformation, and lead efforts to establish global safety standards for artificial intelligence, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.

In his first major international speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, Burnham warned Russian agencies are using "every means at their disposal", including bots and fake websites, to "spread lies and disinformation".

The prime minister noted AI will "multiply" existing threats, and pitched the UK as an "honest broker" on the technology.

Fears about AI have grown after industry insiders recently warned it could threaten humanity.

In Burnham's speech, he accused Russia of running a disinformation campaign.

"The Kremlin spends around Â£1.3 billion each year on manipulating information," Burnham told the UN General Assembly.

"They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC.

"We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community â creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair.

"On top of that we have seen cyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. And we know that AI will multiply the threat."'

He also referenced the 2019 UK general election, in which the government previously said Russia almost certainly sought to interfere.

To counter this, Burnham announced a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt AI-enabled disinformation campaigns by hostile states.

The centre will work alongside intelligence agencies, government departments, law enforcement and social media to bring together expertise to combat "information warfare".

There was no immediate comment from Russia, a representative of which was sitting in the room listening to Burnham.

When the UK government put out a report in 2020 about Russian activity in the UK, including in elections, Moscow described the allegations as "Russophobia".

Addressing a forum about disinformation in Moscow on Tuesday, before the prime minister's speech, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Western media of embracing "anti-Russian cliches and fantasies".

News.title: Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has said Andy Burnham is a man he can do business with, after the two leaders met in person for the first time.

Trump said UK-US relations are "more up now" that Burnham is in power, following their meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Speaking to reporters, Burnham said he had "established a good connection" with Trump and they had "taken that further today" following discussions on issues such as trade and immigration.

But the US president made clear his opposition to the UK's "terrible" deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back a joint UK-US military base on the archipelago's largest island, Diego Garcia.

Burnham, asked by broadcasters if the deal is "dead", later said the UK will "work hard" to find a resolution between the different sides and he is "confident we can find it working with our US partners".

Trump and Burnham met on Tuesday as they attended the United Nations for the annual gathering of world leaders.

Following bilateral talks, Burnham sat alongside Trump and used his opening remarks to say: "You and I have established a good connection in our early discussions and we've taken that further today."

The two men then faced questions shouted from the assembled press pack.

Asked by the BBC if Burnham was a man he could do business with, Trump said: "Yeah I do, I think he's a natural businessperson, we've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting we've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone.

"Yeah, I think so, he gets it, he understands what he has to do."

Burnham later said he had explained to Trump that Britain has been in "too much turbulence" in recent times but it is time to "turn the story" about the country into a positive one.

The US president added that the UK is a country with "great patriotism", and he thinks it is "waiting for good leadership, waiting for success".

Relations between Sir Keir and Trump also began well before becoming increasingly strained earlier this year when the then-prime minister refused to permit the use of UK bases for the initial US-Israel strikes on Iran.

News.title: Plot targeting Manchester's Jewish community disrupted, say police
News.content:
Two men have been arrested over a suspected terrorist plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester, police have said.

The men, both in their 30s, were arrested on Sunday on the eve of Yom Kippur - considered to be the holiest day in the Jewish calendar - when thousands of British Jews were in synagogues already guarded with a heavy security and police presence.

The men were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, according to the Metropolitan Police, which is leading the investigation.

Sources have told the BBC the suspected plot was "fairly imminent" and in the later stages of planning.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the government would "continue to do all in our power to address threats against our Jewish community".

She added: "We cannot expect our Jewish community to live behind higher walls.

"We must also tackle antisemitism at its source and root it out wherever it rears its head."

News.title: 'Poison seller' who sold my daughter deadly drugs should rot in hell
News.content:
A Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals to people who went on to kill themselves should "rot in hell", the mother of a British woman who took her own life has said.

Imogen Nunn, known as Immy, died in January 2023 aged 25 after buying drugs online from Kenneth Law.

Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in online suicide forums. But almost 80 deaths in the UK have also been linked to him.

However, as part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.

Imogen's mother, Louise Nunn, told the BBC she was angry he would not face justice here. "I think we've been let down as families. Our children have been let down," she told the BBC.

It comes as the impact statements of UK families will be read in court in Ontario this week.

News.title: IMF tells advanced economies to 'bring debt down' as borrowing costs rise
News.content:
The world's advanced economies including the UK and US need to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels following weeks of spiralling government interest costs, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

In an exclusive interview, Kristalina Georgieva said global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost".

"[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.

The intervention comes as government borrowing costs have surged in response to wars disrupting the supply of oil, which has fuelled inflation.

Higher global borrowing costs have hit the UK government in the run-up to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first Budget next month, with speculation building over potential tax and spending policies.

The latest figures show borrowing - the difference between tax receipts and government spending - was Â£18.3bn ($24.4bn) in August, almost a fifth higher than the year before and higher than official forecasts. Meanwhile debt interest for the month was the highest August figure since monthly records began in 1997.

Higher borrowing costs have also hit the US, the world's largest economy, which has seen its debt pile surpass $40tn. The amount has doubled within the space of a decade, prompting concerns at home and abroad.

On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Georgieva said the IMF's message to advanced economies was that while there were economic factors occurring outside the control of governments, they did have command over domestic policies.

"There are these two things that must be done: bring debt levels down, put fiscal consolidation as a priority, and make sure that the central banks deliver on their mandate for price stability," she said.

"It is impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to get the courage to take the steps that are necessary. These are politically tough steps to take, but necessary steps to take."

Asked specifically about the UK's higher interest costs compared to other major economies, Georgieva said its position was "not very different" from others.

She pointed to "fairly consistent action" on lowering debt and praised planning and housing reforms, adding that advanced economies "don't have the cash" to boost growth and so had to rely on reforms to encourage the private sector to invest.

News.title: Europe's car makers are in crisis. Will the threat of war rescue them?
News.content:
For European brands, all of this could not have happened at a worse time. The loss of the steady stream of profits from China, and the emergence of Chinese rivals on their home turf, has come after they invested heavily in producing electric vehicles (EVs). But EV sales have not increased as quickly as expected. Executives admit they have struggled to match the low production costs and development speed of the Chinese insurgents.

The result is that European manufacturers are now rushing to cut costs, while wondering what to do with expensive factories capable of producing millions more cars than they are able to sell.

Volkswagen has already announced plans to cut 100,000 jobs over the next few years. Whereas once closing plants in Germany would have been unthinkable, the company has now shuttered one in Dresden and may shut down four more. That includes a site in Zwickau, where VW spent over â¬1bn (Â£857m) converting production lines to build electric vehicles - a process that was completed just four years ago.

Industry estimates indicate that western European car plants have roughly 2.5 million vehicles worth of annual spare capacity.

Little wonder that car makers are jealously eyeing soaring defence budgets across Europe.

Sigrid de Vries says car makers are well placed to help Europe rearm.

"Many of the capabilities that defence needs are needed for and also delivered by the automotive sector," she says. "So automotive manufacturers and suppliers possess industrial assets, they possess manufacturing expertise, logistics capabilities, also advanced technologies. They have vast and also very integrated supply chains that may be relevant for Europe's broader defence preparedness objective."

But it is not that simple â security protocols, political and economic rivalries within Europe plus the fact that unless you're actually at war, the volumes will not replace the mass consumer market, all of which present challenges, she says.

"These are two very different worlds," she says. Governments want to invest in their defence capabilities and that is why it's now, more than ever, interesting for manufacturers and suppliers to see what's possible, but it will not be enough to address the underutilisation of manufacturing capacity we currently see."

News.title: Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market
News.content:
The Liberal Democrats will fight the next general election on a promise to cut taxes for millions of workers, Sir Ed Davey has said in a speech to his party conference.

The Lib Dem leader said that if he gained power, he would raise the annual tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000.

He would also raise the 40p income tax threshold from Â£50,270 to Â£56,000, in a Â£17bn package funded by the economic boost he says would come from the UK rejoining the EU single market and customs union.

He claimed the plan would mean a Â£680 cut for "most taxpayers" but it would not come into full effect until the fifth year of a Lib Dem government - potentially up to eight years away.

The announcement was greeted with sustained applause by Lib Dem MPs and activists in the Brighton conference centre.

The Â£12,570 income tax allowance was frozen by the Conservatives in 2021, resulting in more people being dragged into paying the tax, and Labour has so far resisted calls from trade unions and some of its MPs to unfreeze it.

The Lib Dems said they would raise the threshold to Â£15,000 a year, and increase the starting point for paying employee National Insurance (NI) to the same level.

At their conference earlier this month, Reform UK promised to increase the income tax personal allowance to Â£15,000 within 100 days if they won power.

Sir Ed told the Lib Dem faithful "the difference between us and Reform" is that "their tax cut is paid for through cruelty."

He said "Reform's figures show they'd pay for it by ripping Â£22bn of crucial support away from disabled people."

Explaining his pledge to raise the 40p income tax threshold, Sir Ed argued that more and more people were being dragged into a tax bracket that had originally been intended for higher earners.

"A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses" he said, adding: "That's not fair, it's not right."

Under the Lib Dem plan, based on research by think tank Frontier Economics, external, the economic boost from rejoining the single market would allow the party to spend Â£17bn on tax cuts by the end of the next Parliament.

The party says it would unfreeze personal allowances in the second year of a Lib Dem government, allowing them to rise with inflation, before bringing in big tax cuts in year five when the economic benefits of closer trading with the EU had kicked in.

However, the move would depend on the party being able to negotiate a closer trading arrangement with the EU in just 12 months.

Stuart Adam, of the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, told BBC Verify the Lib Dem package would cost "much more" than the Â£17bn quoted by the party.

Reform has estimated that its policy, to raise the starting threshold to Â£15,000 just for income tax, would cost Â£21bn by the fifth year.

The Lib Dems say their policy would be funded by an extra Â£27bn from its plans for a "growth and defence pact" with the EU.

News.title: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences
News.content:
Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police have said.

The charges are an alleged indecent assault against a teenage girl aged 16 to 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham in 1991 and the alleged sexual assault of an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth in 2004.

These charges are in addition to those brought against Westwood, 68, in October 2025 relating to seven women, which include four counts of rape.

Westwood has previously denied multiple sex offences, including rape and sexual assault, and pleaded not guilty to earlier charges last December.

Westwood is now facing a total of 17 charges involving nine women.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police Service, said: "The women who have made reports have placed their trust in us, and we remain committed to providing them with all available support.

"Independent support is also available through Rape Crisis via its 24/7 Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line."

Westwood is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court at a future date in relation to the two additional charges, the Met Police said.

A trial relating to the original 15 charges is scheduled to begin at Southwark Crown Court on 25 January 2027.

Catherine P Baccas, deputy chief crown prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) London, said: "Today the Crown Prosecution Service has authorised two further charges of sexual assault and indecent assault against Tim Westwood.

"Mr Westwood is already charged with nine counts of indecent assault, two counts of sexual assault and four counts of rape in relation to reported non-recent offences between 1983 and 2016 involving seven women.

"These new charges, following an investigation by the Metropolitan Police, relate to separate reports of non-recent offences in 1991 and 2004 involving two additional women.

"Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring these additional charges to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue further criminal proceedings.

"The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that criminal proceedings are active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial."

News.title: Earl Spencer should pull Diana book from shelves, Piers Morgan says
News.content:
Piers Morgan has called for Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana to be pulled from the shelves over a factual error.

Earl Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, apologised to Morgan for incorrectly describing him in the memoir as the editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group published "highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym" in 1993.

Speaking to the BBC, Morgan said he accepted the apology but that his lawyers would be "laying out that we want the offending pages to be removed from this book. And if that means they pulp the first edition, so be it".

The BBC understands Penguin, the publishers of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, will be amending this one point in future editions of the book.

The photographs of Princess Diana mentioned in relation to Morgan in Earl Spencer's book were published by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993.

At the time, Morgan was working at The Sun and did not join the Mirror as its editor until 1995.

Earl Spencer admitted "his assumption was incorrect" and "apologises to Mr Morgan for this error", a statement said.

News.title: New EU industry rules would damage UK, warns Burnham
News.content:
Andy Burnham has warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK, as he met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies.

The prime minister said he was concerned about how British industry and supply chains could be affected, and raised the subject with von der Leyen when he met her during a UN summit in New York.

Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day".

He said his immediate priority was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach an agreement that would boost the British economy.

The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its supply chains.

Tensions over the proposed scheme have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July.

Burnham said: "We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us.

"We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain.

"We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies hereâ¦ we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem.

"We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'."

News.title: Father admits causing death of his son in hotel fall
News.content:
Foster was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week for the plea hearing to take place.

His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing.

Paphos District Court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side.

Foster decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said.

A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing.

"The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said.

The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence.

In a statement given to the BBC, Alexandrou, said: "This was a momentary lapse of attention, without any intention to cause harm, which had the most devastating and unimaginable consequences.

"We will now present to the court the relevant mitigating evidence and circumstances for consideration ahead of sentencing."

The family have suffered "unimaginable grief" since the "horrific events" and have asked for privacy during this time, added the lawyer.

News.title: Mum and three children die in Bootle house fire
News.content:
A mother and three children have died in a house fire on Merseyside.

Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property in Stone Square in Bootle, Sefton, at 03:45 BST.

Eight firefighters searched the house where they discovered four people in an upstairs bedroom who were showing no signs of life, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.

Another casualty, who was outside the property when crews arrived, was taken to hospital.

Officers from Merseyside Police were at the scene and a joint investigation with the fire service into the cause of the blaze is under way.

The North West Ambulance Service's hazardous area response team also attended the scene of the fire and confirmed the four fatalities.

Chief Fire Officer Nick Searle confirmed the "intense fire [had] spread very rapidly".

News.title: Reform MSPs walk out of parliament in protest against Scottish independence debate
News.content:
Michael Marra, the new leader of Scottish Labour, was among those backing the motion although he said it was more about SNP internal politics and less about practical action to make people's lives better.

His amendment, which was passed, retained Swinney's statement but added that efforts should be stepped up to tackle child poverty.

During the debate, Marra said there had "always been a route to another referendum".

That route was to "build a consensus â the settled will of the Scottish people â and make it overwhelming".

But he said he believed Scotland "can be a fairer and stronger nation without being a separate state".

He added: "I don't believe we have to risk our currency, our defence, our markets and our budgets to deliver a more equal and just Scotland."

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the SNP should accept the result of the "once in a generation" 2014 referendum - which saw Scotland vote by 55% to 45% to remain part of the UK.

"The SNP say that Scotland should decide. We did decide, more than two million Scots said no, and thank goodness for that," he said.

Swinney insisted that a simple majority of pro-independence MSPs represented a mandate for a referendum.

"My party believes it is for the people of Scotland to decide when there is an independence referendum."

Saying that Scotland needs the "fresh start" of independence, he told MSPs the "fundamental right to decide our nation's future remains".

Swinney also raised the demographic change in Scotland since the last independence referendum.

He claimed that by 2029 there would be more than one million people in Scotland who did not have the opportunity to vote because of their age, and by 2030 the youngest voters would not even have been born in 2014.

He added that Scotland's place in the UK and the world "had changed beyond recognition" after Brexit.

News.title: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies aged 67
News.content:
British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died aged 67 after a short illness.

After living in Africa, he joined the BBC in 1986. Doyle became East Africa correspondent in 1993 and made his mark covering the Rwandan genocide a year later.

As West Africa correspondent from 1997 to 2002, he reported on Sierra Leone's brutal civil war and aftermath of Liberia's conflict.

Following Doyle's death, BBC foreign editor Paul Danahar said he was a "legendary figure", as well as a" brilliant, brave, empathetic reporter".

The BBC's Andrew Harding, who worked with Doyle, paid tribute to his former colleague in a 2015 article, published to mark his departure from the national broadcaster.

In the piece Fergal Keane, another prominent BBC correspondent in Africa, recalled their stint in Rwanda in 1994. "He stayed longer than any of us," Keane said of Doyle. "Those who were in that awful place at that awful time will know what Mark Doyle gave for the cause of truth and for the BBC."

In the same article Sir David Richards, who headed British forces struggling to stop Sierra Leone's civil war in 2000, also praised Doyle.

Sir David said his reporting helped convince the UK government of the need for a robust intervention. "Hence the saving of thousands of Sierra Leonean lives that would otherwise have been at huge risk," he said.

In 2004 Doyle won first prize in the UN Correspondents Association/UN Foundation Awards for his coverage of post-war Liberia.

He became BBC World Affairs correspondent before retiring from the BBC in 2015.

One of the most famous sites in a New Jersey shore town is coming down, taking with it decades of fun childhood memories for locals and tourists.

The Ferris wheel that was a focal point of the shuttered Gillian’s Wonderland Pier in Ocean City will soon be demolished.

"Right now, we have a decrepit and decaying site, and we have to do something. You know, time is not on our side,” real estate developer Eustace Mita, who purchased the site in 2021, told news outlet WPVI.

Gillian’s Wonderland Pier opened in 1965 and closed in 2024 — a week before its 94-year-old founder, Roy Gillian, died, CBS News Philadelphia previously reported. Now the iconic Ferris wheel, weathered by years of salt air, will soon be cut apart.

Mita explained that the Ferris wheel’s bolts and major components have been fused due to corrosion, meaning it cannot simply be disassembled and preserved.

open image in gallery The Ferris wheel that was a focal point of the former Gillian’s Wonderland Pier in Ocean City, New Jersey, will soon be demolished ( Getty Images/iStock )

"It would make it impossible to reassemble in place anywhere," he told WPVI.

Locals are grieving the loss of the beloved Ferris wheel, with Andrew Boylan calling it “a big staple of Wonderland.”

"It feels like a lot of memories are being taken away,” Boylan, who spent 13 years working at Gillian’s Wonderland Pier, told CBS News Philadelphia.

Stu Newman, who would go to the pier as a child, said, "I'm an engineer, so I understand that aspect of it, but from a personal side it's going to have a lot of attachment to a lot of people that have ridden that thing decades ago."

"I'm upset because it is a cornerstone of Ocean City and we all have wonderful memories of it,” said Mary Anne Munning, who stopped by the site to take a photo of the Ferris wheel Tuesday before it gets demolished.

open image in gallery The site’s developer explained that the Ferris wheel’s bolts and major components have been fused due to corrosion, meaning it cannot simply be disassembled and preserved ( AFP via Getty Images )

In June, the Ocean City Council voted to designate the former Gillian’s Wonderland Pier as an area “in need of rehabilitation,” bringing Mita one step closer to creating a 252-room oceanfront hotel. The developer initially planned to keep the Ferris wheel part of the property.

"Our thought was we will rehab it, keep it, and actually raise it by 10 feet. That will be a $1.5 million project," Mita told WPVI in 2024.

But Mita’s proposal has yet to be approved, and the city council’s designation has been challenged in court.

Several community groups filed a lawsuit to reverse the council’s decision to designate the site as “in need of rehabilitation,” WPVI reported in August.

Former Today Show host Billy Bush has been hired as a contributor at Fox News, returning to cable television a decade after his career collapsed over a leaked 2005 tape during which Donald Trump bantered with him about sexual assault.

Bush made his debut on Jesse Watters Primetime on Tuesday night and will appear across all Fox platforms, the network announced.

“I’m excited to join FOX News Media and its loyal audience to share my perspective on the people, ideas and moments shaping today’s culture,” Bush said in a statement released through Fox News Media, “as well as the ones trying to undo it!”

The move comes ten years after Bush lost his position as an anchor on NBC’s Today Show following the release of a three-minute video recording. In the clip, captured on the set of Days of Our Lives while Bush was an anchor for Access Hollywood, Donald Trump made crude remarks about women and bragged about groping them. Bush was heard laughing at the comments.

“You can do anything,” Trump said on the tape, which was published by The Washington Post shortly before the 2016 presidential election.

open image in gallery Former ‘Today’ show host Billy Bush is joining Fox News as a contributor, making his return to television ten years after a leaked 2005 video showing Donald Trump joking with him about sexual assault derailed his career ( Getty )

Following the disclosure, Bush issued a statement saying he was “embarrassed and ashamed” of his conduct.

“Of course he said it,” Bush wrote in a 2017 essay in The New York Times, addressing later reports that Trump had questioned the authenticity of the recording. “And we laughed along, without a single doubt that this was hypothetical hot air from America’s highest-rated bloviator.”

In the same piece, Bush directed comments toward women who had made allegations of sexual misconduct against Trump.

open image in gallery More than a dozen women have accused Trump of sexual misconduct — in 2023, a federal jury in New York found Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll over a mid-1990s incident in a Manhattan department store dressing room ( AP )

“To these women: I will never know the fear you felt or the frustration of being summarily dismissed and called a liar,” Bush wrote, “but I do know a lot about the anguish of being inexorably linked to Donald Trump.”

More than a dozen women have accused Trump of sexual misconduct. In 2023, a federal jury in New York found Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll over a mid-1990s incident in a Manhattan department store dressing room, awarding her nearly $90 million in damages. Trump is appealing the verdict.

Bush, 54, who is a nephew of former President George H.W. Bush and a cousin of former President George W. Bush, went on to host the syndicated program Extra for five years and launched the podcast “Hot Mics With Billy Bush.”

Sitting on the floor of a makeshift shelter for survivors of Nepal's deadly recent floods, Tenzin Dolma Ghale said she had nothing left but the clothes she was wearing. Her entire village and members of her family were washed away by the surge of water and debris that killed over 1,450 people and left more than 6,000 missing.

After speaking, she waved a hand and looked at the ground. “It’s all finished,” she said.

Ghale is among millions of people living with the deadly consequences of climate-related disasters. As such disasters intensify, international climate adaptation and disaster preparedness aid programs have been slashed, leaving countries facing billions of dollars in avoidable damage and dwindling recovery funds.

“The reality is that we need trillions of dollars every year, but developed countries have not met their obligation,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of New Delhi-based Satat Sampada Climate Foundation.

Aid cuts weaken disaster monitoring in the Himalayas

The Trump administration’s abrupt cuts to U.S. foreign aid in 2025 eliminated or sharply curtailed programs serving millions of people worldwide, with devastating consequences for many communities. Reductions by other major donor countries deepened the funding crisis.

Among the programs shut was SERVIR-Hindu Kush Himalaya, a joint initiative of the U.S. Agency for International Development, NASA and the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD.

Covering Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan, the program used satellites and geospatial analysis for disaster risk reduction, water resources and land cover. It facilitated flood risk services, collaboration with the Nepal Red Cross Society on risk communication and more than 170 public data sets on glaciers, disasters and vulnerability.

Glacial and disaster preparedness experts praised the organization for its extensive research, cross-border coordination and support of local disaster reduction measures.

Before losing its funding due to USAID cuts, the program addressed mounting risks in a region where climate change has caused rapid glacier melt, shifting monsoons and increasingly frequent floods, landslides and glacial lake outburst floods, or GLOFs. Those changes endangered food, water and energy security for nearly 2 billion people living in or downstream of the region, according to ICIMOD.

Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, according to a new report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with ICIMOD. Yet only around 0.1% of the Himalaya’s estimated 40,000 glaciers are currently monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, the report said.

When funding for SERVIR-HKH ended, so did programs that monitored landslide forecasting, daily flooding, training programs and regional collaboration between countries.

With the program's loss, millions now face a heightened risk of GLOFs, which can release millions of cubic meters of water and debris in just a few hours.

In northern Pakistan, melting glaciers have created 3,044 glacial lakes, with over 30 identified as likely to result in such floods in areas where over 7 million people live, according to the United Nations Development Program.

Afghanistan also faces an increased threat of GLOFs, according to research published by the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

In India — which was not part of the SERVIR-HKH program but borders all of the countries that were and is also home to over half the Himalayas — over 130 high-altitude lakes are at risk of flooding.

South Asia is already experiencing deadly climate-related disasters. The 2022 Pakistan floods killed more than 1,700 people and caused an estimated $40 billion in damage. Flooding in Nepal in 2025 killed nine people and caused millions of dollars in damage. Cloudbursts, landslides, flash floods and extreme rainfall have wreaked havoc in the Indian Himalayas, resulting in the death of over 12,000 people and damage exceeding billions of dollars in the last 15 years.

The region suffered economic losses of at least $7 billion in 2025 due to climate-driven extreme weather, according to the Emergency Events Database maintained by the University of Louvain, Belgium. This database itself is at risk of being shut down as a result of USAID funding cuts.

In a statement to The Associated Press, the U.S. State Department said that the U.S. supports Nepal’s flood warning capacity through programs with the World Meteorological Organization and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The department noted that SERVIR-HKH ended in January 2025 but that its tools remain active through ICIMOD.

The impact extends beyond communities hit directly. The Himalayan region is vital to national economies, with agriculture, industry, tourism and domestic use all dependent upon it.

Cuts to programs like SERVIR-HKH will have cascading effects for years, said Neha Rai, a climate finance expert at ICIMOD.

Rai likened the cuts to climate programs to abruptly halting funds for cancer research, which needs years of sustained research for success.

“Climate risk is also a generational challenge,” said Rai. “You need long-term observations, expertise, you need institutions that cannot simply be switched off and on as short-term priorities.”

Rai said cuts to cross-border programs have also impacted information sharing between governments, scientists and organizations across the region — a critical function in a region where what happens upstream directly affects countries downstream.

Climate finance shrinks as vulnerable countries face rising debt

These cuts are part of a larger trend. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, official development assistance from its Development Assistance Committee members, which includes the U.S., fell 23% in 2025 — the largest annual contraction on record. Traditionally large donors such as the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Japan and Canada have also announced massive reductions, reallocating funds to defense and other domestic priorities.

Global South countries spend approximately 225 times more in debt repayments than what they receive in grant-based climate finance, according to a recent report by the advocacy group, ActionAid International.

“There is a toxic relationship, in fact, between the climate crisis and the debt crisis,” said Teresa Andersen of ActionAid International.

She said countries take loans to recover from climate impacts but then cut investments in clean energy and preparations for future climate-related extreme weather to repay the loans.

The money being provided isn’t nearly enough, and climate often isn’t prioritized, said Richard Sherman, a board member of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, an international climate finance mechanism to assist developing countries vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change.

“There’s plenty of money if it goes to certain priorities, but for climate change right now, we’re witnessing a severe depreciation of the importance to act and make systems more resilient,” he said.

While disaster recovery funds still exist, they're also losing funding and aren’t equipped to handle the expected increase in disasters, he said.

“We’re not expecting developed countries to act as an ATM,” said Sherman. “But supporting vulnerable countries, helping them adapt and become more resilient means they’re less likely to suffer the kind of impacts we have right now.”

___

Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

Democratic voters remain deeply divided over a potential nominee for the 2028 presidential race, according to new polling from Bowling Green State University and YouGov.

The survey placed former Vice President Kamala Harris in a tight race at the top of a crowded pack, with 17 percent support among Democratic voters.

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg closely followed at 16 percent, while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and California Governor Gavin Newsom polled at 14 percent each.

Reviewing the data on “CNN News Central,” CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten described the early primary landscape as exceptionally scattered, comparing the party’s primary base to people who “don’t know what the heck they want.”

“There are four folks within 17 percent, I mean, it’s just completely messy,” Enten said. “The clear thing to take away here is there is no clear leader in this group. This is a field that is messier than any Democratic field in at least 20 years. I would argue, the messiest, least clear Democratic field since 1992.”

open image in gallery According to new polling, the race for the 2028 Democratic nomination remains wide open as voters split their support among early contenders — CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten called the emerging primary field the party’s ‘messiest’ in decades ( Getty Images )

Enten noted that the current primary environment differs significantly from prior cycles, calling the lineup the party’s “messiest” in decades and joking that “it’s messier than an airport the Sunday after Thanksgiving.”

Addressing Harris’s standing, CNN host Kate Bolduan asked how her current support compared with her earlier popularity among Democrats. Enten highlighted her sharp drop in numbers since the summer of 2024.

“You see the 17 percent now, back in July of 2024, just as Joe Biden was getting out of the race, Kamala Harris was polling at 45 percent,” Enten said. “You know, that’s more than twice as much as the support that she has right now.”

open image in gallery Former Vice President Kamala Harris holds a slim lead at 17 percent, topping a crowded early primary field ( Getty Images )

Enten compared her position with President Donald Trump’s early lead ahead of the 2024 Republican primary, when Trump held 49 percent support among GOP voters.

“This is a weak place for a frontrunner,” Enten said. “These are the types of numbers that would really make me think twice about running if I was Kamala Harris, given her universal name recognition.”

The polling metrics were released hours before Harris was scheduled to join Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for a campaign stop in Michigan.

The trip to the battleground state reignited questions about her potential 2028 plans, though Harris has not publicly announced or committed to another campaign.

His voice forceful and proud, he rose in front of the world's largest gathering of leaders on behalf of his nation and announced that he had something important to say. The tiny South Pacific island nation of Nauru, its president said, had altered its name — and reclaimed its heritage in the process.

“I have traveled far,” David Adeang said Tuesday at the United Nations.

What was known to the world for many years as Nauru, Adeang said, was returning to the name and pronunciation of its past: Naoero.

“There are moments in the life of a nation when its people are called to remember who they have always been,” Adeang said in his speech at the U.N. General Assembly in New York. “This is such a moment for us.”

Though the names are similar and, in essence, the same word, the shift in spelling and pronunciation represents the nation's effort to recast — rebrand, even — itself for its own people as much as for the outside world. He called it not a change but an effort to “affirm a truth.”

“For many years, the world has known our country as Nauru. Nauru is how our name sounded to those who found it hard to say, and the world kept it,” Adeang said. “But it is not the name our people used among themselves.”

The nation, an eight-square-mile island with about 12,000 people, became independent in 1968 after longtime colonial rule under the United Kingdom, New Zealand, Australia and Germany. It announced the renaming in August after signaling its intent in February.

The country’s international code is changing from NRU to NRO and its people will be known as dei-Naoero instead of Nauruan. Commonly known abroad by the pronunciation of Now-roo, the new name is spoken as Now-ero.

Across the past century, other nations have renamed themselves or tweaked their names for various reasons, from modernization to rejection of colonialism.

The African nation of Eswatini changed its name from Swaziland in 2018. In Africa, Dahomey became Benin after a 1975 coup and Rhodesia became Zimbabwe in 1980 after shedding colonial rule. Siam became Thailand in 1939 to foster ethnic unity and shed a foreign label.

Turkey, meanwhile, has been officially named Turkiye since 1920 but requested in 2022 that the United Nations use the spelling and pronunciation as its name in English as well — in part to avoid confusion by underscoring that the bird wasn't the word.

The list goes on. Persia became Iran. Burma became Myanmar. Upper Volta is now Burkina Faso, Gold Coast is Ghana and Ceylon is Sri Lanka.

A name, obviously, is a pivotal and intimate expression of a nation's identity on any stage, domestic or international. Adeang's remarks Tuesday reflected this as he carefully pronounced the name to differentiate it from its former pronunciation.

“We do not make this choice to erase our past. We make it because we honor it,” he said. “That name carries the memory of our ancestors, our language, and our identity. It has been there all along. Never lost, never absent. Today, we restore Naoero.”

And then, after completing his address about the issues that face his people — rising seas, economics, respect on the global stage — he concluded his address with three words:

“Say our name.”

___

Ted Anthony has written about international affairs for The Associated Press since 1995.

The Princess of Wales wore a set of earrings which belonged to Princess Diana as she and Prince William attended the world premiere of Tom Cruise’s new film.

William, who is the president of Bafta, and Kate attended the premiere of Digger in Leicester Square, central London, on Tuesday. Kate wore a purple floor-sweeping Jenny Packham dress accessorised with Diana, Princess of Wales’s earrings and the Queen Mother’s amethyst sautoir necklace.

William wore a black velvet tuxedo that attracted a compliment from Mr Cruise, who greeted the prince with the words “great jacket”.

open image in gallery Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales speak with Director Alejandro G. Inarritu and cast member Tom Cruise as they attend the "Digger" world premiere ( Reuters )

The film premiere came as the Prince of Wales’s late mother has dominated headlines due to the publication of her brother Earl Spencer’s book.

The 64-year-old Mr Cruise stars opposite Riz Ahmed, Sandra Huller and Jesse Plemons in the film about an oil tycoon whose company sets off an ecological disaster, forcing the Mission: Impossible star’s billionaire character to embark on a mission to save humanity from his own mess.

The Hollywood star wore a traditional black tuxedo with cummerbund and bow tie, but his patent leather cowboy boots were a surprising nod to his Digger character.

open image in gallery Tom Cruise attended the premiere in patent leather boots ( Getty )

Co-star Mr Ahmed, who opted for a single-breasted black blazer with flap pockets and wide-leg suit trousers, was accompanied by his mother in a traditional sari in red ombre tones.

British actor Mr Ahmed was not the only star who attended the event with his family: Sir David Beckham brought along two of his sons, Cruz and Romeo, with the family trio all in tuxedos.

They posed for photographs alongside William and Kate, who were also seen talking to the cast of the satirical black comedy, including House Of The Dragon’s Emma D’Arcy, Everything Now actress Sophie Wilde and Call Me By Your Name’s Michael Stuhlbarg.

open image in gallery The Prince and Princess of Wales with David Beckham and his songs Cruz, second right, and Romeo, right ( Geoff Pugh/Daily Telegraph/PA Wire) )

The film’s director Alejandro G Inarritu, who won best director Oscars for The Revenant and Birdman, was also on the black carpet.

Digger actress Huller wore a gold deep V-neck gown with cape-like sleeves, while her co-star Wilde walked the carpet in a dark purple off-the-shoulder crinkled dress with sculptural draped layers and a neckline bow.

Known for his exuberance at premieres, Cruise spent time taking photographs with fans and also signed the white shirt of one man who was in the crowd.

open image in gallery The Prince and Princess of Wales greet Tom Cruise at the Royal Film Performance of Digger, at the Odeon Luxe in Leicester Square, central London (Ian West/PA) ( PA Wire )

Also in attendance, Salma Hayek wore a silk-caped black maxi dress while actress Jodie Turner-Smith wore a peach-toned backless pleated dress with ruffled sleeves.

Ted Lasso actress Hannah Waddingham also posed for photographs wearing a sparkly black strapless gown alongside her partner Nick Beresford-Cleary.

Digger will be released in cinemas in the UK on 2 October.

News.title: England learn more in scrappy Sri Lanka win than in summer of white-ball walkovers
News.content:
You do not expect spinners to dominate at Chester-le-Street, but this hot summer has produced strange events, none more so than Jacks recording the second-best figures by an England spinner in one-day international cricket having previously only taken three wickets in 16 games at home.

Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka’s debutant leggie who was playing club cricket in East Anglia a year ago, laid down a marker as he impressed with three for 44 starting with the wicket of Root, his first dismissal in one-day international cricket since February.

England’s 89-run win was completed by Jacks taking three for none in four balls as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 176, their run chase a timid effort when they had a sniff of victory after restricting England to 265 and preventing them from hitting a six for the first time in an innings since 2019.

Vice-captain Jacks has evolved under Harry Brook’s leadership from an opening batsman to middle-order finisher who can chip in with the ball. “He is just a good leader with bat ball and in the field. He is buying into everything we want to do,” Brook said. “We are always talking about adapting to conditions and he has done it really well since coming back in. He could have moaned and groaned about batting in the middle order and playing as an all-rounder but has accepted that will be his place for a long time.”

Brook thought England made “just about par” on a very dry pitch and was reluctant to shower too much praise on batting consultant Kevin Pietersen, whose spin class the day before concentrated on making runs on a slow surface. “It will take time, more than one day. He’s not a miracle worker but it helps the more opportunity we get,” Brook said.

England were stretched and Pietersen will be happy. He told them to think about their approach, that in this type of game “rotation of strike is incredibly important”. He was right, they ran well, apart from Rehan Ahmed, and did not hit a six in an innings for the first time in seven years.

When England batsmen tried to force the pace they perished. Ben Duckett, Root and Brook all had opportunities to build an innings without seeing it through and it required Jacks to tip the total to more than 250. He batted within himself at first, but hit four fours in a row in the 47th over in a late burst that took England to a winning score.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.
