World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 22, 2026
World.content:
Monrovia — South Africa Pushes for Permanent African Seat on UN Security Council

South Africa is leveraging ongoing intergovernmental negotiations on UN reform to advance the African Union's demand for permanent representation. Speaking at the 81st UN General Assembly, South Africa's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Mxolisi Sizo Nkosi, highlighted Security Council reform as a core priority for Pretoria as it rallies support across member states.

The Security Council currently comprises 15 members: five permanent and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. South Africa maintains that the body must expand to reflect contemporary global realities, specifically addressing Africa's historic absence from the permanent category.

UN Voices Deep Concern Over Escalating Security Crisis in Ethiopia

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The UN has expressed strong concern over a deteriorating security situation in Ethiopia, pointing to the formation of a new coalition of armed groups, widespread instability, and repeated drone strikes.

Speaking at a press briefing on September 21, UN Secretary-General Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the UN was "deeply concerned" by the ongoing escalation. The warning comes amid heightened tensions across the country, including fresh clashes between federal forces and regional troops in northern Tigray.

South West Somalia Steps Up Flood Preparations Ahead of El Niño Rains

South West State President Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe convened a high-level ministerial committee and the Somalia Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) to review emergency preparations ahead of expected El Niño rains.

Officials outlined risk mitigation plans aimed at preventing flood damage, safeguarding communities, and enhancing disaster response capabilities across the state. President Madobe urged government agencies and humanitarian partners to streamline coordination and ensure emergency equipment is pre-positioned in high-risk zones.

South African Women Need Protection, Not Warnings, Says Human Rights Watch

The discovery of several women's bodies on the outskirts of South Africa's commercial capital, Johannesburg, has caused fear, anxiety and outrage across the country. All the women were found naked or partially clothed, according to police. Some of the bodies had bruising. At least three suspects are already in custody as authorities continue to examine possible links between the killings

Writing for Human Rights Watch, researcher Stacey-Leigh Manuel emphasized that these horrific killings are not isolated incidents, but rather symptom of South Africa's ongoing national emergency regarding gender-based violence.

World.title: Niger: Junta Strips 5 More Exiled Critics of Nationality
World.content:
press release

Nairobi — Latest Crackdown Heightens Rights Concerns Amid Renewed Political Tensions

Niger's junta has provisionally stripped five more exiled opposition figures of their nationality, extending a controversial policy increasingly used against critics of the military authorities, Human Rights Watch said today.

On September 17, 2026, Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani, who has led Niger's junta since the July 2023 coup, signed a decree removing the nationality of five prominent Nigeriens living in exile. The decree derives authority from a 2024 order creating a national terrorism database with overbroad inclusion criteria and inadequate due process requirements and safeguards for redress. The order jeopardizes privacy and data protection rights and increases the risk of statelessness.



"The Niger junta's use of a terrorism database to deprive people of their nationality without any meaningful legal safeguards raises serious human rights concerns," said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. "Nationality is a fundamental legal status, not a privilege that governments can take from people for political reasons."

The five affected are former Prime Minister Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou; Amadou dit Ange Barou Chekaraou, Oumarou Moussa Ibrahim, and Ousmane Abdoul Moumouni, all former advisers to President Mohamed Bazoum, who was ousted in 2023 and remains arbitrarily detained; and Boubacar Seyni Souley, a social media activist critical of the junta.

The September 17 decree accuses the men of various offenses, including disseminating information capable of disturbing public order, providing intelligence to foreign powers, electronic defamation, demoralizing the armed forces, and threatening state security.

The decree raises questions about compliance with Niger's existing legal framework. The 1984 Nationality Code does not provide for "provisional loss" of nationality. Where deprivation of nationality is permitted, the law requires the authorities to notify the person concerned and give them one month to submit a written defense before the measure is published in the official journal.

"Nothing of the sort is happening here," the Alliance of Sahel Democrats, a coalition of Nigerien, Malian, and Burkinabè diaspora political opposition groups advocating a return to constitutional rule, said in a statement on September 18. The alliance also noted that the September 17 decree is depriving individuals of their nationality while they are still being prosecuted, in contravention of the 2024 order, which states that deprivation of nationality can only be imposed after a conviction.

According to Niger's press agency, the junta's latest action brings the number of people provisionally deprived of Nigerien nationality under the 2024 order to 25. In October 2024, the junta provisionally stripped nine people linked to former President Bazoum of their nationality. In June, authorities revoked the citizenship of Mariama Djibrine, an opposition figure living in exile.

In a September 19 statement, the G25-Niger, an opposition coalition of civil society groups and media organizations formed in 2025, said the 2024 order "is being used as a tool of political repression ... to crack down on opponents and other dissenting voices."

Since taking power in 2023, Niger's military junta has entrenched authoritarian rule and consolidated sweeping and unchecked powers, systematically weakening institutions capable of holding the military authorities to account.

In the past year alone, the military authorities have dissolved all political parties and several independent unions, suspended dozens of civil society groups, detained journalists under a broad cybercrime law, criminalized consensual same-sex relations, announced Niger's withdrawal from the International Criminal Court, and prolonged the country's political transition without any roadmap toward democratic elections. In addition to Bazoum, the junta continues to arbitrarily detain Moussa Tchangari, a prominent human rights defender.

The authorities have also taken steps to curb criticism from abroad. In June, Niger's foreign affairs minister instructed diplomatic missions to monitor online criticism of the military authorities, signaling growing scrutiny of the diaspora's discussions of the country's political and human rights situation.

The political climate in Niger has become increasingly tense in recent weeks, Human Rights Watch said. On August 28, mutinous soldiers attacked a military base at the international airport in Niamey, Niger's capital, and the presidential palace, with hours of gunfire. The mutineers also briefly seized the headquarters of the state-run national television, disrupting broadcasts. General Tiani called in Russia's government-controlled Africa Corps, whose intervention, including the use of armed drones, helped loyalist forces suppress the mutiny.

Close 

Niger is a party to the United Nations Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, which restricts states from depriving people of their nationality when doing so would leave them stateless. Colleagues of the five affected by the September 17 decree said that at least four of them only possess a Nigerien passport.

Those who are without a nationality as well as their families risk being deprived of legal and social protection abroad. It could prevent them from returning to Niger, which is their right under international human rights law.

"The Niger junta has been depriving perceived political opponents of their nationality without meaningful due process, and contrary to Niger's obligations to prevent statelessness and protect fundamental rights," Allegrozzi said. "The junta should immediately revoke the decree and suspend the use of the easily abused terrorism database."

World.title: Djibouti: Djibouti Frees Top SA Investigative Journalist Micah Reddy
World.content:
South African investigative journalist Micah Reddy of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists was detained on Saturday, but is now on his way back to South Africa.

Micah Reddy, the South African investigative journalist who was detained by government authorities in Djibouti on Saturday, 19 September, was released on Tuesday and is on his way home to South Africa, unharmed.

His family announced this on Tuesday following two days of anxiety after he and his local fixer Kooki Mahmoud disappeared from their hotel in Djibouti at about 1pm on Saturday. Reddy's family said in a statement that Mahmoud had also been released without charge.

"It is with immense relief and delight that we share the news that he is on his way back to South Africa, unharmed," the family said.

Reddy, a journalist and Africa Coordinator at the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), had been held in the custody of Djiboutian authorities "from 1pm on Saturday, 19 September 2026", the announcement added.

"Despite numerous efforts to establish his whereabouts and condition, no official information was provided until today," the family said.

World.title: Sudan: Drone Strikes Destroy More Than 330,000 Learning Materials in Sudan's North Kordofan State
World.content:
New York/Nairobi/Khartoum — Drone strikes on two warehouses in Shikan locality, North Kordofan, on 20 September destroyed over 292,000 school textbooks, 40,000 Arabic Language and Mathematics Review Books, and other learning materials intended for distribution to children.

The materials were to be distributed from October 2026, marking the start of the new school year, including to schools in West Bara, Bara and Um Dam, with the loss expected to affect the learning of thousands of children.

"The destruction of these learning materials is a setback for children at a time when every effort is being made to get them back into the classroom," said Angela Kearney, UNICEF Representative in Sudan. "Many children have missed years of schooling due to the conflict. With schools already facing shortages of teachers, desks and learning materials, this loss will further undermine children's access to quality education. Every child has the right to education, and that right must be protected."

Delivering education supplies to the conflict-affected areas in Sudan is often challenging, making the loss of these materials particularly significant. Access to safe learning opportunities remains essential to helping children learn, recover and build their futures.

UNICEF calls on all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure and uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law. Education supplies and facilities must be safeguarded to ensure children can fulfill their right to education.

World.title: North Africa: Egypt Declares Suez Canal Secure As August Revenue Surges to $567 Million
World.content:
CAIRO — Egypt's Suez Canal Authority (SCA) has declared the waterway safe, with maritime traffic flowing normally as August revenue rose 56.7 percent year-on-year to $567.1 million, up from $326 million in the same month of 2025. SCA Chairman Osama Rabie announced the figures during a ceremony in Alexandria marking World Maritime Day 2026, organized by the Maritime Transport Sector of the Ministry of Transport.

The revenue increase represents a notable rebound for a canal that has endured significant disruptions in recent years. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty previously said Red Sea tensions had cost Egypt roughly $11 billion in lost Suez Canal income. The latest numbers point to a recovery for one of the country's most vital sources of foreign currency.

The canal transited 1,358 vessels in August 2026, a 27 percent increase from 1,070 vessels in August 2025. Net tonnage rose 51.1 per cent to 68.3 million tonnes, up from 45.2 million tonnes a year earlier.

Rabie emphasized that navigation remained stable and services continued at high efficiency. He added that canal pilots were carrying out their duties with the highest levels of readiness and professionalism.

Despite the strong year-on-year gains, traffic has not returned to pre-disruption levels. Average canal transits stood at about 40.8 vessels per day between January and August 2026, compared with 73.7 per day in 2023. Canal revenue reached $4.67 billion in fiscal year 2025/2026, a 23 percent increase, though vessel transits and cargo tonnage remain below the canal's peak performance.

The Suez Canal remains a critical artery for global trade, linking the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea and offering the shortest maritime route between Asia and Europe.

World.title: Liberia: A Decade On - the World Is Still Listening to Liberia's Ebola Story
World.content:
Ten years after Ebola swept through Liberia and claimed thousands of lives, the world is still turning to this small West African nation for answers. On Sunday, in a wide-ranging conversation, Chris McCall of The Lancet's World Report, the news section of one of the world's oldest and most trusted medical journals, sat down with Gregory T. Blamoh, Secretary General of the Liberia National Red Cross Society (LNRCS), to revisit an outbreak that reshaped the country's approach to public health emergencies.

The conversation was part of a broader examination of how nations once devastated by epidemics have turned hard-won experience into lasting institutional memory.

"Our success in the Ebola response was collective," Blamoh said. "Every Liberian was involved and learned from the response. Systems have been put in place, and every Liberian is fully aware of Ebola. And if we were to have any recurrence, the impact will not be as devastating as the first outbreak."

Community volunteers built that collective response on the ground, many mobilized through the LNRCS.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

During the 2014 outbreak, Red Cross volunteers trained, equipped, and trusted by their neighbors stood on the front lines, working across four areas of intervention that remain central to the organization's emergency work today: Safe and Dignified Burial, Risk Communication, Contact Tracing, and Psychosocial Support.

Ten years on, those four pillars remain embedded in Liberia's emergency preparedness architecture.

The LNRCS has continued training volunteers, strengthening early warning systems, and keeping communities informed work that has left the country better prepared for future public health emergencies.

Among the most sensitive and, at the time, most misunderstood interventions was Safe and Dignified Burial. Ebola spreads readily through contact with the bodies of the dead, making traditional burial practices a serious transmission risk.

Working in full protective equipment, 240 LNRCS-trained burial team members took on the difficult task of safely managing the remains of 3,820 Ebola victims while preserving as much dignity and cultural respect as possible.

It required constant, careful engagement with grieving families, community members, and traditional leaders, building the trust needed to explain why long-held burial practices had to change to protect the living.

Alongside the burial teams, Red Cross volunteers led sustained awareness campaigns, going house to house, market to market, and community to community to explain how the virus spread and how it could be stopped. In a crisis defined as much by fear and misinformation as by the disease itself, these conversations became one of the response's most powerful tools, correcting rumors, dispelling myths, and building trust.

Close 

The experience underscored a lesson that still shapes humanitarian response today: communities are not simply recipients of information, but essential partners in saving lives.

Volunteers also formed the backbone of contact tracing, systematically identifying and monitoring people who had been in contact with confirmed cases, following them through the 21-day incubation period, and alerting health authorities at the first sign of symptoms. This community-level monitoring helped catch potential cases early and contain chains of transmission before they could grow work that demanded discipline, persistence, and close coordination with health authorities.

The response also recognized the psychological toll of the outbreak on survivors, families, communities, and responders themselves.

Psychosocial support was woven into the Red Cross response, offering counseling and community-based care to help people navigate grief, stigma, fear, and trauma effects that, for many communities, lingered long after the outbreak was officially declared over.

A decade later, Liberia's Ebola experience continues to demonstrate the value of preparedness, community trust, local leadership, and volunteer action. The Red Cross volunteers at the center of the response were more than emergency workers; they were neighbors and trusted voices who translated public health messages into action that saved lives.

Today, the systems and community networks strengthened during the Ebola response continue to inform Liberia's readiness for future emergencies. As Blamoh put it, the experience "isn't just history; it's a roadmap other nations are learning from."

Ten years later, the world is still listening to Liberia. And Liberia's lessons still matter.

World.title: Nigeria: Central Bank Cuts Interest Rate
World.content:
"It emphasised that the recalibration of the corridor does not constitute a change in the current monetary policy stance, but rather an operational reset to enhance the effectiveness of monetary policy and support the transition to an inflation targeting framework," CBN said.

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has cut the benchmark interest rate to 23 per cent.

CBN Governor Olayemi Cardoso disclosed the committee's decision at the conclusion of the bank's two-day, 307th Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting, held from 21 to 22 September in Abuja.

This decision followed two consecutive retention of the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) at 26.5 per cent, holding it in May and July previously, following a 50-basis-point reduction in February from 27 per cent.



Speaking after the meeting, the CBN Governor stated that the committee decided to reset the MPR and recalibrate the policy corridor as an important operational realignment aimed at strengthening monetary policy transmission.

"The committee decided to reset the MPR and recalibrate the policy corridor as an important operational realignment aimed at strengthening monetary policy transmission and reinforcing the primacy of the monetary policy rate.

"It emphasised that the recalibration of the corridor does not constitute a change in the current monetary policy stance, but rather an operational reset to enhance the effectiveness of monetary policy and support the transition to an inflation targeting framework," CBN said.

The MPC also adjusted the asymmetric facilities corridor around the MPR to +50/-300 basis points, a move aimed at discouraging banks from keeping idle funds with the CBN and encouraging increased lending into the economy.

Furthermore, the committee maintained the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) for commercial banks at 45 per cent, retained the rate for merchant banks at 16 per cent, and kept the CRR on non-TSA public-sector deposits at 75 per cent for liquidity management considerations.

CBN cut the interest rate amid its continued efforts to moderate Nigeria's headline inflation.

Since CBN maintained the rate in May, inflationary pressure has generally eased, with headline inflation standing at 15.39 per cent in August, down from 15.43 per cent in July, 15.91 per cent in June and 15.93 per cent in May, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).

The rise in inflation recorded in April followed the escalation of the Middle East conflict, which began in February and contributed to higher global oil prices.

However, despite the recent easing in inflation, CBN's decision comes amid a renewed increase in fuel prices across the country, a development that could put fresh upward pressure on the prices of goods and services.

World.title: Kenya: Kenyatta Clears Way for New Jubilee Leadership
World.content:
Nairobi — Former President Uhuru Kenyatta has formally cleared the way for a leadership transition in the Jubilee Party, asking members to accept former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang'i to take his place as the party prepares for the 2027 General Election.

Speaking during the Jubilee Party handover, Uhuru said he would move to a senior advisory role while remaining a member of the party.

He then publicly asked Jubilee members to back Matiang'i, who has already been endorsed by the party as its presidential candidate for the 2027 election.

"Let me take that upper position, to be like a senior advisor there," Uhuru said, adding that he would remain available to guide the party.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He told delegates that once he moved to the senior position, his "younger brother" should take over the position he had been occupying.

"And together with all our Jubilee delegates, let us now go and organize ourselves to give him the work for 2027," Uhuru said.

Uhuru made the message even clearer, directly asking Jubilee members to accept Matiang'i.

"I ask you with respect to accept and welcome him. You agreed that I move to that top position, right?" he told the delegates.

"And agree to welcome Fred Okeng'o Matiang'i to take my place. Will you accept that?"

The crowd responded in the affirmative.

Uhuru described Matiang'i as a young leader from Kisii with the qualities he believes Jubilee needs as it prepares for the next election.

"I see there is this young man from Kisii over there called Fred Matiang'i," Uhuru said.

He described him as a person with wisdom, hardworking and someone who "loves Kenyans" and has "no malice."

Uhuru also urged Jubilee members to begin organising early, saying the political season had already started.

He called for the party to identify candidates for elective positions across the country, including MCAs, governors, senators and MPs, as well as a presidential candidate.

"Let us go and look for a President who will lead us like this," Uhuru said.

Despite stepping aside from the top party position, Uhuru insisted that he was not abandoning Jubilee.

"Even now, me as I am, over there, and I'm going nowhere. I am still a Jubilee member," he said.

He said he would remain involved in the party and use his experience to advise its leadership.

"I want to join hands with you so we can organize ourselves," Uhuru said, adding that he had no interest in political insults and wanted Jubilee to work with other Kenyans.

Matiang'i welcomed the endorsement noting that the moment "is humbling."

Close 

"I am deeply humbled and the best gift that we can give Uhuru is ensure that we keep on with this party and its activities as we head to 2027," he said.

The move follows a High Court ruling that barred retired presidents from continuing to hold formal leadership positions in political parties beyond six months after leaving office. Uhuru had earlier said he was ready to facilitate a lawful handover in line with Jubilee's constitution.

The transition has already triggered competition within Jubilee, with Deputy Party Leader Jeremiah Kioni offering himself for the position of party leader and insisting that the next leader should be chosen through the party's democratic structures.

Uhuru, however, said the process should be about organising the party and preparing for 2027.

"Is it running away that I have run away, or is it organizing ourselves that we are organizing ourselves?" he asked.

He also urged Jubilee members to avoid political insults and instead explain to Kenyans what they intend to do if elected.

"Go and tell Kenyans how you will serve them," Uhuru said.

He added: "A vote is not a marketplace. A vote is a vision."

World.title: ‘Big Sister’ warning resurfaces as Massachusetts expands home visits after Clancy trial
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Twenty-seven years before Massachusetts proposed to dramatically expand a taxpayer-funded program sending nurses into the homes of families with newborns, legendary conservative firebrand and grassroots women’s leader Phyllis Schlafly posed a question that her daughter says now sounds remarkably familiar.

"Are the American people willing to allow government agents to come into their homes to ‘advise’ them how to care for their babies?" Schlafly wrote in a March 1999 column titled, "Watch out for ‘Big Sister’ as Well as ‘Big Brother.’"

The warning has resurfaced as Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey seeks $2 million to expand the state’s Welcome Family program, which offers nurse visits following childbirth. The program currently serves approximately 3,000 births annually, with the expansion intended to make visits available following roughly 68,000 births statewide per year.

BLUE STATE GOV IGNITES ONLINE FIRESTORM WITH PLAN TO SEND GOV'T INTO HOMES OF NEWBORN BABIES: 'LUNATIC LIBS'

The push comes in the aftermath of the Lindsay Clancy case, which put a searing spotlight on maternal mental illness. Clancy does not dispute that she killed her three young children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, inside their Duxbury home in 2023.

Clancy's defense argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible, while prosecutors argued she knew her actions were wrong. The jury deadlocked, resulting in a mistrial.

For Anne Schlafly, chairman of Eagle Forum and Phyllis Schlafly’s daughter, her mother’s warning has now taken on new resonance.

"My mother was very prescient about the things that could happen if we let government intrude into our family lives," Schlafly told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TARGETS HEAD START BUREAUCRACY IN MOVE ADVOCATES SAY PUTS PARENTS IN THE DRIVER'S SEAT

"Her point was a government agent or an agent of the government has no business in your home, in your castle, snooping around and determining whether or not you’re raising the children the way the government wants you to raise the children," she said. "After all, the home is our castle."

Phyllis Schlafly’s 1999 column focused on Healthy Families America and similar home-visiting initiatives, warning about programs that screened families for risk factors, connected parents with health and social services and offered parenting guidance inside the home.

She also questioned whether programs officially described as "voluntary" would always operate that way in practice.

Massachusetts today describes Welcome Family as voluntary. Nurses assess the health of the "parents and caregivers" and newborn, answer questions about newborn care, screen for postpartum mental health concerns and connect families with additional services.

MICHIGAN LAWMAKER MOVES TO SHUT DOWN 'GUARDRAIL-FREE' CASH HANDOUT PROGRAM FOR NEW MOTHERS

Notably, Massachusetts lists "ensuring that your home is safe" among the subjects Welcome Family nurses may advise parents about, though the program’s family information page does not specify particular home safety criteria.

The state has called Welcome Family an "entry point into the system of care" for families with newborns. Healthy Families America, the program at the center of Schlafly’s 1999 column, is also among the models Massachusetts lists within its broader Home Visiting Initiative, though it is separate from Welcome Family.

Healey described her vision for the expansion in broader terms during an interview on Boston Public Radio.

"Everybody in the state, when you have a baby, you’re going to have a home visit within days, weeks and that will be an opportunity for a healthcare provider to make an assessment to see if you need some additional support and resources," Healey said.

FIERY VIEWS ON LINDSAY CLANCY AT WORK COULD GET YOU FIRED — AND BE PERFECTLY LEGAL, EMPLOYMENT LAWYER WARNS

Anne Schlafly questioned what meaningful consent looks like shortly after childbirth.

"Is it really voluntary if you don’t have true informed consent?" Schlafly said. "If you have just given birth, you’ve been in labor, you’ve been under sedation, can you really recognize what you were signing up for supposedly on a voluntary basis?"

"I think mothers need to have the full disclosure that this would be a government agent in the home," she added.

The scale of the proposed expansion also concerns Schlafly.

"If government is going to expand their reach and hire a whole bunch of more people and use taxpayer money to send out all these agents to the families, I mean, that’s quite an expansion," she said. "This idea of coming in to inspect and see what’s going on in your home smacks of Big Sister and Big Brother both."

Massachusetts does not characterize the visits as inspections, but as voluntary health and support services.

State officials point to results from the existing program. In 2025, Welcome Family offered 1,620 postpartum depression screenings, with 208 screening positive. The state says every person who screened positive received a referral for services.

Schlafly said she does not object to families choosing to accept that help.

"If people want to have this help from Governor Healey, then they can avail themselves of it," she said.

Her dividing line, she said, is whether parents retain the ability to refuse.

"I think any time you make it compulsory, the line has been crossed," Schlafly said. "I would say the only way that this Massachusetts program could be acceptable is if the parents could opt out at any time."

Massachusetts’ published materials describe participation as voluntary.

Fox News Digital reached out to Healey’s office for comment and clarification about parents’ ability to decline visits, information collected during visits and whether information may be shared with other state agencies.

Nearly three decades after her mother warned about "Big Sister" entering the family home, Schlafly said she believes she knows what her mother would tell Massachusetts parents today.

"There’s no doubt that Phyllis Schlafly would advise parents to reject busybodies who want to inspect their home," she said. "The home is a sacred and private area, and Governor Healey has no business in the homes of Massachusetts parents."

World.title: Kamala Harris says 'attack on DEI is an attack on maternal care' in appearance with El-Sayed

Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Tuesday declared that an attack on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) is an attack on maternal care as she joined Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit to rally support ahead of the November midterm elections.

Harris made the remarks during a campaign roundtable with El-Sayed and several healthcare advocates focused on Black maternal health and healthcare costs.

"An attack on DEI, to recognize diversity, equity and inclusion, is an attack by definition on maternal care, including the need to protect Black women in connection with their pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care," Harris said.

She noted that maternal mortality rates are disproportionately higher among minority groups, with the risk of death increasing up to four times for Black women and three times for Native women.

MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS LEADERS MUST ADDRESS ‘UNPAID DEBTS’ TO BLACK COMMUNITIES

"One in 12 women in America currently lives in a maternal care desert with limited or no access to maternal care," she added.

Harris then took aim at political leaders who tout "family values," arguing that efforts to end DEI programs strip away protections aimed at supporting certain communities during pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care.

BIDEN-ERA DIRECTIVE FOR DIPLOMATS TO PEDDLE DEI ON FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SCRAPPED BY STATE DEPARTMENT

"As one of the most — some would say the most financially strong economies in the world — we have the distinction of also having one of the highest rates of maternal mortality in the world," she said.

"So, it raises the issue of disparities and also hypocrisy when there are leaders who otherwise walk around every day talking about their family values."

Harris also turned her criticism toward President Donald Trump’s health care legislation, which she referred to as the "Big Bad Bill," arguing that it cut Medicaid spending with the support of former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee facing El-Sayed.

DR. OZ UNVEILS MEDICAID OVERHAUL, CLAMPS DOWN ON $2B FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS AND MANDATES WORK FOR ABLE-BODIED

"Medicaid is the largest funder for maternity care in America," she said. "Donald Trump cut Medicaid funding by a trillion dollars. These are the facts Mike Rogers supported that cut through that ‘Big Bad Bill.’"

Harris closed by reaffirming her support for El-Sayed in the Senate race, pointing to his position on maternal health and saying she believes he would be a "champion" on the issue.

World.title: Former WWE star Kurt Angle says 'I believe that I had a better career in TNA'
World.content:
Kurt Angle is probably best known for his WWE run as he racked up six world titles and became the fifth Grand Slam champion in the company’s history. He also came into the company with an Olympic gold medal on his resume, which is just as impressive.

Pro wrestling fans who follow the sport closely know that Angle was a beast in Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA). He was a six-time world champion, a two-time tag team champion and an X Division champion during his near-decade run there.

Angle put on some great matches in TNA with Abyss, Samoa Joe, A.J. Styles and the like.

Angle added that Joe’s background as a ground-and-pound grappler worked well with his freestyle wrestling background. Even with Styles flying around the ring at times when he was young, Angle said the two were able to mesh well.

World.title: From Austin to New York, pro-China network fuels week of anti-US protests as Xi meets Trump
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As President Donald Trump readies for high-stakes negotiations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a network of pro-China organizations funded by pro-communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham is taking to the streets from New York City to Austin, creating the image of rolling street unrest that lawmakers warn China can exploit to project a perception of chaos in the United States.

Yesterday, Singham’s wife, Jodie Evans, wore a trademark fuchsia straw hat and protested across the street from the United Nations on E. 47th Street, between First and Second Avenue, under an arch at Katharine Hepburn Garden, smiling widely next to agitators from the far-left CodePink nonprofit she co-founded and her American-born husband helped fund from his base in Shanghai. As part of their elaborate weeklong calendar, the activists railed against the U.S. military and its "all-out climate and environmental devastation." and then they marched to the offices of Open AI to demonstrate against data centers they allege "drive war" and "economic degradation."

The week’s protests reflect a pattern of rapid mobilization around breaking news and political flashpoints. The sequencing of events — combined with messaging sharply critical of the United States and silent about China’s human-rights, environmental and civil-liberties record — raises questions lawmakers debated last week about whether some activists function as "Trojan horses" for foreign adversaries such as China. Recently, Evans posted a video lauding China for building an economy that helps citizens "grow and thrive." Last year, Singham delivered a speech in China supporting the Chinese Communist Party and Xi's "new world order."

SOCIALIST, COMMUNIST GROUPS COORDINATE, PROMOTE ‘SPONTANEOUS’ ANTI-ICE PROTESTS IN AUSTIN

Lawmakers have warned that the cumulative visibility of such actions shape public perceptions, project an image of instability and give foreign adversaries a potential messaging – and negotiating – advantage as Trump prepares for high-stakes talks with Xi this week.

"The American people need to know that this is not just an organic movement," Rep. Jason Smith, R-Mo., chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, told Fox News Digital. "There has to be more transparency across all areas with these kinds of activities."

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on China, told Fox News Digital the network’s grassroots image belies the serious funding infrastructure behind these groups. "In these situations where you have groups that portray themselves as grassroots, it's really more Astroturf, very fake," he said.

He said the protests "raises serious concerns" about malign foreign influence in the U.S., especially "when you see them actively speaking out against American interests."

The protests are publicly framed as separate events involving immigration, climate change, artificial intelligence, militarism and Israel. But their shared sponsorships show how organizations within the broader Singham network move quickly from one issue to another, using national organizations, local chapters, social-media promotion and shared venues to create a cumulative impression of coordinated street activism.

Moolenaar called for "clarification and transparency" regarding the organizations’ finances and questioned whether they should continue receiving tax-exempt status, adding that their political involvement may violate "campaign rules and political rules here in the United States."

LAWMAKERS RAISE ALARM OVER NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S $278M NETWORK SPREADING CCP PROPAGANDA IN THE U.S.

HASAN PIKER DEFENDS PRO-COMMUNIST, ANTI-ICE SINGHAM NETWORK ACTIVISTS AS 'WONDERFUL PEOPLE'

The significance of the week’s activity is heightened by the scale of Singham’s financial support for the network. A Fox News Digital investigation has documented how Singham has pumped $285 million through a donor-advised fund and shell companies into a broader network of six major nonprofits, media outlets and activist organizations that have promoted anti-American and pro-China messaging.

In that network, Singham has given CodePink $1.33 million, while doling out $22.44 million to the People’s Forum, a hub for the protest activity this week, and $1.098 million to BreakThrough BT Media, a media arm of the network that is flooding social media with images and videos from the coordinated protests this week.

As Fox News Digital reported exclusively, the Justice Department’s Southern District of New York has convened a federal grand jury investigation into Singham’s financial network, sources say. Prosecutors are examining whether Singham, the organizations he funded or their leaders engaged in alleged wire fraud, bank fraud or money laundering, according to sources. Singham hasn’t been charged with a crime, and the investigation doesn’t establish that he personally directed each protest. Singham, the People's Forum, CodePink and BreakThrough News haven't responded to repeated requests for comment.

The sequence began Sunday night in Austin, where socialist and communist organizations rapidly promoted an anti-ICE protest after the shooting of Venezuelan national Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez. The Democratic Socialists of America, Freedom Road Socialist Organization and Party for Socialism and Liberation amplified calls for demonstrators to gather at 8121 Research Blvd. in Austin.

Although media accounts described the protest as organic, the mobilization moved through an existing national activist infrastructure. The Singham network's Party for Socialism and Liberation and the Freedom Road Socialist Organization circulated video and protest messaging, while Democratic Socialists of America promoted the gathering as "spontaneous" and called supporters to the streets. The protest later spread beyond Austin, with activists in Pearsall, Tex., pledging to put "boots on the ground."

In response to Fox News Digital’s reporting on the protests, the Party for Socialism and Liberation published a video with an activist "rejecting" criticism of its Austin protests as a "nefarious" coordinated event and called the protests the result of "righteous anger."

The Party for Socialism and Liberation, Democratic Socialists of America and Freedom Road Socialist Organization didn't respond to requests for comment.

CHINESE PROPAGANDA, SINGHAM NETWORK, FOREIGN DARK MONEY LINKED TO CAMPAIGNS AGAINST DATA CENTERS

On Monday, the network’s actions moved to New York City, where Singham’s wife, Evans, and her cadre of CodePink activists began a week of demonstrations tied to Climate Week and the United Nations. CodePink co-founder Susan Medea Benjamin has led previous protests, including demonstrations supporting China.

After the environmental activism led by Evans outside the UN, CodePink agitators joined an "Unplug OpenAI" protest outside OpenAI’s offices on Lafayette Street, linking artificial-intelligence data centers to the "military-industrial complex." The group’s weeklong schedule promised "disruptions" and "bird-dogging," a tactic in which seemingly regular people plant themselves in restaurants, conferences and other events to heckle and harass public officials and even ordinary citizens, peppering them with questions and shaming rhetoric without any real interest in a dialogue.

Early Tuesday, CodePink celebrated its "fearless cofounder" Evan’s birthday with an Instagram collage of photos from her decades of activism, including the image of a smiling Evans in her pink straw hat, standing beside fuchsia balloons from a campaign called "China Is Not Our Enemy" that the group launched after receiving the donations from Singham. Another photo included her beaming smile next to controversial Marxist influencer Hasan Piker, as the two joined a caravan to support the Communist Party of Cuba.

Later in the day, CodePink activists moved their campaign inside the People’s Forum, a Manhattan hub for communist organizing for a screening of a film, "Earth’s Greatest Enemy," by a fiercely anti-U.S. film company, Watermelon Pictures, chronicling the U.S. military as "one of the most significant drivers of environmental destruction," the "world’s largest institutional polluter."

Back in Austin, a short while later at about 5:30 p.m. Eastern Time, the Singham network's BreakThrough News propaganda network posted edited video clips from the Austin protests, headlined: "SECOND DAY OF PROTESTS IN AUSTIN AFTER ICE SHOOTS VENEZUELAN DELIVERY DRIVER."

For Wednesday, Evans and CodePink promise more protests against the U.S. military's "role in climate issues."

On Thursday, as Xi meets with Trump in the White House, the People’s Forum, CodePink, the Palestinian Youth Movement and other groups in the Singham network are hitting the streets to protest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In social media posts, the groups are advertising a Thursday march from Bryant Park to the United Nations, calling on New Yorkers to "reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project."

That day, Evans and CodePink also plans to participate in a teach-in on "War & Climate: What U.S. Imperialism Demands of Our Climate Justice Movements" before joining the anti-Israel agitation. Organizers are lashing out against the "genocide" in Gaza and blasting "ecocide."

By Friday, as Xi readies to leave town, the protests will go full circle back to Austin, with the Singham network’s Party for Socialism and Liberation planning a protest at 6 p.m. at City Hall with the simple message: "Now is the time for us all to be brave, to follow the example of Minneapolis earlier this year, and TAKE TO THE STREETS!"

World.title: Super Bowl-winning coach reveals 'Cold War' with Broncos' Sean Payton over alleged spying | Matt Calkins
World.content:
Seattle Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald didn't cheat. He took advantage of the Broncos' negligence. But apparently that's not the way Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton saw it.

During a recent interview with Graham Bensinger, Macdonald revealed that he and his staff found around 100 plays that fans had posted on X after filming Broncos training-camp practices in 2024. And given that Macdonald's first game of that season was against Denver, he scouted those plays in order to gain an advantage.

It worked. Seattle came out with a 26-20 win in Russell Wilson's first game back at Lumen Field.

But apparently Payton didn't take too kindly to the Seahawks coaches' scouting tactics.

Macdonald told Bensinger that Payton found out about the plays they pulled from social media midway through the season and "lost his mind."

"He called [Seahawks general manager John Schnedier] and basically threatened to come out publicly and do a whole Patriots Spygate type of thing," Macdonald said. "And I'm sitting there like 'Oh my God, we didn't cheat!'"

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So why didn't Payton make it public? Because according to Macdonald, Schneider threatened to sue if he did. The result was what Macdonald described as a "Cold War" type standoff, with both teams keeping their fingers on the proverbial button without actually pressing it.

After the season, Macdonald said he ran into Payton at his Indianapolis hotel during the week of the NFL Combine. Preparing for confrontation, he instead got meekness, with Payton essentially acting like nothing had happened.

"I was kind of like over him, and he was just like, 'Hey coach,' and he totally backed down in that moment," Macdonald said. "I was like, 'Oh, man. That's great'."

A couple things here. The first is that Macdonald didn't do anything wrong. This was nothing like Spygate, in which there was a deliberate attempt to circumvent the rules. This was just the Seahawks being savvy enough to know where to obtain plays that had been made public.

I don't know what the specific rules are regarding filming with the Broncos, but Seattle doesn't allow anyone to record camp practices after the individual periods have ended. That's called prudence. It's a rule all teams should have in place.

The second is that, assuming all this is true, it's another ding on Payton's reputation. This was a guy who was already suspended for the 2012 season due to the Saints' Bountygate scandal, in which the team paid players to knock targeted opponents out of the game.



He took what appeared to be a swipe at his former quarterback Russell Wilson after Jaxson Dart replaced him as the Giants' quarterback, saying "I was talking to (Giants co-owner) John Mara not too long ago I said 'we were hoping that change would've happened long after our game."

Now there seems to be a petty attempt to call out cheating when no cheating took place.

"He's not my biggest fan," Macdonald said of Payton.

Of course, it would have been interesting to see if Macdonald would have been willing to tell this story a year ago at this time. Winning a Super Bowl gives you the cachet to say close to anything you please.

World.title: Trump’s focus on the press distracts Republicans from pocketbook issues
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Zigzagging from issue to issue, President Donald Trump has left his political allies struggling to keep pace with his pronouncements and lost precious time to drive a compelling message ahead of the midterm congressional elections, Republican strategists and people who’ve worked with him said.

The takeaway from recent polling is that voters worry most about high prices and the cost of living. But Trump has at times veered off pocketbook issues and made moves that are peripheral to the top-of-mind concerns of voters who will soon decide which party controls Congress.

The latest instance of Trump stepping on his party’s own messaging came on Friday.

In the hour before he held an Oval Office event focused on reducing prescription drug prices, Trump announced he was barring three news outlets from the White House grounds because he disliked their coverage. That caught even some members of his own staff off guard.

The media ban has dominated the news cycle for days, and rather than steer the conversation back to the savings Americans would reap from his policies, Trump amplified the furor.

Some Republican candidates in competitive races are increasingly distancing themselves from the president, believing that voters want a different focus and tack than what Trump is offering.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., who is typically a staunch Trump defender, released an ad criticizing Trump’s mass deportation agenda. And GOP candidates in Iowa and Michigan have spoken out against the Iran war and its effect on prices.

Nearly two-thirds of adults lack confidence in the national news media, according to an NBC News survey in June sponsored by More Perfect, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to advancing democracy. That makes the press a ripe target, though it isn’t clear that Americans want Trump to do something about it.

In an NBC News poll this month, registered voters cited inflation, government corruption, threats to democracy, jobs and the economy, the Iran war, immigration and healthcare costs as issues that loom largest; news coverage was not presented as an option.

“The president is out there touting his new arch,” Maura Gillespie, a Republican strategist, said of Trump’s plan to build a soaring arch near Arlington National Cemetery. “None of that addresses the gas prices being over $4. None of that addresses the younger voters who are struggling to afford their first home. None of that is landing.”

“Republicans need to steer their messaging away from Trump and divert their lane from him and focus on their constituents, because that’s the only thing that’s going to get them elected,” she added.

Trump often complains that news coverage fails to credit him for his successes. Labor and stock markets have proved resilient in Trump’s term, though wages are lagging inflation.

“The story no one is writing is how well the economy is doing in spite of the president’s lack of discipline,” said a person close to the administration, who added that Trump, 80, is growing “more impulsive with age.”

Speaking at the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump spooled out a list of accomplishments on his watch. He struck a triumphal tone as he cast the U.S. as a nation in the midst of a renaissance.

“Our economy is the envy of the world,” he said. “Our military is the most powerful on earth. Our technology is second to none and we’re leading in virtually everything. Our energy is fueling the planet. America is rising, our nation is growing, our power is expanding, our country is doing better than ever before.”

A White House spokesman, Kush Desai, said in a statement: “The Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the president’s long-term economic agenda on the home front. Continued private-sector job growth, booming investments, and month-over-month prices of beef, chicken, prescription drugs, and other essentials declining in the last two inflation reports are all proof that America’s positive economic momentum continues.”

In recent months, Trump has slalomed back and forth through the issues.

In April, he threatened to destroy Iran’s civilization. Hours later, he backed off. He called Iran’s leaders “very rational” in June, “scum” in July. In his United Nations speech, Trump revived his apocalyptic threat. He warned that he may need to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into hell” if the regime doesn’t agree to a deal to end the war.

This month he announced that he would send every American a $5,000 check if Republicans win the midterm elections; a key Republican senator whose committee oversees spending plans told reporters he had seen no details of how Trump’s idea would work.

“He’s very unpredictable. He calls it trusting his gut,” a second Republican senator told NBC News, who, like others in this piece, requested anonymity to speak candidly.

The press ban

The latest thunderclap from Trump’s social media feed was his eviction of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds.

A number of high-level White House aides were unaware beforehand that Trump had imposed the ban, and they struggled to explain it in the hours after it went into effect, according to conversations with four White House officials. Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles was absent from the building Friday when he announced the new directive, according to a person familiar with the situation, potentially leading to some of the confusion from the staff.

Still, aides sought to defend Trump’s move.

“Nobody close to the president was surprised at his action to hold the fake news accountable,” a senior White House official said.

Even Vice President JD Vance seemed at a loss as to how to explain the policy. Trump said specifically that he was “banning” the three outlets. But Vance, speaking to reporters Monday before heading to a campaign stop in North Carolina, said: “So, he’s not banning media outlets. What he’s doing is saying, ‘We’re not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda.’”

01:21 Rubio defends White House media outlet ban 00:00 00:00

In an interview with the “TODAY” show, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked whether media outlets should be banned because Trump doesn’t like their coverage. Rubio defended the president’s decision, saying, “There aren’t a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it’s called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They’re just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House.”

MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett were all denied access to the White House on Saturday.

Klein and Haslett both had their White House press credentials confiscated when they sought to enter the grounds.

In his remarks Friday, Trump said, “We are banning them, yes we are, and there may be others to follow.” But a Trump adviser told NBC News on Tuesday “there are not” conversations happening inside the White House about expanding the ban to other disfavored outlets.

The TV networks have set up what’s known as a “pool”; they take turns covering the president as he goes about his public activities and sharing footage with other news outlets. CNN was supposed to provide TV pool coverage on Monday, but the White House barred them from their duties.

In response, the four other networks that are part of the TV network pool — NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox — refused to step in for the exiled CNN, meaning there was no TV pool coverage.

The repercussions were soon evident, potentially impeding Trump’s ability to deliver his message. Newsmax, a conservative outlet, tried to air the president’s remarks at a ribbon-cutting ceremony, but he couldn’t be heard.

“There’s no microphone because the pool cameras aren’t there. So maybe, Tim, this is one example of it backfiring just a little bit,” the Newsmax host said, adding, “So obviously, the ramifications are here. Can’t hear what the president is saying.”

Signs in solidarity with news organizations on the media ban list were placed in the White House press quarters on Saturday. Megan Shannon / NBC News

Trump’s ban is now before a judge. All three outlets filed suit against Trump on Monday, arguing that their eviction violates both due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, set a hearing for Wednesday afternoon on the plaintiff’s motion for a temporary restraining order.

Trump has long lamented his media coverage. During his first term, the White House barred a CNN reporter, Jim Acosta, from the grounds following a contentious public exchange with Trump. CNN sued and the judge in the case — also Kelly — ordered the Trump administration to return Acosta’s press pass. In the end, the administration relented and restored the pass permanently.

In the new term, Trump has also talked privately about barring individual reporters and news outlets from the White House, but he refrained, according to two people familiar with those discussions.

By acting now, he may be distracting from a promising message for his party ahead of the midterms. Internal White House polling shows that Trump’s effort to reduce the cost of prescription drugs is his most popular issue, according to a White House official.

“He can and should be talking about the things that voters say are really important to them. And this [the media ban] is not it,” said Douglas Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee. “It seems to have come out of nowhere and it seems to have caught a lot of people by surprise.”

“We’re less than 45 days out from the election and for the last three days no voter has heard anything about what Donald Trump wants to do to lower prices,” he added. “That’s a problem for any Republican on the ballot.”

The second Republican senator rattled off a series of issues that he’d like to see Trump spotlight.

“He can go out and talk about the reduction in crime,” the senator said, “or controlling the border, or eliminating rules and regulations.”

“But he’s probably not.”

‘Be quiet’

A recent run of setbacks has soured the mood inside the West Wing, a senior White House official said. Even though Trump now has a handpicked chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, the board defied Trump’s wishes last week and raised interest rates.

The Supreme Court has blocked Trump’s attempt to use the Postal Service to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms, something Trump had hoped to do.

Gas prices have spiked since the Trump administration and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28, creating a slow-rolling backlash within the GOP.

Growing numbers of Republicans in tight midterm races are finding ways to distance themselves from Trump, whose approval rating in a new NBC News poll stood at 41%, a second-term low.

Rep. Ashley Hinson, an Iowa Republican who faces a tough race for the Senate, called for an “immediate end” to the Iran war in a social media post Monday. That’s an about-face from Hinson, who has voted against resolutions directing Trump to stop the war six different times.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.”

On Friday, Trump got some unsolicited advice from an iconic figure in the cultural world. Pat Boone, the 92-year-old singer-songwriter, released a video on X that offered a heartfelt suggestion to the president.

“Right now, I feel like you’re very tired,” Boone said, looking straight at the camera. “And I’m worried that many of us haven’t prayed enough for you because I think you’re wearing out and you’re feeling the pressure and expressing yourself in ways that are not becoming to you — that are not presidential.”

“So may I recommend something very highly: that you be quiet.”

World.title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular charged with rape of teen girl
World.content:
“Looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular has been charged in connection with the rape of a teenage girl at his family’s house in Cape Cod last May, according to a criminal complaint.

Clavicular, 20, whose real name is Braden Peters, was charged with rape, drugging someone for sexual intercourse and procuring liquor for someone under 21 years old. The complaint was filed on Sept. 8 in Orleans District Court in Barnstable County, Massachusetts.

Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, an 18-year-old influencer known online as Alorah or Alorah Ziva, alleged that in May 2025, while she was in Massachusetts, Peters called her an Uber to his family’s Cape Cod house. Once there, he got her drunk on vodka while they livestreamed on Twitch and then raped her, according to a criminal complaint from the Chatham Police Department. His mom and grandmother were allegedly in the house.

00:19 Clavicular charged with rape and drugging in Massachusetts 00:00 00:00

The charges come months after Mendoza sued Peters in Miami, accusing him of sexual battery in connection with the events of May 2025. The civil lawsuit also separately alleges he injected her face with a non-FDA-approved fat-dissolving substance during a November livestream in Florida.

A source familiar with the matter confirmed that the charges against Peters are in connection with Mendoza’s allegations.

Peters’ attorney at the time Mendoza’s civil lawsuit was filed said that he denies the allegations and “intends to vigorously defend himself.” The influencer defended himself in a series of posts on X on Monday night; he included a section of a video Mendoza previously posted in which she spoke about meeting Peters in May 2025 and called him “super nice.” Peters also shared what appears to be a handwritten letter Mendoza sent him, in which she said she was “thankful for you helping me.”

“How about dont finance cars you cant afford,” he wrote in one post. “Happens to all successful young men, people try to come for your money. Greed is evil.”

Mendoza’s lawyer told NBC News they have “no comment at this time as the police are handling the criminal matter.” Peters’ attorneys declined to comment.

The Bulwark first reported the criminal charges. Peters’ representative, Mitchell Jackson, said the outlet was “exaggerating” in its article and that Peters had not been served with an arrest warrant. An email to the general mailbox of The Bulwark seeking comment was not immediately returned late Monday.

“Braden Peters has not been physically served. As usual the Bulwark is exaggerating,” Jackson said in a text message Monday night. A source familiar with the matter confirmed that Peters had not been served as of Tuesday morning.

According to the Massachusetts criminal complaint, Mendoza told police she met Peters on Instagram in May 2025, while Mendoza was a minor, and they developed an online business relationship. Her civil lawsuit alleges that Peter offered to help make Mendoza well known online, and paid her $1,000 to make four “looksmaxxing” videos.

Eventually, the criminal complaint says, Peters ordered Mendoza an Uber to his family’s residence in Chatham, Massachusetts, a seaside town at the southeastern tip of Cape Cod.

Mendoza said Peters’ mother and grandmother greeted her when she arrived at the house on May 23, 2025, early in the evening, according to the criminal complaint. She then went into Peters’ bedroom, where they livestreamed on Twitch while drinking alcohol. According to the criminal complaint, Mendoza told police she felt “peer-pressured” to drink.

She said Peters “instructed her to say that the alcohol is water, so that neither his Twitch account nor live stream gets banned,” according to the criminal complaint. After making out on Peters’ couch, Mendoza said she fell asleep in Peters’ bed, according to the criminal complaint.

Mendoza told police that she woke up the next morning to Peters having sex with her, according to the criminal complaint.

“She stated that because it was already occurring, she did not tell Mr. Peters to stop,” the criminal complaint says. “Ms. Mendoza advised that she did not consent to the sexual intercourse.”

Mendoza told police she did not say anything to Peters as he was on top of her because she was in “shock,” and that she never verbally consented to the sex. She said that after Peters finished having sex with her “he was so cold” and ordered her an Uber home, according to the criminal complaint.

In her civil lawsuit, Mendoza additionally alleged Peters had sex with her when she was drunk “to the point where she was unable to give consent.” The criminal complaint did not mention that allegation.

Mendoza did not receive a sexual assault forensic exam after the encounter, according to the criminal complaint.

According to the criminal complaint, she initially told police she told a friend about the encounter but could not provide the friend’s contact information at the time. When police called her back later, she told them she “did not tell anyone the full extent of what occurred,” according to the criminal complaint.

Police attempted to contact Peters multiple times in response to the allegations, per the criminal complaint, but he did not contact authorities as of Aug. 30.

Mendoza said she saw Peters again in November 2025 after they ran into each other at a networking event in Miami, her civil lawsuit says. Peters then allegedly invited Mendoza and her friends to his place in Delray Beach, Florida, for a streaming session on Kick.

Mendoza alleged that during the livestream, Peters injected her with a syringe of Aqualyx, a fat-dissolving compound he did not reveal was not approved by the Food and Drug Administration, which he said would reduce fat in her face, without her consent, according to the civil lawsuit.

“The video shows that Peters had problems injecting Mendoza. In fact, Mendoza’s right cheek has perforated,” the civil lawsuit says, adding that Peters allegedly suggested that the syringe contained methamphetamine.

Peters and Mendoza saw each other a handful of times after that, including instances where Peters paid bouncers to let Mendoza into bars and purchased alcoholic drinks for her, according to the civil lawsuit.

In July, Peters filed a motion to dismiss several counts and challenged the sexual misconduct claim, which was added in an amended complaint. That motion is still pending. Peters is set to be deposed on Oct. 1, and the case remains pending.

Over the last few years, Peters has gained enormous fame as something of a godfather of “looksmaxxing,” an online phenomenon among young men. “Looksmaxxing” is the general practice of trying to maximize your physical appearance through a wide range of dieting, exercise and grooming habits. It promotes men with sharp jawlines, low body fat and symmetrical faces.

“Looksmaxxers” sometimes attempt to achieve the optimal male physique through extreme measures, including “bone smashing,” or using a hammer to intentionally break facial bones so they grow back more defined. Experts have called the trend potentially unhealthy and dangerous.

The new charges against Peters are not his first run-in with the law.

Peters and two other people were charged in April in Florida with shooting at an alligator. He and another person pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public and were given six months of probation and ordered to serve 20 hours of community service, according to NBC South Florida.

He was also hospitalized in April in Miami after a suspected overdose, according to his representative. He said in a livestream at the time, after being released from the hospital, that “I ain’t gonna be doing any more substances for a little while, hopefully for forever.”

World.title: ICE officer who shot Venezuelan man wasn't wearing body camera, sources say
World.content:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in Austin, Texas, on Sunday was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News.

An ICE officer shot Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old native of Venezuela who federal officials said has a deportation order, in the upper torso on Sunday afternoon while Garces Perez was working for DoorDash, according to local authorities and his attorney.

The officer who shot Garces Perez joined the ranks of ICE last year, after previously serving as a border patrol officer within U.S. Customs and Border Protection, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

The shooting was the latest involving federal agents enforcing President Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration and has sparked protests in Texas, as well as calls for accountability and a transparent, independent investigation.

The Austin Police Department on Tuesday released dash cam and body camera footage from an off-duty officer and a responding officer who arrived at the scene after the shooting, but neither shows the lead-up to the incident. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis and Austin Mayor Kirk Watson have both previously stated that local officers were not involved in the shooting itself.

Garces Perez's lawyer said Tuesday she hopes "the relevant agencies will make all available footage public so there can be a clear and complete understanding of what happened."

The lack of body camera footage from the ICE officer who shot Garces Perez — a detail first reported by The Atlantic — is likely to escalate concerns about the shooting.

Law enforcement officers retreat as people protest ICE on Sept. 20, 2026, in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell / Getty Images

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had said earlier this month that all ICE officers would be equipped with body cams by the end of September.

"We're getting close," Mullin said at a press conference in New York. "By the end of September, I'm pretty sure we will be there."

Representatives for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to inquiries on the ICE officer not wearing a body camera.

Garces Perez's medical condition has also been subject of controversy. Following his hospitalization on Sunday, the Venezuelan man was taken into ICE custody, with DHS alleging that he's in the U.S. illegally with a final deportation order.

Democratic Rep. Joaquin Castro of Texas said Garces Perez was transferred back to a hospital on Monday after complaining about not having feeling on the left side of his body and believing that the bullet was still lodged in his back.

On Tuesday, Castro said Garces Perez had been transferred back to ICE's South Texas Detention Complex in Pearsall, noting he's scheduled to visit the man Wednesday.

"Today, he tells me he is receiving only Tylenol and ibuprofen for pain," Garces Perez's attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, wrote on X on Tuesday. "He remains in isolation, on a flat bed, and without the tablet he previously used to communicate."

Lincoln-Goldfinch filed a habeas petition seeking Garces Perez's release from ICE custody on constitutional grounds. On Monday, U.S. District Court Judge Orlando Garcia ordered Garces Perez to attend an in-person hearing on the habeas claim next Wednesday, Sept. 30, effectively blocking ICE from deporting him until then.
