World.title: This 'fire amoeba' pushes the limit of what's possible for complex life
World.content:
This 'fire amoeba' pushes the limit of what's possible for complex life

toggle caption Felix Mikus

Angela Oliverio, a microbiologist at Syracuse University, studies the edge of what's possible.

"There's a very deep curiosity and desire to understand life at its limits and at its most extreme," she says. "And where that boundary is and what truly are our constraints."

It's not unlike ultra-elite athletes who push themselves "to the absolute max of what we think is humanly possible," she says. "But in this case, we're just expanding it to life more generally" — specifically, microscopic life.

Sponsor Message

Oliverio studies organisms called extremophiles, so named because they thrive in unusually harsh conditions, like high temperatures. The title holders in this regard are simple organisms like bacteria and a group called Archaea, with certain species living at or above 212°F, the boiling point of water.

But Beryl Rappaport, a PhD student in Oliverio's lab, says that until now, that same ability to beat the heat has been less studied in eukaryotes — a group whose members include many different species, from humans to single-celled amoebas. These organisms have more complex cells that contain a nucleus and other structures.

Rappaport says part of the reason may simply be that scientists haven't found the right eukaryotes yet. "So few have been described, especially in detail. We have a lot to learn from them."

Now, she and her colleagues have added a remarkable new organism to the pantheon: a species they call the fire amoeba that nudges a key temperature limit for complex cells upwards by another five or so degrees. The findings were published in the journal Cell.

This may seem like a modest improvement, but Oliverio considers the sub-4-minute mile for runners, which was long thought to be impossible. Once one athlete achieved it, however, it was just weeks before it happened again.

"It wasn't so much the incremental amount that this record was broken by, as much as the proof that it was possible," she says.

A little cell that likes it hot

To make this discovery, the researchers and their colleagues went on something of a fishing expedition in Lassen Volcanic National Park in northern California.

"It's one of the least-visited national parks in the US," says Oliverio.

"It's super beautiful," adds Rappaport. "Very mountainous. All of the pines. A lot of butterflies flitting around. It did experience some pretty rough fires in the past decade, so a lot of new understory growth. And then just these little steaming geothermal pockets."

Sponsor Message

One such pocket is a tributary of a little waterway called Hot Springs Creek, "that you would almost miss because it's surrounded by a lot of tall grasses," says Rappaport.

The research team decided to take some samples there by using extra-long barbecue tongs to grip a series of vials that Rappaport dipped into the steaming water.

toggle caption Kristen Skruber

Later, in the lab, she put the water samples under a microscope, filmed them, and sped up the footage. And that's when she saw something moving. It seemed to protrude, retract, and fluidly change its shape — as if it were performing a single cell's version of hot yoga.

"That's definitely an amoeba," she recalls thinking. "That's characteristic amoeba movement."

This amoeba, however, was able to replicate at temperatures up to 145°F. This is a new record for a complex organism. It can also continue moving around up to 147°F and protect itself in waters as hot as 158°F. When Rappaport and her colleagues studied its genome, they realized they had a new species on their hands.

The team named it Incendiamoeba cascadensis, which translates to "fire amoeba of the Cascade mountain range."

An extremophile with lessons to share

The next question the researchers investigated was how the fire amoeba can thrive at such high temperatures.

When they compared the genome of the new species to those of other amoebas, they observed that the fire amoeba had ways of keeping its proteins and membranes stable at higher temperatures.

It's a finding that could be used to expand the search for life. "Thinking about not only what are the limits of life and what is possible here, but also what might be possible elsewhere," says Oliverio.

In addition, she argues the amoeba's temperature resilience could offer clues to help create heat-resilient crops or drugs that are stable across a wider range of temperatures.

"I can tell you from experience it's really hard to find a really cool exotic organism and actually turn it into something that has a major impact on other species," says Debashish Bhattacharya, an evolutionary biologist at Rutgers University who wasn't involved with the research.

"But there's always the potential of finding something amazing, that's for sure," he adds.

Sponsor Message

Bhattacharya says that in other extremophiles, their genomes have become more compact. "It's called genome streamlining," he says, "so they can then compete with bacteria which have smaller genomes and live in these harsh environments."

This isn't the case with the fire amoeba, which has a larger genome than its relatives. "It's taken a different path," says Bhattacharya, "so I think that's really interesting."

Oliverio finds it similarly interesting. And now that the fire amoeba has been documented, she thinks it's just the start. More scientists, she hopes, will now go looking for other complex organisms with these extreme abilities.

"Perhaps the upper temperature record will be broken again soon," she says.

World.title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over deadly 2019 Easter bombings
World.content:
Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over deadly 2019 Easter bombings

toggle caption Eranga Jayawardane/AP

COLOMBO, Sri Lanka — A Sri Lankan court found 15 men guilty on Tuesday of involvement in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, which killed more than 260 people and wounded about 500.

The April 21 attacks targeted three churches and three hotels across the island nation during Easter services and celebrations. The Islamic State group-inspired bombings, among the deadliest in Sri Lanka's history, killed 42 foreigners and devastated communities across the country.

In 2021, authorities filed 23,270 charges against 24 suspects accused of planning or inspiring the attacks. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and firearms and explosives offenses under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.

Sponsor Message

None of those believed to have directly participated in the attacks are alive.

Sri Lanka has not carried out executions since 1976, meaning death sentences typically result in life imprisonment.

Two Sri Lanka-based Islamic militant groups were accused of carrying out the bombings.

Sri Lanka's Catholic Church has claimed, without providing evidence, that those identified so far as perpetrators are not the masterminds behind the bombings, and that there was a bigger conspiracy behind the attacks.

In July, a former police chief and a former senior defense ministry official were also sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.

World.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue Trump. And, Paramount settles in massive merger lawsuit
World.content:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue Trump. And, Paramount settles in massive merger lawsuit

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

CNN, MS NOW and Politico have filed a lawsuit against President Trump for violating their constitutional rights. His administration cut access to the White House for the networks' journalists, accusing them of covering him unfairly. The lawsuit argues that the news organizations' First Amendment rights protect them from punishment by the federal government for their speech. Major TV networks supported CNN, which was supposed to provide shared pool coverage of Trump's departure from the White House and visit to the United Nations in New York City. CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox were not listed for pool coverage in the White House daily briefing.

toggle caption JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

🎧 Trump has pressured news organizations throughout his second term with lawsuits and regulatory threats. This latest move has sparked a strong, unified response, NPR's Brian Mann tells Up First. Beyond the major networks, organizations including The New York Times, NPR and The Washington Post announced they would suspend use of pool photographs and audio until further notice. A hearing for the lawsuit is set for Wednesday. With just over 40 days before the midterm elections, many of Trump's Republican allies are urging him to focus on voter issues instead of his grievances with journalists.

Sponsor Message

Trump is set to address world leaders today at the United Nations General Assembly. With approval ratings below 40% — partly due to economic concerns stemming from the war in Iran — Trump is seeking to boost his image just ahead of the midterms. The president's high-profile week of diplomacy will also see him hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping in the nation's capital.



🎧 Trump plans to present himself as a peacemaker and highlight various deals he's brokered globally, according to conversations NPR's Franco Ordoñez has had with the White House. Ordoñez says Trump is likely to defend his Iran policy and highlight his new security agreement with Denmark regarding Greenland. The Iranian president will also be at the event and is set to speak tomorrow. Richard Fontaine, who served in the George W. Bush administration, told Ordoñez that meaningful diplomacy will happen in private meetings rather than at the U.N. Security Council or General Assembly. Trump has scheduled one-on-one discussions with Gulf leaders, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez.

Paramount's owners have agreed to concessions with 12 Democratic state attorneys general to resolve an antitrust lawsuit that threatened the biggest merger in Hollywood history. Pending a judge's approval, Paramount will operate Warner Bros. Studios and Paramount Pictures separately for now. Together, they will release at least 30 films per year for the next two years and 32 films per year for the following three years, with financial penalties for noncompliance. They will also invest an extra $300 million each year to produce movies in the U.S. Paramount has also agreed to create a board to establish editorial independence for CBS, which it runs, and CNN, which is currently run by Warner Bros.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Some politicians and many Hollywood writers, actors and workers fear this merger will lead to layoffs and price gouging, NPR's Mandalit del Barco says. These critics doubt Paramount's promises and oppose consolidating power with the Ellisons, who bought Paramount last year. Alvaro Bedoya, an adviser to a group involved in the Block the Merger coalition, tells del Barco he is upset that attorneys general surrendered after Paramount's threats to move its studios out of California. Screenwriter Jacob Tobia, who had two TV shows he sold canceled during media consolidations, tells NPR that he predicts this deal will harm artists. Paramount CEO David Ellison defends the merger as beneficial for workers and consumers.

Picture show

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

Typhoon Halong swept through western Alaska last October, damaging homes, infrastructure and the Nunalleq archaeological site near the coastal village of Quinhagak. This site, roughly the size of two Olympic swimming pools, contains significant artifacts of the Yup'ik, a Native culture that predates Western contact. The storm scattered many of the items that served as important links to Quinhagak's past. The artifacts that remain underground are also at risk because the storm eroded more of the land buffer between the Bering Sea and where they're buried. Archaeologists are now rushing to recover as many objects as possible before the next storm hits. These photos show the extent of the work archaeologists are doing to save these artifacts.

Behind the story

by Rhitu Chatterjee , Health Correspondent

toggle caption Malte Mueller/Getty Images/fStop

Note to reader: This piece includes mentions of suicide.

I've been reporting a lot about how a growing number of Americans are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support and mental health advice. Earlier this year, I told the story of Sophie Rottenberg, a 29-year-old woman who died by suicide in 2025 after using ChatGPT as a therapist.

Years of reporting on suicide have taught me that human connection is key to preventing suicide. So, I was heartened to learn that in May, OpenAI launched a new ChatGPT feature called Trusted Contact. It's optional, and allows users to list the name and contact information of someone they trust for the bot to alert in case of a mental health crisis.

Sponsor Message

A spokesperson from OpenAI told me by email that the feature is available to all adult users. I assumed ChatGPT would proactively invite users to designate a contact — just like doctors' offices ask for an emergency contact.

But when I opened ChatGPT on my phone, it didn't alert me about Trusted Contact. A handful of users I checked with said the same.

So, I decided to see whether ChatGPT informs new users about this feature. One of my NPR colleagues, Megan Lim, volunteered to help. She downloaded ChatGPT on her phone and created an account and began using the voice feature. When it didn't mention Trusted Contact, Megan asked it directly.

"Do you have a Trusted Contact feature?" she said.

"I'm not seeing a general trusted contact feature," ChatGPT replied. "Maybe you're thinking of another app that has a trusted contact option?"

OpenAI spokesperson Gaby Raila told NPR by email that the new feature isn't available on ChatGPT voice, but they are working on it. The company didn't provide NPR with data on how many people are using Trusted Contact, but Raila said that the company has seen "good adoption" on ChatGPT text.

But if people don't know about the feature, how can it help them? You can read or listen to what I learned through my reporting in this story.

If you or someone you know is in crisis or if you're thinking about hurting yourself, you can call or text the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. It's 988.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption Mosa'ab Elshamy/AP

Wildlife officials say they suspect that 10 lions that were found dead in Tanzania's Ngorongoro Conservation Area on Friday were poisoned. Students, it is time to grab your mics. NPR's College Podcast Challenge is back for 2026. Students can submit their podcast by Jan. 17, 2027, for a chance to win a af $5,000 grand prize. Listen to how the contest has transformed the lives of past participants. A new study published in Science Advances suggests that the usage of betel nuts, mind-altering seeds popular in parts of Asia, may date back to hunter-gatherers.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Sask. premier unsurprised that Trump now says U.S. will continue with Canadian potash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said it is "not surprising" that U.S. President Donald Trump has appeared to recommit to using Canadian potash, even as he mused about importing large quantities of the mineral from Belarus.

"It wasn't realistic," said Moe, speaking with CBC's Power & Politics on Tuesday.

"[Belarus is] shipping all of their potash east, not to the western world, and that's been indicated to be the case."

Moe's comments came after Trump announced on social media Monday that the United States was working on a " massive Deal" to purchase potash from Belarus, with pricing substantially lower than what is paid for potash from Canada.

Experts have already highlighted the potential deal's challenges, with Josh Linville of ⁠StoneX saying he doubts Belarusian potash will play a major role in supplies for U.S. farmers ⁠or in lowering prices.

"I'm afraid the impact would be limited. We ⁠have ⁠not struggled to find potash," Lineville told Thomson Reuters. "We ​have more than enough to go around. It is phosphate and nitrogen that we need help with."

WATCH | Trump says U.S. working on deal to buy potash from Belarus: Trump says U.S. working on deal to buy potash from Belarus | Duration closed caption 1:37 U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that Washington is working on a deal to purchase potash from Belarus for less than what the U.S. currently pays to Canada.

On Tuesday at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Trump appeared to pivot away from that announcement.

"We'll continue to go with Canada, but Belarus would like to sell it for a much lower price," Trump said.

Potash is a key component in fertilizers. In 2024, almost a third of the world's potash came from Canada, all of which was mined in Saskatchewan.

According to Natural Resources Canada, since Potash and Agri Development Corporation of Manitoba (PADCOM) started commercial production in June, 11 of the 12 active potash mines in Canada are located in Saskatchewan.

Moe has described Saskatchewan's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters.

He called Belarus' product "blood potash," because its proceeds go to "support Russian aggression" in Ukraine.

WATCH | Fact check: Could Trump replace Canada's potash with Belarus: Fact check: Could Trump replace Canada's potash with Belarus? | Duration 1:56 Canada produces more potash than any other country in the world, all from 10 active mines in Saskatchewan. U.S. President Donald Trump says he's working on a deal to buy potash from Belarus at a cheaper price. But could Belarus replace our supply? Here are the facts.

On Tuesday, Moe repeated that criticism, saying Trump's comments were not realistic or ethical.

"Saskatchewan provides a reliable [potash] supply, has all of the infrastructure set up to provide that supply and is going to have more potash available in the years ahead, so it only makes sense to do business," Moe told Power & Politics host David Cochrane.

Saskatchewan's premier declined to speculate why Trump made his announcement. Moe said he doesn't understand a number of the president's policy positions.

Instead, Moe alluded to potential pressure from Midwestern, agricultural states ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. In his initial post on social media about the potential deal, Trump said it would be "very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."

World.title: Facing criticism, Carney says he has a 'very clear mandate' to push through major economic changes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government received a clear mandate from voters in the last general election — and in subsequent byelections — to "build Canada strong," and he's pressing ahead with changes to federal project approvals and the Labour Code despite criticism from some circles.

The comments come a day after the government tabled Bill C-39, a 246-page omnibus bill that seeks to end what critics maintain is an unwieldy approvals process for major projects and establish a one-year timeline for federal reviews.

The legislation also includes a provision clarifying that the labour minister can step in and end a work stoppage if it's deemed in the "national interest," which has drawn heat from organized labour leaders who say it infringes on the right to strike.

Carney said Canada is facing U.S. economic assaults and threats to its sovereignty and Ottawa's top priority is to turbocharge development to keep the economy going and people working.

"We've been very clear that we would focus on what we can control, and first and foremost is building at home, building Canada strong, building in a way that builds for all," Carney said.

"The government was elected on a very clear mandate."

Carney established the Major Projects Office to help shepherd proposals like port expansions, mines, hydroelectric links and pipelines through the federal approvals process. More than two dozen projects and initiatives have been added to the list since it was established last year.

This latest legislative program is designed to streamline approvals for more projects needing a federal green light.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Carney said projects currently face a maze of bureaucratic red tape with multiple agencies sometimes responsible for different aspects of an approval.

Pointing to the more than decade-long fight to build a new rail bypass after the Lac-Mégantic disaster, Carney said he's taking steps to make the approvals process "much more efficient."

"A decision delayed is a project denied," Carney said. "If you're going to say no — decide it within a year."

WATCH | Carney on the changes proposed in Bill C-39: Carney says he has a mandate to open airports to private investment | Duration closed caption 1:58 Asked about whether his government has a mandate to do things like privatizing airports and making Labour Code changes, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'yes,' based on Parliament passing his government's budget legislation.

Carney said timelines under the last government were so long that businesses effectively "stopped building."

"That's not good for Canadian independence. It's not good for Canadian workers. It means fewer jobs. It means a more expensive life for Canadian families," Carney said.

"This government has elected to turn that around."

Regarding union criticism that C-39's labour provisions gut workers' rights, Carney said the bill "absolutely reinforces the right to strike," but it does include new clauses clarifying when a minister can step in to end job action.

Before this legislation, Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code stated that the minister could direct the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB) to "do such things as the minister deems necessary" to maintain or secure industrial peace in federally regulated workplaces.

With the proposed legislative changes, the wording would be somewhat less vague: a minister can direct an end to strikes within its jurisdiction if that action "adversely affects or may adversely affect the national interest."

WATCH | Major projects bill 'reinforces the right to strike,' Carney says: Major projects bill 'reinforces the right to strike,' Carney says | Duration closed caption 2:04 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, will reinforce the responsibility of employers to 'negotiate in good faith' and create transparency around labour negotiations.

The government insists this provision will be deployed only in extraordinary circumstances, but unions maintain that the language is ripe for abuse and will incentivize employers to hold out on cutting a deal with workers while waiting for the government to step in.

"A right you cannot exercise is not a right," said Bea Bruske, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress.

"Canada's unions fought for the right to strike, and we will fight to defend it.”

NDP Leader Avi Lewis said he's concerned about what could be federal overreach in the collective bargaining process.

"The NDP stands shoulder-to-shoulder with Canada's labour movement," he said in a statement.

WATCH | Canadian Labour Congress on Labour Code changes: Any new restrictions on right to strike are 'unacceptable': Canadian Labour Congress | Duration closed caption 0:46 Speaking to reporters about the new Liberal major projects bill, Canadian Labour Congress president Bea Bruske says while Canada's workers want to help in the U.S. trade war, 'we cannot have our elbow up against Trump with our hands tied behind our backs at bargaining tables.'

Some industry groups, meanwhile, are thrilled with Ottawa's economic proposals.

"The legislation directly targets two longstanding barriers to Canada's prosperity: slow and unpredictable project approvals and labour instability affecting critical supply chains," said Adam Legge, the president of the Business Council of Alberta.

"These actions signal a renewed and much appreciated focus from Ottawa on creating the conditions to grow, invest, hire and compete."

The federal Conservatives have not said how their caucus will vote on this new legislation — and it did not feature prominently in their question period attacks on Tuesday — but leader Pierre Poilievre has criticized what's been proposed.

He said a "real bill" designed to turbocharge the economy would "scrap all anti-development laws."

World.title: Trump flexes 'American power' on UN's biggest stage
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump is telling the world that he will keep using military power to advance his country's interests, including stopping what he calls "hostile foreign adversaries" from gaining influence in the Western Hemisphere.

During his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump threatened Iran with annihilation, laid claim to Venezuela's oil as the spoils of victory, and justified U.S. strikes on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean.

He also warned countries that more such interventions could follow.

"We have acted with decisiveness and speed to reshape the world stage and solve problems that have plagued us for far too long," said Trump.

"We're reasserting American power, including American military power, where necessary in our region and around the world, to create a safer future for all of us."

Trump's 37-minute speech to the annual gathering of world leaders only briefly touched on Russia's long-running war against Ukraine. He pleaded for an end to the conflict but offered no new initiatives toward peace.

WATCH | Trump says his 'big decision' on Iran is either a deal or annihilation: Trump raises possibility of Iran deal — or that he could 'drive them into hell' | Duration closed caption 4:48 U.S. President Donald Trump, who spoke the United Nations on everything from artificial intelligence to Cuba's 'failed state,’ says he has a 'big decision' ahead on Iran. Trump said he believes 'we'll make a deal' but also raised the possibility he could 'annihilate the Islamic Republic' and never give them a chance to harm other nations again.

He devoted a notable portion of his speech to the Western Hemisphere. That echoes his new national security strategy, published last December before Trump ordered the mission to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and joined Israel in launching the war against Iran.

The official strategy document, which drew praise from the Kremlin, argues for reviving the Monroe Doctrine, the 19th-century declaration of U.S. supremacy over the Western Hemisphere.

'Vicious gangs, bloodthirsty cartels'

Previous U.S. administrations have allowed much of the region to be "dominated by vicious gangs and bloodthirsty drug cartels, destabilized by uncontrolled migration and infiltrated by hostile foreign adversaries — foreign, sick, demented adversaries," said Trump.

"But not anymore," he continued.

"Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere, and if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States."

He boasted about the deal that gives the U.S. control over much of Venezuela's oil productions. "To the victor belong the spoils," he declared.

Trump's speech to the General Assembly lasted 37 minutes, and it included scathing criticisms of the UN. (Heather Khalifa/The Associated Press)

The speech made clear not only the importance of the Western Hemisphere to Trump's worldview, but also his perception of the region as a potential threat, says Shannon O'Neil, a senior vice-president at the Council on Foreign Relations, a think-tank based in Washington, D.C.

The message sets the U.S. up "to assert control, if not dominance, in this hemisphere," O'Neil told reporters in an online panel discussion Tuesday.

She sees the Trump administration's approach to the governments of Latin America as "really trying to put their finger on the scale to encourage and support those that were ideologically aligned."

Canada gets a pass

The speech did not mention Canada, evidence that the U.S. president has bigger preoccupations than the trade war with his country's northern neighbour.

Trump did, however, take on its southern neighbour, calling Mexico the epicenter of drug cartel violence.

"It's unacceptable for the United States to share a 2,000-mile border with a territory controlled by enemy cartels. So Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity," he said.

Trump also said his administration is seeking "fundamental change" in Cuba.

WATCH | Here's what Cuba's UN delegation did during Trump's speech: Cuban delegation walks out of UN after Trump calls country 'failed state' | Duration closed caption 0:34 Members of Cuba's delegation walked out after U.S. President Donald Trump called their country an 'absolutely failed state' during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

"The communist regime is under great pressure," he said. "We'll not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep."

Members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall as Trump spoke.

'Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic?'

Trump also said he faces a "big decision" on Iran.

He said one option is making a deal that allows Iran to become a "far greater country" than ever before.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"

That was Trump's way of laying out both a path for a negotiated solution and the consequences of not following that path, says Mara Rudman, a former U.S. deputy special envoy for the Middle East.

"Fairly clumsy is maybe the kindest word I can use," Rudman told CBC News Network shortly after the speech.

Trump and some of his top officials met Tuesday with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

Trump was due to meet the leaders of Gulf countries on the sidelines of the General Assembly on Tuesday.

"My anticipation is that they are urging him, however quietly, to go down the path of negotiation," said Rudman, who served as a national security advisor in both the Clinton and Obama administrations.

Trump predicted that a deal with Iran will happen immediately after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Rudman sees that as evidence that the midterms — which polling suggests put the Republican Party at risk of losing both the U.S. House and Senate — are weighing on the president.

"I think his audience was the American people and not the Iranians or anyone else in the world, despite the fact that he was speaking at the UN," she said.

Trump also used the General Assembly podium to call fears over the risks posed by artificial intelligence a hoax and to repeat some of his long-running sharp criticisms of the United Nations, the main theme of his speech last year.

He also called the International Criminal Court a rogue organization. The court was created jointly by 125 countries in the early 2000s to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity. The U.S. has never ratified the court's treaty.

World.title: Hamilton-born NHL prospect collapsed after coaches didn't submit workout for review: university
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hockey coaches at Arizona State University (ASU) didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before an outdoor workout last month that saw NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapse, leaving him in hospital in critical condition.

James Rund, the university official leading the review, wrote that the Hamilton-born 21-year-old collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during the Aug. 20 training session at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus.

The report, which calls for a " a blue-ribbon advisory panel," said the temperature was about 30 C, and the student athletes were involved in "calisthenics, bodyweight exercises such as pushups and planks, and running."

The hockey coaches asked permission for Timothy Zeisel, who was there for the workout and had " spoken with the ASU Hockey team in the 2025-26 season about topics of leadership and teamwork," to speak to the team. However, the coaches didn't " submit a plan of training activities for review by ASU’s strength and conditioning coaches" before training began.

Near the end of the workout, "Matthew appeared to struggle, and then in rapid succession stumbled, dropped the medicine ball and fell to the ground. He attempted to get up and resume running but fell to his knees," wrote Rund, ASU's senior vice-president of educational outreach and student services.

Mayich in stable, critical condition, lawyer says

The Mayich family's lawyer, Rob Carey, said on Tuesday that "Matthew is in stable but critical condition still. The family is still praying for a miracle, but nothing has significantly changed. But even if that happens, we will never have the young man who came to Arizona last month, a hockey star and (by all accounts) a wonderful person."

In an interview last week from Phoenix, Ariz., with CBC News, Mayich's father, John Mayich, said "we know Matthew's a fighter and we're hoping he pulls through this."

Before the workout, Matthew was "perfectly healthy," said his mother, Christina.

Carey said that " when Matthew went down, there was no plan and no preparation, so he was treated in a way that hurt his chances rather than helped them."

"A month later, nobody's been named, nobody's been suspended, nobody's been fired for violating the very policies ASU published today, and the university wants to appoint a committee."

He added that "a committee isn't going to tell us why grown men with a rulebook in their hands let this happen to a young man at his first real workout in the desert. That's what an investigation is for, and it's why we're going to ask the county attorney to do one."

Carey said in early September that based on his own investigation, he believes Mayich endured a "military-style, brutal, gruelling workout" with no breaks and no water for over an hour.

"You have an elite NHL-drafted athlete showing up on the first coach-led workout, the very first day the team could organize formally, and he left the field with no chance of recovery," Carey said. "Obviously there's something wrong."

Rund said ASU would "be undertaking a comprehensive review of its practices to identify and implement best practices regarding the planning, conduct and monitoring of athletic activities. and the response to emergencies that arise during athletic activities."

A drone shot of Arizona State University campus in Tempe on Sept. 17. Mayich participated in the training session Aug. 20 at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus. (Andrew Hernandez/CBC)

In early September, a spokesperson for the ASU Police Department said they were investigating what happened to Mayich, which is a "standard procedure" for an incident of this severity.

The report said ASU would have a panel of experts provide best practice recommendations for:

Planning and approval of outdoor athletic activities, including strength and conditioning activities, practices and competitions.

Staffing, monitoring and conduct of outdoor athletic activities, including adjustments to address changed conditions or adverse reactions.

Preparation for and response to adverse events or reactions occurring during outdoor athletic activities.

Use of outside consultants in the planning and delivery of strength and conditioning, and practice activities.

Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020. He was selected in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft by the St. Louis Blues.

Doug Armstrong, the Blues' president of hockey operations, said in a news release in late August, "The entire Blues organization is keeping Matthew Mayich close to our hearts as we pray for his comfort and recovery while he continues to undergo medical treatment in Arizona."

The organization also extends its "deepest support" to his family, friends and teammates during this difficult time, Armstrong said.

'A tremendous hockey player'

During his six seasons with the Huskies and one as a member of the Hamilton Jr. Bulldogs, Mayich established "himself as a tremendous hockey player and, more importantly, an outstanding person both on and off the ice," the Hamilton Steel Hockey Club, formerly the Huskies, said.

The statement was sent to CBC Hamilton on behalf of the organization, former Huskies president Mike Spadafora and former Huskies head coach Chris Travale. Spadafora is currently the councillor for Hamilton's Ward 14 and running for re-election in the Oct. 26 municipal vote.

"Without fail, whenever [Mayich] is asked, he comes back every year to speak and skate with a new crop of young kids," Travale said. "His message is always about so much more than hockey — it’s about relationships, friendships, and the experiences you have along the hockey journey."

Mayich's father said Matthew "didn't care if he was at a small rink in Hamilton or a big rink in St. Louis with a lot of people — he just loves the game."

The incident has made waves in the sports world, prompting the Professional Hockey Players’ Association to speak up about the lack of protections for young athletes.

"When athletes feel pressure to remain silent about an injury, illness, exhaustion or concern because they fear the consequences of speaking up, the system has failed them," said PHPA executive director Brian Ramsay in a statement on Sept. 10 that doesn't directly name Mayich.

"Athletes should never have to choose between their health and their careers. Period."

World.title: Indigenous leaders call for change in Sask. health care after woman's death during childbirth
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains details about death in childbirth.

First Nations leaders say a declining health-care system and systemic racism within that system both contributed to a mother's death from complications during the birth of her twins.

"No matter where you are in life, you should have fair and equitable treatment. Everybody should be treated the same," Meadow Lake Tribal Council vice-chief Richard Derocher said on Tuesday, speaking alongside the family of Chelsea Bear at a news conference in Saskatoon.

Bear, a member of Flying Dust First Nation, went to hospital on Aug. 10 in Meadow Lake, in pain and bleeding, but was sent home without receiving proper care, her family said. She was 36 weeks pregnant and her pregnancy was considered high-risk.

The next day, the pain and bleeding increased severely, and Bear returned to the hospital. She was ultimately taken to Saskatoon, where the first twin was delivered stillborn and the second baby was born very weak, her family said.

Bear died after their deliveries, in the early hours of Aug. 12. She was 36 years old and left behind four other children, in addition to the surviving twin, Gracie, who is still in the neonatal intensive care unit in Saskatoon.

Her family said she died from hemorrhaging blood due to placental abruption — which is when the placenta separates too early from the uterus.

They said that if Bear would have received proper care when she first went to hospital, she and both her babies would still be alive.

Chelsea Bear died on Aug. 12 while delivering her twin babies. One of her babies died and the second remains in the neonatal intensive care unit in Saskatoon. (CBC News)

"She must have been so scared, I was thinking, just losing all the blood.… It must have hurt her," Chelsea's mother Deb Bear said at a news conference Tuesday in Saskatoon.

"I just don't want this ever to happen to anybody else."

Bear's family is the second Indigenous family to speak out and call for change after the death of a mother during childbirth in Saskatchewan this year.

Jaali Sutherland-Weenie, from Beardy's & Okemasis Cree Nation, died on April 26 after first going to the hospital in Rosthern with severe back pain and vomiting, then being sent to Saskatoon. Her family said she was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, a blood pressure condition. Her baby girl survived.

Sutherland-Weenie's family said they believed she would have been treated differently if she were not Indigenous.

Systemic racism alleged

On Tuesday, near the end of a lengthy news conference, Derocher said that speaking about Bear's death is complicated "because of all the things that are not being said" when people are "trying to be as nice as possible."

He and Meadow Lake Tribal Council Tribal Chief Jeremy Norman both said they were on a conference call with representatives of the Saskatchewan Health Authority that took place after MLTC reached out to them about Bear's death.

They said they expressed frustration that they weren't getting answers and told the SHA they were considering holding a news conference.

Norman said an SHA representative "basically told us, keep quiet, because it's so hard to get doctors in our region, it's so hard to get people to come and work in the north."

Meadow Lake Tribal Council Vice-Chief Richard Derocher says issues like systemic racism in health care need to be discussed. (CBC News)

Derocher said those words "burnt me hard," and are another example of the systemic racism that happens every day, when First Nations people are asked "to keep silent, do not speak of this issue, do not bring it forth."

He and the other chiefs also spoke about how they have seen the quality of health care declining for everyone in Saskatchewan over the past two decades — in everything from hospital care to long-term care — and how they want to work with the province to make positive changes.

SHA to conduct patient safety review

The SHA declined an interview request, but issued a statement extending their condolences to the family and community for the "profound and tragic loss."

The statement didn't directly answer a question about Norman and Derocher's account of the conference call where they said they were asked to keep quiet. The statement said the SHA met with the MLTC to hear their concerns, but at the time of the meeting, "the SHA had not received consent from the family to discuss the specifics of their case with MLTC."

"We have since received the family's consent and will continue our discussions with MLTC in the coming days," the SHA's statement said.

The health authority said it would be conducting a thorough patient safety review.

"The SHA acknowledges the complex and dynamic conditions that our maternal health and obstetrical clinical teams operate within, and appreciate their commitment, clinical expertise and professionalism."

Independent investigation called for

The MLTC chiefs and Flying Dust First Nation Chief Tyson Bear are calling for more than a patient safety review.

"We are calling for a thorough, independent, transparent investigation, so Chelsea's family can get the answers they deserve," Chief Bear said.

Chelsea Bear's death was not an isolated incident in the health-care system, the chiefs said.

In a news release, they highlighted that it is the sixth quality-of-care incident that the Meadow Lake Tribal Council has tried to raise with the SHA this year.

"We're here for a better health system. We're here to make change," Tribal Chief Norman said.

"It's unfortunate things like this have to happen before we look at making change, before we really dig in to say, 'What's the problem?'"

World.title: Texas camp where 27 girls died in 2025 flood investigated for manslaughter, negligent homicide
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Camp Mystic faces a criminal investigation that could include manslaughter or negligent homicide charges in the deaths of 27 girls amid devastating flooding in Texas last year, court documents show.

In applications for search warrants executed last week, investigators sought to obtain the electronic communications of the camp's owners, saying they could provide evidence of manslaughter, negligent homicide, child abandonment or other crimes. No charges have been brought, and a representative of the camp did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Brant Johnston with the Texas Rangers wrote in an affidavit that Camp Mystic had inadequate emergency plans, failed to conduct emergency drills or training, and in some cabins did not have enough adult counsellors. Its owners neglected to take precautions by relocating children from low-lying cabins despite having monitored late-night flood warnings, Johnston wrote.

"Young campers cannot reasonably be expected to independently recognize a rapidly developing, life-threatening hazard or to organize and execute an evacuation absent direction from an adequate number of adult supervisors," Johnston wrote.

He concluded: "Camp Mystic, LLC was aware of and consciously disregarded a substantial and unjustifiable risk of death to the campers in their care."

WATCH | Why the Texas camp was so vulnerable: Texas flash flood: Why Camp Mystic was so vulnerable | Duration closed caption 2:29 Several campers and staff were killed when a flash flood slammed into a summer camp for girls along the Guadalupe River in central Texas. CBC’s Eli Glaser examines how Camp Mystic’s location and layout may have contributed to the devastation.

Twenty-five campers and two teenage counsellors at the Christian all-girls camp were killed as the raging Guadalupe River surged beyond its banks before dawn on July 4, 2025. Camp Mystic owner Richard Eastland also died in the flood.

For decades, Camp Mystic was a summer staple and an institution for generations of families, who dropped off their girls at the sleepaway camp to ride horses, canoe, fish and attend Bible studies. The camp did not reopen this year, and it has filed for bankruptcy reorganization.

All told, the destructive flooding killed at least 136 people along a several-kilometre stretch of the river, raising questions about how things went so terribly wrong.

A sheriff's deputy pauses while combing through the banks of the Guadalupe River near Camp Mystic, Saturday, July 5, 2025. (Julio Cortez/The Associated Press)

Attorneys for some of the victims' families welcomed the search warrants but said they should not have been necessary.

"For more than a year, families of the 27 angels killed at Camp Mystic have fought, begged, and pleaded with the Eastland family for accountability and answers," Christina Yarnell and Brad Beckworth, attorneys for the family of victim Cile Steward, said in a written statement.

"Instead, the Eastlands have held hostage the information and answers owed to parents who deserve, more than anyone, to know the details surrounding their daughters' final moments."

Steward's body still has not been found.

Johnston wrote in the warrant that he made several visits to Camp Mystic and that he and other investigators have conducted interviews with witnesses, flood victims and people associated with the camp. But several people, including members of the Eastland family and other top camp officials, refused interviews, Johnston wrote.

The Eastland family and other camp leaders have testified in courtrooms and in front of the state legislature in the months since the flood, however, with camp director Edward Eastland offering a tearful apology.

World.title: P.E.I. orchard owner 'fed up' after children damage apples during U-pick visit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The owner of a P.E.I. apple orchard made a post on social media to remind guests to be respectful at the U-pick. This comes after kids ruined over 100 apples at Wintermoor Orchard last week. CBC’s Camryn Farquharson has that story.

After a group ruined more than 100 apples, this P.E.I. orchard owner took to social media

A Prince Edward Island orchard owner’s social media post about children damaging apples has blown up online, sparking a conversation about how visitors treat U-pick farms.

Mark Ashley, co-owner of Wintermoor Orchard in York, said he wrote the post after coming home to find rows that staff had just cleaned now littered with apples.

"There was an incident in the orchard with several mothers and a decent amount of kids, and I wasn't here for it," Ashley said.

"But when I get back and I looked out at the damage that had occurred and the waste of food … I was just kind of fed up at the time, and after a long day of work too. And I said I'm going to post something about this."

Ashley said his partner was alerted to children climbing trees, smashing apples and seemingly playing with a wooden sword in the orchard.

He said his partner went down to ask them to stop. Minutes later, he said, other visitors reported that the children were back at it while their parents remained "oblivious."

So his partner went down to talk to them again.

"The children basically were made to apologize. The parents actually should have apologized," he said. "Had I been there, I would have used it as a teaching moment."

Ashley estimates about 100 to 120 apples were on the ground afterward.

While he said it’s not a huge financial loss, the damage means staff have to clean the same rows twice. He said it also shows a lack of basic respect.

"Just because there’s no sign doesn’t mean it’s an opportunity to let your kids just do what they want," Ashley said.

Ashley says he now plans to add small signs around his orchard reminding parents to supervise their children. (Camryn Farquharson/CBC)

Ashley said he posted on Facebook to raise awareness among parents and to talk about a broader problem he hears about from other orchards, corn mazes and even a lavender farm that closed after children mistreated a blind goat.

The post has drawn hundreds of thousands of views, thousands of reactions and about 1,000 comments, he said.

Ashley eventually had to turn off comments and spent the evening deleting racist and vitriolic replies. Some commenters assumed the family involved were immigrants. Ashley said they did not appear to be.

Now, Ashley plans to put up small signs around the orchard reminding visitors of some basic rules, including that parents must supervise their children, and that climbing trees, shaking branches and stomping apples are not allowed.

"I don't want to hire more people. I don't think that's the solution," he said. "That just means that I'm hiring somebody to supervise someone else's children."

'These things can happen'

The incident struck a chord with Matt Boyle, who runs The Grove Orchard & U-Pick in Warren Grove.

"We know how much effort and work goes into growing these crops … but [I'm] not shocked because these things can happen," Boyle said.

He said his orchard faced more frequent damage in its earlier years, sometimes daily, until they changed how they operate.

Now, with around 20,000 visitors a season, he said incidents are down to fewer than a handful.

Matt Boyle with The Grove Orchard & U-Pick says his farm used to see much more damage in the past but has reduced incidents by explaining rules to visitors, adding signage and hiring more staff. (Camryn Farquharson/CBC)

Boyle said the difference comes down to communication at the beginning of each visit, as well as staffing.

Every visitor gets a spoken introduction that covers the orchard’s history and rules. There are also signs in the rows.

On busy days, about 10 staff are on duty, with four workers constantly cleaning rows and picking up dropped fruit and cores.

"Whenever people see the amount of respect that it’s treated with, I feel that most people have the obligation and feel the obligation to also do so," Boyle said.

He said his team is adding more signage, including instructions on how to pick an apple without damaging the tree.
