A dialogue that froze once already

President Ghazouani called for a national political dialogue on 27 November 2024. It is the sixth such exercise since 2004, the Institute for Security Studies, a South African research body, notes.

Preparations broke down early this year. Moussa Fall, the coordinator appointed to run the process, suspended the preparatory sessions in March 2026 over the presidential-term question.

The deadlock broke in July 2026, when negotiators struck the words on durations and mandates from the dialogue’s reference document. Alwiam, a Mauritanian news site, reported the compromise on 14 July 2026.

That history is why the new calls landed badly. Talks had been suspended until both sides accepted that no theme would be tied to a third term, Gourmo Lo told RFI.

One party walks out, another was already out

The Rally of Progressive Democrats, an opposition party, suspended its part in the process on 16 September 2026. Its statement called the campaign a public call to violate the constitution, the weekly Le Calame reported.

A second party, Mauritania Forward, had already stepped back on 27 August 2026. Its reason was different: the detention of Lebat Ould Mayouf, a retired general on its executive bureau.

His party says it has been given no explanation for the detention, and no court ruling in the case has been reported. The coalition raised it again in writing on Thursday, 17 September 2026.

It said third-term calls and curbs on freedoms could threaten the dialogue, and demanded the release of those it calls political prisoners. Mauritania’s national news agency, AMI, carried the text in full.

What Ghazouani has actually said

The president addressed the question himself at a press conference with national media on Friday, 24 July 2026. More than three years of his term remain, he said at the presidential palace in Nouakchott.

“I will not support anything contrary to the constitution or that does not have the will of the people,” Ghazouani said. Trust Magazine, a Mauritanian outlet, published the remarks the next day.

His government has been less categorical. The government spokesman, Culture Minister Al-Hussein Ould Meddou, addressed the same question in June 2026.

The president would not close the door if the national dialogue approved a third term, Ould Meddou said. The Mauritanian site Zoom reported the remarks on 11 June 2026.

Other voices have joined the argument. Mohamed Jemil Ould Mansour leads the Front for Citizenship and Justice, known as Jemaa, and is not part of the opposition coalition.

He called the third-term initiatives noise and provocation in a Facebook post on 20 August 2026. Their promoters had no justification, he wrote.

Biram Dah Abeid, an anti-slavery campaigner and member of parliament, came second to Ghazouani in 2019 and again in 2024. He said he leaves the president facing the constitution, his oath and his conscience, Le360 Afrique reported.

What it means for outsiders

Nothing on the ground changes for the small foreign community in Nouakchott this month. Mining and gas staff, aid agencies and European Union missions carry on as before.

The offshore blocks off Mauritania and Senegal, with the Tortue field straddling the maritime boundary. File map. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

The signal to watch is institutional. Mauritania’s reputation for orderly politics sits behind projects such as the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas field, shared with Senegal.

The cost of living is the other pressure in the room. Annual inflation reached 8.9 percent in August 2026, with consumer prices up 1.2 percent on July, the national statistics agency ANSADE reported.

What to watch

President Ghazouani asked the parties in July 2026 to launch the dialogue and finish it before the end of the year. Sahara Media reported that he proposed a start in October or November 2026.

Two markers will show which way this goes. One is what the ruling party’s standing commission recommends on a constitutional change.

The other is whether the suspended parties return to the table. The opposition says it is waiting to hear the president answer the calls directly.

World.title: Namibia Social Security Commission Benefits Rise From 1 October 2026
World.content:
Namibia · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened The Social Security Commission, Namibia’s state worker fund, raises maternity, sick leave, death, retirement and disability benefits from 1 October 2026.

— How big Maternity pay rises to N$20,000 (about US$1,230); death, retirement, disability and first-year sick leave to N$15,000 (about US$925).

— Who announced it Justice and Labour Relations Minister Fillemon Wise Immanuel, at a media briefing in Windhoek on Tuesday 22 September 2026.

— The catch Second-year sick leave rises only to N$13,000 (about US$800), below the N$15,000 (about US$925) cap for the first year.

— Who pays Employers and employees each pay 0.9% of basic salary, capped since 1 September 2026 at N$112.50 (about US$7) a side.

— What comes next The contribution ceiling reaches N$16,000 (about US$985) on 1 March 2029, after steps in 2027 and 2028.

Namibia’s Social Security Commission benefits rise on 1 October 2026. Maternity pay goes to N$20,000 (about US$1,230) and most other payouts to N$15,000 (about US$925).

Namibia’s Social Security Commission (SSC) will raise five worker benefits from 1 October 2026. The maternity payout climbs from N$15,000 (about US$925) to N$20,000 (about US$1,230).

Fillemon Wise Immanuel, Namibia’s justice and labour relations minister, announced the rises on Tuesday 22 September 2026. He spoke at a media briefing in Windhoek, the capital.

The SSC is the state body that collects payroll contributions from registered employers and employees. It pays them back as benefits when a worker gives birth, falls ill, retires or dies.

What the benefit increase covers

The maternity benefit rises by N$5,000 (about US$310). Sick leave pay increases from N$11,250 (about US$695) to N$15,000 (about US$925) for the first 12 months.

For the final 12 months of sick leave, the benefit rises from N$9,750 (about US$600) to N$13,000 (about US$800). Death, retirement and disability benefits each increase from N$12,000 (about US$740) to N$15,000 (about US$925).

The Namibian and the Windhoek Observer, two Namibian newspapers, reported the same figures on Tuesday. The new levels apply to workers registered with the commission.

The Namibian dollar is pegged one for one to the South African rand. Conversions here use a rate of 16.24 to the US dollar on 22 September 2026, from European Central Bank reference rates.

The contribution ceiling is already moving higher

The maximum basic salary used for contributions rose from N$11,000 (about US$675) to N$12,500 (about US$770) on 1 September 2026. The commission had deferred that step from 1 March 2026.

The increase was gazetted in July 2026, after the date written into the notice had already passed. The commission said the new contributions would not be applied retrospectively.

The ceiling then climbs to N$14,000 (about US$860) on 1 March 2027 and N$15,000 (about US$925) on 1 March 2028. It reaches N$16,000 (about US$985) on 1 March 2029.

Employers and employees each pay 0.9% of basic salary, so the combined rate is 1.8%. At the current ceiling that caps each side at N$112.50 (about US$7) a month.

Namibia’s maternity benefit rises to N$20,000 (about US$1,230) on 1 October 2026 (file photograph.)

Why the government says it is moving now

Immanuel said the increases are meant to protect the dignity of workers and give them greater income security. He named illness, childbirth, disability and death as the moments the fund exists for.

“An expecting mother is not worried about how to meet her household needs,” the minister said. He described contributions as an investment in workers and their families rather than a deduction from pay.

“It is a promise that when predictable risks strike, there is social protection,” Immanuel said. He added that the scheme also helps families who lose a breadwinner with funeral costs.

Simson Shilongo, the commission’s deputy chairperson, told the briefing the new levels deliver meaningful social protection. Ben Nangombe, its acting chief executive, set out how contributions are calculated.

Who gains and who pays

Workers gain directly through higher maternity, sick leave, death, retirement and disability payouts. New mothers receive N$5,000 (about US$310) more than under the old cap.

Employers pay more as the salary ceiling rises, because each side’s contribution tracks basic pay. The maximum monthly contribution per side rose from N$99 (about US$6) to N$112.50 (about US$7).

The fund is financed by those payroll contributions from employers and employees. It paid out N$367.3 million (about US$22.6 million) in benefits over the past year, according to The Brief, a Namibian business outlet.

The maternity, sick leave and death fund accounted for N$302.3 million (about US$18.6 million) of that total. Maternity claims alone came to N$213.1 million (about US$13.1 million).

What it means beyond Namibia

Namibia’s scheme is built on payroll contributions, so benefits follow registration with the commission. Employees must be registered, and self-employed people may join voluntarily.

South Africa, by contrast, pays its main social grants from the national budget. That money flows through the South African Social Security Agency rather than a payroll fund.

The Namibian model ties what a worker receives to what has been paid in on their behalf. It also means employers carry part of the cost of every increase.

For more on how African governments are navigating social and economic pressures, see Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The next ceiling increase takes effect on 1 March 2027, when the maximum basic salary rises to N$14,000 (about US$860). Payroll systems have to be updated at each step.

Further increases follow on 1 March 2028 and 1 March 2029. The published schedule gives employers time to plan and locks in a steady rise in contributions.

The 2022 revision, the one these levels replace, lifted maternity pay to N$15,000 (about US$925) from N$13,000 (about US$800). The new maternity cap is a third higher than that.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do Namibia’s Social Security Commission benefits increase? The new levels apply from 1 October 2026. Justice and Labour Relations Minister Fillemon Wise Immanuel announced them in Windhoek on Tuesday 22 September 2026. How much will the maternity benefit rise to in Namibia? It rises from N$15,000 (about US$925) to N$20,000 (about US$1,230) from 1 October 2026. What is the new contribution ceiling for Namibia’s social security scheme? The maximum basic salary used for contributions rose to N$12,500 (about US$770) on 1 September 2026. It reaches N$16,000 (about US$985) on 1 March 2029. Who pays into Namibia’s social security scheme? Employers and employees each pay 0.9% of basic salary. Since 1 September 2026 each side’s monthly contribution is capped at N$112.50 (about US$7).

World.title: Angola Single-Use Plastics Ban Takes Effect After One-Year Grace Period
World.content:
Angola · POLICY

Key Facts — What happened Plastic bags thinner than 50 microns, plastic straws, drink stirrers and cotton buds were banned from 22 September 2026.

— The law Presidential Decree 170/25 was signed on 22 September 2025 and gave producers and traders exactly 12 months to adapt.

— What it costs Company fines run from 1 million kwanzas (about US$1,100) to 30 million kwanzas (about US$33,000), doubled for repeat offences.

— Who enforces ANIESA, the economic inspection authority, polices medium and large firms; municipal administrations check small shops and stalls.

— The catch Health, oil and gas, fishing, cosmetics, farming, construction and personal hygiene sit outside the decree entirely, awaiting their own rules.

— What comes next A second phase on 22 September 2028 targets polystyrene cups, non-recyclable plates, cutlery and PET bottles under 500 millilitres.

Angola’s single-use plastics ban took effect on Tuesday 22 September 2026, one year to the day after the decree that created it. Companies caught breaking the rules face fines of up to about US$33,000.

The waterfront in Luanda, Angola’s capital and largest city. File photograph (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Angola banned the production, import, sale and use of several everyday plastic items on Tuesday 22 September 2026. The Angola single-use plastics ban makes the southern African country the latest on the continent to put a date on disposable plastic.

What the Angola single-use plastics ban covers

The first phase outlaws plastic bags thinner than 50 microns, plastic straws, drink stirrers and cotton buds with plastic stems. They can no longer be made, imported, sold or used anywhere in the country.

A separate clause goes further in sensitive places. All single-use plastic is barred from beaches, conservation areas, museums and sites listed as world cultural or natural heritage.

Iury Sousa Santos, Angola’s Secretary of State for the Environment, set out the rules at a press conference in Luanda. “The bags we commonly have on the market are not recyclable,” he told reporters.

“They are often dumped in the open, and our recycling capacity at national level is still very limited,” he added. The Portuguese news agency Lusa reported the remarks.

Why the ban starts on this date

The rules come from Presidential Decree 170/25, signed on 22 September 2025 by President João Lourenço. The decree gave producers and traders exactly 12 months to adapt.

That grace period is why the ban bites now rather than a year ago. A second set of bans follows 36 months after the decree, on 22 September 2028.

The decree implements a national plan approved on 29 May 2025 by Presidential Decree 122/25. The plan is known in Portuguese as PLANEPP and runs from 2025 to 2027.

Who actually enforces the rules

Two different bodies police the ban. Medium and large companies answer to ANIESA, the National Authority for Economic Inspection and Food Safety.

ANIESA sits under the Ministry of Industry and Commerce. Small shops and market stalls are checked instead by municipal administrations, Angola’s local government bodies.

The decree lets the police assist inspectors on the ground. The ministry or the municipality then rules on each case, after the trader has been heard.

Shredded plastic at a processing plant. File photograph (Photo: Rio Times media library)

What the fines actually are

Penalties are written in national minimum salaries rather than fixed sums. Angola’s minimum wage has been 100,000 kwanzas (about US$110) a month since 16 September 2025.

Individuals face a quarter of one minimum salary up to 50 salaries. That works out at 25,000 kwanzas (about US$27) to 5 million kwanzas (about US$5,500).

Companies face 10 to 300 minimum salaries, or 1 million kwanzas (about US$1,100) to 30 million kwanzas (about US$33,000). A repeat offence doubles both ceilings.

Conversions here use a rate of about 916 to the US dollar, the XE mid-market rate on 22 September 2026. Non-compliant imports are forfeited to the state, and licences can be suspended for up to two years.

The scale of Angola’s plastic problem

Angola generates about 19,000 tonnes of solid waste a day, Iury Sousa Santos told the Luanda press conference. Almost 24 percent of that is plastic, or roughly 4,560 tonnes.

Less than a tenth of all waste is recycled. Most of the rest goes to landfill or ends up in ditches, rivers and the sea.

What the rules mean for business

Carlos Manuel Rodrigues, Angola’s Secretary of State for Industry, said the country has 33 plastic bag factories. He told reporters they had adjusted without heavy investment.

He added that the government will issue no import licences for the banned items. That makes the border, rather than the shop shelf, the first line of control.

Importers and packaging firms now have to check their product lines against the banned list. Several sectors are outside the decree altogether and will get their own rules later.

Those carve-outs cover health, oil and gas, fishing, cosmetics, agriculture, civil construction and personal hygiene. Biodegradable and compostable packaging is also excluded, if it is certified.

A continental pattern

Angola is not acting alone. Guinea, in West Africa, began enforcing its own ban on Monday 21 September 2026, one day earlier.

Ethiopia outlawed single-use plastic bags on 31 January 2026 under its solid waste law. Enforcement there falls to the country’s Environmental Protection Authority.

The wave fits a wider pattern traced in Africa: The New Scramble. Environmental rules, resources and market access increasingly overlap.

What to watch next

The next fixed date is 22 September 2028, when polystyrene cups, non-recyclable plates, cutlery and small PET bottles go. Until then, the question is whether inspections happen at all.

An opinion column in Forbes África Lusófona on 2 September 2026 asked whether the responsible bodies are ready. Its author argued that measurement and selective collection remain the weak link.

The minimum wage is also the dial on every penalty. Each rise in Angola’s wage floor lifts the whole scale of fines with it.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did Angola’s single-use plastics ban take effect? It took effect on 22 September 2026, twelve months after Presidential Decree 170/25 was signed on 22 September 2025. What products are banned in the first phase? Plastic bags thinner than 50 microns, plastic straws, drink stirrers and cotton buds with plastic stems. What fines can companies face for breaking the rules? From 10 to 300 national minimum salaries, which is 1 million kwanzas (about US$1,100) to 30 million kwanzas (about US$33,000). Who enforces the ban in Angola? ANIESA, the National Authority for Economic Inspection and Food Safety, covers medium and large firms. Municipal administrations cover small businesses.

World.title: UK Court Hears First Rwanda Genocide Charges Against London Doctor
World.content:
United Kingdom · COURTS

Key Facts — What happened Dr Vincent Brown, 65, appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court in London on 22 September 2026 on seven genocide-related charges.

— The allegations Prosecutors say he directed and incited killings in Kigali during the first week of the genocide in April 1994.

— His answer Brown entered no plea, spoke only to confirm his details, and denies any involvement, his lawyer told the court.

— The catch The charges are allegations only. Nothing has been proved, and Brown keeps the presumption of innocence.

— What comes next Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring granted bail with a security and sent the case to the Old Bailey for 9 October 2026.

— The first The Crown Prosecution Service says these are the first Rwanda genocide charges ever brought in the United Kingdom.

Dr Vincent Brown, a 65-year-old doctor from north London, appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 22 September 2026. He entered no plea, and the allegations against him have not been proved.

The City of London, with the Tower of London at right. File photograph, not taken at the hearing. (Photo: Colin and Kim Hansen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The first Rwanda genocide charges ever brought in the United Kingdom reached a London courtroom on 22 September 2026. Dr Vincent Brown, 65, appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court, entered no plea and keeps the presumption of innocence.

What the court was told

Brown, formerly known as Dr Vincent Bajinya, faces one count of conduct ancillary to genocide. He also faces six counts of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity.

Prosecutor Jane Stansfield told the court that Brown headed the department of family health at Rwanda’s National Office of Population in 1994. Witnesses, including his neighbours, described him as a leader or supervisor of violence carried out by others, she said.

The prosecution alleges six killings in Kigali over four days in April 1994, among them a young woman and her baby son. Prosecutors also allege that a taxi driver was stoned to death by a group Brown directed.

Brown spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address. He did not enter a plea, and no court has tested any of the allegations.

His lawyer, Sam Blom-Cooper, told the court that Brown welcomed the chance to clear his name. “These are appalling crimes, terrible murders that were committed back in 1994,” he said.

“But this, finally, does represent the beginning of the end for Dr Brown,” Blom-Cooper added. A second defence lawyer, Frank Brazell, told the Associated Press that Brown had always maintained his innocence.

Brazell said the evidence against his client was fabricated and that Brown had urged British authorities to prosecute him. Reuters reported that Brown denies involvement and says he left Kigali in the middle of April 1994.

The charges and the law behind them

All seven charges are brought under section 52 of the International Criminal Court Act 2001, the Metropolitan Police said. That section covers conduct ancillary to genocide and other atrocity crimes committed outside the United Kingdom.

It applies to British nationals, British residents and people subject to United Kingdom service jurisdiction. Brown has lived in Britain for more than two decades, Reuters reported.

The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), the public body that decides whether to bring criminal charges in England and Wales, authorised the case. It said the charges followed a file of evidence from the Metropolitan Police War Crimes Team.

Frank Ferguson heads the CPS division that handles special crime and counter terrorism cases. He set out the decision in a written statement on 21 September 2026.

“The charges relate to allegations that Dr Brown took part in the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994,” Ferguson said. He added that Brown is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others.

Ferguson also stressed that the proceedings are now active. “The defendant has the right to a fair trial,” he said.

The Kigali Convention Centre in the Rwandan capital. File photograph of the city today. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Bail and the next hearing

Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring, the senior district judge for England and Wales, granted Brown bail on 22 September 2026. The condition was a security of 25,000 pounds (about US$33,400) paid by his family.

Conversions in this article use a rate of 1.34 dollars to the pound. That is the European Central Bank reference rate for 22 September 2026.

Because of the seriousness of the allegations, Goldspring sent the case to the Central Criminal Court, known as the Old Bailey. Brown is due to appear there on 9 October 2026.

Reuters reported that prosecutors said they wanted to appeal against the bail decision. The Associated Press reported later that day that Brown had been released on bail.

A case two decades in the making

Brown was first arrested in 2006, when Rwanda sought his extradition along with four other men. A British court finally refused those extradition requests in 2017.

The Metropolitan Police War Crimes Team opened its own investigation in September 2019. It acted on a formal request from the Government of Rwanda about killings in the Rugenge district of Kigali.

The force called the seven-year inquiry complex and extensive, involving numerous deployments and significant international cooperation. Brown denied any role in the killings when police interviewed him in 2020, prosecutors told the court.

Originally from Kigali, Brown lives in Islington in north London, the Metropolitan Police said. He once worked for a charity that helped refugee nurses and midwives find work in Britain.

Other investigations continue

Commander Helen Flanagan is a senior officer who leads Counter Terrorism Policing London. “This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes,” she said.

She added that a number of other investigations into other individuals in the United Kingdom remain ongoing. They concern similar offences related to the genocide in Rwanda.

Reuters reported that six other people remain under investigation. Two of them have been arrested on suspicion of genocide and crimes against humanity, according to the same report.

Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo called the prosecution a long overdue step toward accountability. She speaks for the government that formally asked Britain to investigate the case.

Background to the 1994 genocide

The genocide began after a missile attack on 6 April 1994 brought down a plane carrying Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana. Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira died in the same attack.

An estimated 800,000 people were killed over the following 100 days, most of them from the Tutsi minority. Moderate Hutus were also targeted, and courts in several countries have since tried suspects.

What to watch next

The Old Bailey hearing on 9 October 2026 is the next step in the Rwanda genocide charges. Brown will have an opportunity to enter a plea at a later stage.

The CPS has asked that nothing be reported or shared online that could prejudice the proceedings. Brown is entitled to the presumption of innocence, and the allegations against him remain unproven.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Vincent Brown and what is he charged with? Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, is a 65-year-old doctor living in north London. He is charged with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six counts of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity. The charges are allegations that have not been proved. Did Vincent Brown enter a plea at Westminster Magistrates’ Court? No. He spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address. He denies involvement, and his lawyer told the court that he wants to clear his name. When and where is the next hearing? Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring sent the case to the Central Criminal Court, known as the Old Bailey. Brown is due to appear there on 9 October 2026, after being granted bail with a security of 25,000 pounds (about US$33,400).

World.title: Gabon Debt Interest Costs Set to Jump 37 Percent in 2027
World.content:
Gabon · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Interest and other financial charges on Gabon’s debt are set to reach 667.3 billion CFA francs (about US$1.18 billion) in 2027.

— The catch That 37 percent jump covers interest and fees only. Repayment of principal is budgeted separately, at 1,879.5 billion CFA francs (about US$3.31 billion).

— The numbers The draft budget totals 6,223.1 billion CFA francs (about US$11 billion), up 13.2 percent on the revised 2026 budget.

— The borrowing The government plans to raise 1,144.1 billion CFA francs (about US$2.01 billion) on international markets next year, Reuters reported.

— What comes next Gabon’s National Assembly now takes up the bill, while ministers negotiate a new International Monetary Fund programme they want agreed by December.

Gabon debt interest charges are set to rise almost 37 percent next year, the 2027 draft budget shows. Repayment of principal is counted on a separate line, and it is rising faster still.

The International Monetary Fund headquarters in Washington. Gabon asked the Fund for a new lending programme in March 2026. File photograph. (Photo: Marek Ślusarczyk Tupungato Photo portfolio, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Gabon debt interest is about to take a much bigger bite out of the state budget. The Central African oil producer’s 2027 finance bill projects 667.3 billion CFA francs (about US$1.18 billion) in such charges.

That is 36.9 percent more than the 487.6 billion CFA francs (about US$859 million) set aside in the revised 2026 budget. Gabon’s Council of Ministers adopted the bill on Friday 18 September 2026, in the oil city of Port-Gentil.

What the figure covers, and what it leaves out

The 667.3 billion projection covers interest and other financial charges only. It does not include repayment of principal, which the budget books on a separate line.

Principal repayments are set at 1,879.5 billion CFA francs (about US$3.31 billion) for 2027. Clearing unpaid bills to suppliers and lenders takes a further 142.9 billion CFA francs (about US$252 million).

Add interest and principal together and Gabon’s 2027 debt service reaches 2,546.8 billion CFA francs (about US$4.49 billion). On the same basis the revised 2026 budget came to 1,796.8 billion CFA francs (about US$3.16 billion).

Total debt service is therefore rising 41.7 percent, faster than the interest line alone. Principal by itself is up 43.6 percent.

All conversions here use a rate of 567.75 CFA francs to the US dollar, as reported by Reuters on 21 September 2026.

Gabon uses the Central African CFA franc, shared by the six states of the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa. That currency is pegged to the euro and differs from the West African CFA franc.

Where the budget stands

The whole 2027 budget is set at 6,223.1 billion CFA francs (about US$11 billion). That is 13.2 percent above the revised 2026 budget of 5,495.2 billion CFA francs (about US$9.68 billion).

Gabon debt interest alone absorbs about 10.7 percent of that budget. Interest and principal together absorb about 41 percent of it.

Budgeted public investment falls to 1,058.4 billion CFA francs (about US$1.86 billion) next year. That is 110.7 billion CFA francs (about US$195 million) less than the revised 2026 figure.

Manganese ore. Gabon is one of the world’s largest manganese producers, and mining and oil revenue underpin the state budget. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

How the government plans to pay

The bill counts on 1,144.1 billion CFA francs (about US$2.01 billion) from international markets. Reuters reported that plan on 21 September 2026.

Another 600 billion CFA francs (about US$1.06 billion) is to come from the regional market in Central Africa. Budget support and bank loans make up much of the rest.

Gabon returned to international bond markets on 30 July 2026. It priced a seven-year Eurobond of US$920 million with a 9.375 percent coupon, above its US$750 million target.

Moody’s, the credit rating agency, rates Gabon Caa2 with a negative outlook. A coupon above 9 percent shows what lenders now charge the country.

How big the debt has become

Gabon’s debt stock stood above 8,600 billion CFA francs (about US$15.1 billion) at the end of October 2025. Agence Ecofin, a Geneva-based African business news service, reported that it had grown 20.6 percent.

The International Monetary Fund is the Washington lender that governments turn to in difficulty. Its staff projected Gabon’s public debt at 94.3 percent of gross domestic product in 2027.

Those projections rest on data available to 2 April 2026. They predate the revised 2026 budget and the July Eurobond.

The same series runs 70.9 percent in 2024 and 78.9 percent in 2025. It reaches 86.1 percent in 2026.

Fitch Ratings, another credit rating agency, publishes lower numbers. It puts the ratio at 80.6 percent in 2026 and 87.6 percent in 2027.

The talks with the Fund

Gabon formally asked the International Monetary Fund for a new lending programme in March 2026. Both sides are aiming for a deal before the end of this year, Gabonreview reported in July 2026.

Thierry Minko, the minister of economy, finance, debt and state holdings, wants Libreville to set the terms. Any deal will be above all Gabon’s own programme, designed by Gabonese people, he said in French.

He was speaking in an interview published by the news site Gabon Media Time in February 2026. The Fund itself is a small creditor here.

Gabon owed it about 247 billion CFA francs (about US$435 million) at the end of August 2026. That figure has been falling, and payments due during 2027 come to roughly US$144 million.

Who feels the squeeze

Bondholders and other creditors collect the rising interest. Gabonese ministries are left with less room for anything new.

Public investment is the clearest casualty in the 2027 plan. The state payroll, at 963.9 billion CFA francs (about US$1.70 billion), is not being cut.

President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema leads the government behind the plan. He took power in a coup in August 2023 and was elected in April 2025 with 90.35 percent of the vote.

He was sworn in on 3 May 2025 for a seven-year term, ending a 19-month transition. His ministers must now fund their promises while the interest bill climbs.

What happens next

The bill now goes to Gabon’s National Assembly, the lower house of parliament. Its budget session opened on Tuesday 1 September 2026 and runs into December.

The Assembly’s finance committee has just finished two days of training for the task. L’Union, a daily newspaper in Libreville, reported that on 22 September 2026.

Members can still change the numbers before a final vote. The direction of the debt line, though, was set by borrowing already done.

Investors will watch the terms of any new Eurobond. They will also watch whether a programme with the Fund is agreed before the year ends.

Other African governments are turning to global capital markets as traditional revenues fall short. That wider pattern is explored in Africa: The New Scramble.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Gabon’s debt interest bill in 2027? The 2027 draft budget projects 667.3 billion CFA francs (about US$1.18 billion) in interest and other financial charges. That is 36.9 percent more than the revised 2026 budget. Does the 37 percent rise cover all of Gabon’s debt service? No. It covers interest and other financial charges only. Repayment of principal is budgeted separately at 1,879.5 billion CFA francs (about US$3.31 billion) for 2027. How much does Gabon plan to borrow abroad in 2027? The bill counts on 1,144.1 billion CFA francs from international markets, about US$2.01 billion. That uses a rate of 567.75 CFA francs to the US dollar, reported by Reuters on 21 September 2026. What does the International Monetary Fund expect for Gabon’s debt? Fund staff projected public debt at 94.3 percent of gross domestic product in 2027, using data available to 2 April 2026. Fitch Ratings puts the 2027 ratio at 87.6 percent.

World.title: Plan RELANCE Funding: Burkina Faso Turns to Banks and Microlenders
World.content:
Burkina Faso · FINANCE

Key Facts — What happened Finance Minister Aboubakar Nacanabo met commercial bank and microfinance chiefs in Ouagadougou on Tuesday 22 September 2026 to discuss funding Plan RELANCE.

— How big The 2026-2030 national development plan carries a five-year cost of 36,190.7 billion CFA francs (about US$63.2 billion).

— Who pays The government expects to cover about two thirds from its own resources, with partners abroad and private finance covering the rest.

— The banks’ number Bank association chief Djakaridjia Ouattara put the related financing need at about 10,000 billion CFA francs (about US$17.5 billion).

— The targets Broad banking penetration is to reach 47.4 percent by 2030, up from 37.9 percent in 2024.

— The catch Private-sector credit shrank 4.1 percent in 2025 after a 2.2 percent fall in 2024, the International Monetary Fund says.

Burkina Faso’s finance minister asked the country’s banks and microlenders on Tuesday 22 September 2026 to help fund Plan RELANCE. The five-year development plan carries a cost of 36,190.7 billion CFA francs (about US$63.2 billion).

Burkina Faso’s government has asked commercial banks and microfinance lenders to put money behind Plan RELANCE. Economy and Finance Minister Aboubakar Nacanabo met their leaders in Ouagadougou, the capital, on Tuesday 22 September 2026.

What the minister asked of the banks

Plan RELANCE is the country’s national development plan for 2026 to 2030. The Council of Ministers adopted it on 29 January 2026.

Its cost is put at 36,190.7 billion CFA francs (about US$63.2 billion) over the five years. That is an average of 7,238.1 billion CFA francs a year (about US$12.6 billion).

The CFA franc is the currency Burkina Faso shares with seven neighbours in the West African Economic and Monetary Union. The Central Bank of West African States issues it, and it is pegged to the euro.

Conversions here use a rate of 572.2 CFA francs to the US dollar on 22 September 2026. That follows from the euro peg and the European Central Bank’s reference rate for the day.

The state expects to carry about two thirds of the bill from its own resources. Partners abroad and private finance are meant to cover the remaining third.

Nacanabo said banks could act above all in the plan’s fourth pillar, which holds its largest state investments. He also pointed to the third pillar, covering schools and health facilities.

“Private financing can catalyse all the surplus financing,” the minister said, according to the Ouagadougou news site Minute.bf. He named innovative instruments and public-private partnerships as the route.

The number the bankers put on the table

Djakaridjia Ouattara chairs the Professional Association of Banks and Financial Institutions of Burkina Faso, the lobby for the country’s commercial banks. He said the banks had committed to back the plan.

“We have made the commitment and shown our full readiness to support our country’s development plan,” Ouattara said.

He put the related financing need at about 10,000 billion CFA francs (about US$17.5 billion) across the five years. He said that sum is not a demand addressed to the banks.

It is part of the financing the plan needs, which lenders will help cover alongside the state and other sources. Ouattara speaks for the banks that would supply that money.

Microlenders want long money and guarantees

Saïdou Soungalo Yaméogo heads the Professional Association of Microfinance Institutions of Burkina Faso. Its members lend small sums to people and firms that commercial banks rarely reach.

“Our finding is that operators need long-term financing while we hold short-term resources,” Yaméogo said. He asked for long-term refinancing lines and guarantee schemes.

The sector counts more than two million members, and sees digital services as the way to reach rural areas. It proposed a standing forum with the ministry to set out its role.

Why credit is the hard part

The International Monetary Fund, the Washington-based lender to governments, reviewed Burkina Faso’s economy in June 2026. Its board discussed the report on 26 June 2026.

“Private sector credit contracted 4.1 percent in 2025 after a 2.2 percent drop in 2024,” the report said. That is the opposite direction from the plan’s credit target.

The Fund also said limited access to finance for households and firms keeps holding private business back. The plan sets out to change that.

Burkina Faso’s economy grew 5.3 percent in 2025, the Fund reported, lifted by gold. The Fund forecasts growth of 3.6 percent in 2026, as farm output falls.

A gold processing plant in Burkina Faso, where mining supplies most export earnings. File photograph.

Gold accounted for nearly 90 percent of exports in 2025, the Fund said. The current account swung to a surplus of 6.3 percent of gross domestic product that year.

The Fund projects that balance swinging back to a deficit of 2.0 percent of output in 2026. Gold prices and insecurity both feed that turn.

Mining also ties Burkina Faso to a wider contest over African minerals and hard assets. That thread runs through our coverage of Africa: The New Scramble.

The targets Plan RELANCE sets

The plan wants broad banking penetration at 47.4 percent by 2030, up from 37.9 percent in 2024. Use of financial services is to reach 88 percent, from 79.7 percent.

Credit to the economy, measured against gross domestic product, is to rise from 30.8 percent to 38.1 percent. Those three numbers are the plan’s scorecard for the financial sector.

The ministry said it had raised 1,936.63 billion CFA francs (about US$3.4 billion) for the budget by 30 June 2026. That was 58.05 percent of the target for the period.

The state daily Sidwaya reported the figure on 29 July 2026, after a review meeting chaired by Nacanabo. It is the yardstick for the plan’s domestic funding.

What to watch next

The first test is whether Tuesday’s commitments turn into loan products and project finance. The microlenders have asked the ministry for a standing forum to define their role.

The second is lending itself, after the two years of contraction the Fund recorded. A return to growth in credit would be the clearest sign the plan is working.

The third is the full-year revenue figure, against the 58.05 percent booked at the half-year mark. Burkina Faso’s own money is meant to carry most of the bill.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Burkina Faso’s Plan RELANCE? Plan RELANCE is Burkina Faso’s national development plan for 2026 to 2030, adopted by the Council of Ministers on 29 January 2026. It carries a cost of 36,190.7 billion CFA francs (about US$63.2 billion). What did the finance minister ask the banks to do? Economy and Finance Minister Aboubakar Nacanabo met bank and microfinance chiefs in Ouagadougou on Tuesday 22 September 2026. He asked them to help finance the plan, above all its investment and social pillars. How much of the plan will the state pay for? The government expects to cover about two thirds from its own resources. The plan document puts those resources at 23,135.7 billion CFA francs (about US$40.4 billion), or 63.9 percent of the cost. What are the financial inclusion targets? Broad banking penetration is to rise from 37.9 percent in 2024 to 47.4 percent in 2030. Use of financial services is to reach 88 percent, and credit to the economy 38.1 percent of output.

World.title: BNI Mining Risk Day Opens as Côte d’Ivoire Freezes Small-Scale Mine Permits
World.content:
Côte d’Ivoire · MINING FINANCE

Key Facts — What happened BNI, the bank the Ivorian state controls, opened its third Risk Day in Abidjan on Tuesday 22 September 2026.

— The theme Mining as an engine of growth, and how to lend to it without damaging the bank’s own loan book.

— Who spoke Youssouf Fadiga, BNI’s director general, told staff that risk control is a culture rather than a box to tick.

— The state push On Thursday 17 September 2026 the National Security Council set a six-month freeze on new small-scale mining permits.

— The catch The bank announced no mining loan, no amount and no deadline; the day was an internal training exercise.

— Why it matters Côte d’Ivoire mined 59.2 tonnes of gold in 2025 and wants far more of that money banked at home.

BNI mining risk filled the agenda in Abidjan on Tuesday 22 September 2026. Côte d’Ivoire’s state-controlled bank spent the day on how to lend to miners safely.

The Bourse Régionale des Valeurs Mobilières, West Africa’s regional stock exchange, in the Plateau district of Abidjan. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

BNI mining risk got a full day of attention in Abidjan on Tuesday 22 September 2026. The Banque Nationale d’Investissement, controlled by the Ivorian state, opened its third Risk Day in the Cocody district.

What the bank actually did

This was not a loan, a rating or a published report. It was a day of in-house training at the bank’s own integrated centre, opened by its director general, Youssouf Fadiga.

The theme, in the bank’s own wording, was the mining sector as an engine of growth. The sub-theme was building a loan book that is profitable, resilient and creates value.

“Every growth opportunity comes with responsibility,” Fadiga told the room, in remarks reported by the Ivorian news site Abidjan.net. He said mining lending demands close knowledge of operators, production cycles and business models.

Bernardin Tabé, who runs risk management at the bank, said risk culture is not his department’s job alone. He noted that an earlier edition of the event had dealt with real estate.

Why a state bank is talking about mines

BNI is not a small player in the country. The Ivorian state holds about 81 percent of its capital, according to the government directorate that manages public shareholdings.

Its balance sheet reached 3,166 billion CFA francs at the end of 2025 (about US$5.5 billion), a rise of 34 percent. Net profit came to 46.8 billion CFA francs (about US$82 million).

Those figures are BNI’s own, presented in June 2026 and reported by the Abidjan daily Fraternité Matin. The bank says the result lifted it to second place among Ivorian banks by assets.

The CFA franc used in West Africa is pegged to the euro at a fixed parity. Conversions here use 572 to the US dollar, the mid-market rate on 22 September 2026 from er-api.com.

A permit freeze five days earlier

On Thursday 17 September 2026 the National Security Council met at the presidential palace in Abidjan. The council is chaired by President Alassane Ouattara and coordinates security policy.

Its communique announced a six-month moratorium on issuing semi-industrial and artisanal mining permits. It also ordered 21 new river patrol units and heavier penalties for illegal gold panning.

Industrial mining is untouched by the freeze, which covers only semi-industrial and artisanal operations. The communique was signed by Fidèle Sarassoro, the council’s executive secretary.

Land disturbed by artisanal gold mining at Tarkwa in Ghana, the kind of small-scale digging Côte d’Ivoire now wants to control. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

No start date for the moratorium has been reported. Six months counted from the decision would take it to March 2027.

Where the exploration permits actually came from

A decree of Wednesday 4 February 2026 gave Kangue Mining Côte d’Ivoire SA a research permit near Odienné, in the north-west. It covers gold, copper and lithium, and runs for four years.

The same cabinet meeting gave the company a second gold research permit in Korhogo and Niakaramandougou. Research permits allow drilling and sampling, not extraction.

Lithium matters because it goes into batteries, and West Africa is being scouted hard for it. Whether anything is found at Odienné will take years of drilling to establish.

The prize Côte d’Ivoire is chasing

The country mined 59.2 tonnes of gold in 2025, eighth in Africa. Mamadou Sangafowa-Coulibaly, the minister of mines, petroleum and energy, wants second or third place by 2035.

He said so on Wednesday 16 September 2026 in Abidjan, at a meeting on a new state precious-metals company. He added that its refinery should start work in the first half of 2027.

The mines ministry also says the country ranked first in West Africa on the Fraser Institute’s 2026 mining attractiveness index. The Canadian research group surveys mining executives each year.

What BNI mining risk means for investors

BNI named no mining client, no loan and no target at the event. The signal is that a state bank is building the machinery to lend to mines.

Mining projects in frontier economies often raise their money abroad rather than from local lenders. Fadiga argued that data and artificial intelligence can help BNI spot risk signals earlier.

He added that those tools must serve rigorous governance and informed human decisions. This fits the wider contest traced in Africa: The New Scramble.

The next test is whether the moratorium is lifted or extended in 2027. The second is whether BNI ever writes a mining loan it is willing to name.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was BNI’s third Risk Day about? It was an in-house training day in Abidjan on Tuesday 22 September 2026. The subject was how to finance mining without losing control of credit risk. BNI announced no loan and no target. What did Côte d’Ivoire decide about mining permits in September 2026? On Thursday 17 September 2026 the National Security Council announced a six-month moratorium on issuing semi-industrial and artisanal mining permits. It also ordered tougher action against illegal gold panning. When did Kangue Mining get its Odienné exploration permit? A decree of Wednesday 4 February 2026 granted Kangue Mining Côte d’Ivoire SA a four-year research permit. It covers gold, copper and lithium in the Odienné department.

World.title: NMDPRA Licence Revocation Warning for Nigeria Petrol Stations Over Under-Dispensing
World.content:
Nigeria · REGULATION

Key Facts — What happened Nigeria’s midstream and downstream fuel regulator told every filling station to recalibrate its pumps on Tuesday 22 September 2026.

— Who ordered it The NMDPRA, the federal authority created by the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 to license fuel depots, pipelines and retail outlets.

— The penalty Persistent or serious under-dispensing can bring sanctions up to revocation of an outlet’s licence, the circular said.

— The catch The sealings described below date from February and July 2026, and no revocation under the new warning has been reported.

— Why it matters Fuel retailing is a cash business in Africa’s largest oil producer, and pump prices feed straight into inflation and transport fares.

— What comes next Four marketer associations were asked to tell members to check dispensers and totalisers at once.

Nigeria’s midstream and downstream fuel regulator has told every filling station in the country to recalibrate its pumps, warning that persistent short measures can cost an outlet its licence.

A hand holding a fuel nozzle at a service station. File photograph (Photo: Rio Times media library)
