“I was screwed over again,” Garibashvili writes.

However, he continues, on 4 January 2026 he was unexpectedly informed that the terms had changed and that he would face five years in prison. By that point, he had already pleaded guilty, been released on bail and was awaiting the formalisation of a plea agreement.

20-year relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili

In one of the key parts of the letter, Garibashvili discusses his longstanding relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party. He says that because of his 20-year political and personal relationship with Ivanishvili, he did not want to enter into a political confrontation with him.

“I silently walked to the political slaughterhouse and went to prison because I did not want to enter into confrontation,”the former prime minister writes.

He says that by making this decision, he sacrificed himself to protect the team and the country.

“I made my sacrifice and also spared the team and the country. In return, I was screwed over for a third time,”Garibashvili says.

‘Authorities suffered more from my arrest than I did’

Garibashvili says that in February he communicated with the authorities through an intermediary. Their main message, he says, was that the ruling team had suffered more from his arrest than Garibashvili himself.

He says this left him with the impression that the authorities were preparing a new provocation because his detention and the campaign against him had failed to produce the result they had expected.

“They failed to discredit me sufficiently in the eyes of the public; they failed to achieve the effect they had expected from my arrest and the accompanying propaganda,” the former prime minister writes.

‘My reputation was not significantly damaged’

Garibashvili says there was no further communication with him until July, when the authorities made a new proposal.

According to Garibashvili, this time the authorities acknowledged that his arrest had damaged the ruling team itself, while the former prime minister’s reputation had not suffered significantly.

Garibashvili writes that public sympathy for him had grown, particularly among some Georgian Dream voters.

He says this was also because other people convicted of offences against the authorities had been released with suspended sentences, making his five-year prison term difficult for the public to understand.

Admitting to new corruption charge

According to the former prime minister, it was after this that the authorities developed a new fear that he would return to politics after his release from prison. Garibashvili says he was asked to admit to a new corruption charge.

He says the aim was twofold: to destroy his reputation once and for all and further prevent any possibility of his return to politics:

“Because of this, they demanded that I admit to a new, dirty corruption charge so that, on the one hand, my name would be completely destroyed and, on the other, they could further guard against the risk of my return to politics.”

‘My imprisonment was political from start to finish’

Garibashvili gives a clear assessment of his own case:

“Based on all this, my imprisonment was political from start to finish, from the very first day, and everything that has been done against me is politically motivated and has nothing to do with a legal process.”

The former prime minister says he believes he is in prison because of “absurd suspicions, fears and envy”.

He describes it as an injustice committed not only against him but also against his family.

Response to state propaganda

The second part of the letter contains direct and strongly worded accusations and criticism of the authorities.

Garibashvili says that “false and dirty propaganda” against him has continued over the past two weeks.

The former prime minister describes statements by government representatives as “hypocritical” and “false”.

“As I see it, you have got rather carried away and really settled into your role. Don’t be hypocrites! First take the log out of your own eye, and then talk about corruption,” Garibashvili writes.

He says the public is well aware that the campaign being waged by the authorities is a “farce”.

Irakli Garibashvili

‘You have made state institutions a laughing stock’

Garibashvili also accuses the authorities of damaging state institutions. He says their actions both at home and abroad have made state institutions “a laughing stock”.

“You have given enemies at home and abroad grounds to talk,” he writes.

He says the ruling team’s policies have plunged the country into “continuous chaos and an endless crisis”.

Garibashvili also says the authorities’ own voters have been left confused by their policies, while a sense of hopelessness, instability and uncertainty about the future has taken hold in society.

Parallel with Saakashvili era

The sharpest part of the letter is Garibashvili’s comparison of the authorities’ actions with the rule of Mikheil Saakashvili.

“You are already following Saakashvili’s path and bringing back the methods of rule used by the United National Movement,” Garibashvili writes.

The former prime minister argues that the authorities’ current policies are ultimately harming both Georgian Dream itself and the country.

“You have caused enormous, irreparable damage to your own state, your government and the ruling party itself,” he says.

The letter ends with a warning:

“You are doing evil. Be careful!”

The case against Garibashvili

Garibashvili was first charged with corruption in October 2025. Investigators accused him of large-scale money laundering.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, Garibashvili provided false information in his asset declarations in an attempt to make illegally obtained income appear legitimate.

In January 2026, Garibashvili pleaded guilty and reached a plea agreement with prosecutors. The court sentenced him to five years in prison.

In a second case, the former Georgian prime minister is accused of accepting a particularly large bribe. Prosecutors allege that he received 750,000 lari (approximately $289,000) from a scheme involving classified procurement by the Defence Ministry.

The new case followed statements by Garibashvili in which he accused the authorities of pressuring him and demanding that he admit to a new charge.

The case concerns the procurement of medical equipment and supplies for the Defence Ministry. According to prosecutors, the ministry carried out three classified procurements from late 2022. At the time, Juansher Burchuladze was defence minister and Irakli Garibashvili was prime minister. Prosecutors, however, plan to reach a plea agreement with Burchuladze, saying the decision was made in view of the extent of his co-operation with the investigation.

World.title: Armenia marks 35 years of independence: the country’s gains and losses, according to AI
World.content:
Armenia’s 35 years of independence: an AI assessment

Armenia is marking Independence Day. Thirty-five years ago, on 21 September 1991, an overwhelming majority of the population (94.39%) voted in a referendum to leave the USSR and establish an independent democratic state.

JAMnews asked artificial intelligence to analyse Armenia’s journey over the past 35 years.

According to the AI assessment, the past 35 years present a highly mixed picture. Armenia has made significant progress in democratisation, international integration and the development of state institutions.

At the same time, Armenia has suffered major losses. Wars have cost thousands of lives, driven emigration and resulted in the loss of territory. Above all, the country has yet to fully resolve its security concerns.

“The greatest achievement is the survival of an independent state. The greatest loss is the human cost and demographic price Armenia has paid over 35 years,” the AI concluded.

From survival to state-building

“35 years can be divided into three major stages.

1991–1998: survival and state-building — the declaration of independence, war, blockade, an energy crisis and economic collapse, but also the creation of the foundations of state institutions.

1999–2017: stabilisation and economic growth — macroeconomic stability, rapid growth and infrastructure development, but also emigration, corruption, a closed political system and the unresolved Karabakh conflict.

2018–2026: democratic transformation, war and a new foreign policy strategy — the 2018 “Velvet” Revolution, the 2020 war, the loss of Nagorno-Karabakh, the exodus of Karabakh Armenians from their homeland in 2023, the arrival of more than 100,000 forcibly displaced people in Armenia, and efforts to build a new security system and new foreign policy relationships.”

Key achievements

“Building an independent state”

The greatest achievement is that Armenia has existed for 35 years as an internationally recognised independent state, with its own Constitution, state institutions, army, currency, diplomatic system and international commitments.

Developing an international presence

Armenia joined the UN in 1992 and later joined numerous international organisations. This means that the Armenian state acts as an independent subject in international relations and makes its own decisions.

Building an army and defence system

During the war of the 1990s, Armenia established its armed forces. This became one of the key institutions underpinning its independent statehood.

Economic recovery and long-term growth

After the severe crisis of the early 1990s, the economy began to recover in 1994, followed by rapid growth in the 2000s. According to the World Bank, Armenia’s economy grew by an average of around 6.3% a year between 2000 and 2023. During this period, the economy shifted significantly from agriculture towards industry and services.

Development of the technology and services sectors

IT, services, finance and tourism now play a much larger role in the economy than they did during the early years of independence. This is particularly important for a small landlocked country.

Some improvement in living conditions

The World Bank notes an increase in life expectancy and improvements in several social indicators. Extreme poverty has been virtually eliminated. However, “ordinary poverty” remains a serious problem, particularly in rural areas.

Political change and the ability to transfer power

The peaceful transfer of power in 2018 demonstrated the potential for mass civic mobilisation and political change. Subsequent elections, including the 2021 early parliamentary election, were competitive and well organised, according to international observers, although political polarisation persisted.

Strengthening civil society and national identity

Independence created an environment in which the Armenian language, state symbols, national culture and the idea of statehood became the foundations of an independent country rather than a Soviet republic.”

Losses and setbacks

“Human losses

The First Karabakh War, the four-day war of 2016 and especially the 2020 war claimed thousands of lives and left deep trauma across Armenian society.

Consequences of the 2020 war

Armenia lost control over a significant part of the territories of Nagorno-Karabakh and its previous security system. After 2020, Armenia’s security environment changed radically. In 2024, the prime minister himself described 2020 as a moment when Armenia found itself on the verge of losing its independence.

The loss of homeland for Karabakh Armenians and population displacement

After the military escalation in September 2023, more than 100,000 people moved to Armenia. The International Committee of the Red Cross noted that Armenian social services and the accommodation system struggled to cope with such a large influx of displaced people. For Armenian society, this became not only a territorial loss but also a major demographic, social and psychological one.

Emigration and demographic problems

Mass emigration, which began in the early years of independence, became one of Armenia’s most persistent long-term problems. The World Bank identifies low birth rates, an ageing population and significant emigration as serious constraints on the country’s economic future.

Social inequality and poverty

Despite years of strong economic performance, economic growth has not always translated evenly into higher living standards. According to the World Bank, as of 2022, around half of the population still lived below the international poverty line of $6.85 a day. This threshold applies to upper-middle-income countries.

Weak institutions and political polarisation

Over 35 years, Armenia has not achieved full judicial independence, eliminated corruption or overcome political polarisation. A 2026 analysis by Human Rights Watch says that, despite reforms, serious problems remain concerning the independence of the judiciary, the media and the police, as well as the protection of human rights.

Excessive reliance on external security partners

For 35 years, Armenia has had to build its security system amid difficult regional and geopolitical conditions. Its long-standing reliance on Russia for security and, in recent years, the need to diversify its partnerships show that full strategic autonomy remains a work in progress.”

Independence as a fact

“Armenia has managed to create and preserve an independent state, but it has not yet transformed that independence into a state system that is sufficiently secure, demographically sustainable and socially prosperous.

It is important to distinguish between independence as a legal and statehood fact and independence as a real characteristic of a state. Armenia achieved the former in 1991. The latter — economic, military, demographic, institutional and diplomatic independence — remains an ongoing process.

At the same time, the picture of recent years is not limited to losses. In 2025, Armenia and Azerbaijan made progress towards a peace settlement. The prospect of restoring regional ties has also created an opportunity for a new stage to begin, although it is still too early to assess its long-term results.”

Armenia’s 35 years of independence: an AI assessment

World.title: Why are pensions in Abkhazia so low? Officials explain
World.content:
A 71-year-old resident of Abkhazia Marina Kachubeevna recently submitted documents to apply for Russian citizenship. Without a Russian passport, she cannot receive a Russian pension, which is relatively generous by local standards.

Her Abkhaz pension, which totals 6,000 roubles [$65] a month including all basic payments and supplements, is not enough to live on. So the woman has to continue working to have money of her own.

“I have wonderful children. My son and daughter-in-law never refuse me anything. When I started having health problems last year, they took full responsibility for paying for my medicines and doctors.

But every time I have to ask them for money for the pharmacy or basic personal needs, I feel uncomfortable. I don’t want to be a burden. At 71, I want to remain independent and be able to buy even small gifts for my grandchildren myself, without having to ask my children for the money,” Marina Kachubeevna says.

This desire to ease the financial burden on her family is the only reason she decided to apply for Russian citizenship.

Intergenerational solidarity and the reality of pension payments

The story of Marina Kachubeevna reflects broader systemic trends in Abkhazia’s social welfare system.

At present, around 33,000 people receive the basic old-age pension of 6,000 roubles. As the chairman of the republic’s Pension Fund, Denis Gularia, acknowledges, this amount falls far short of what is needed to live on.

However, Gularia points to a traditional model of social support in Abkhaz society, based on assistance from relatives.

“There is such a concept as intergenerational solidarity: children should help their parents. Of course, some pensioners do not have children, but this is the kind of society we have. Neighbours help each other as much as they can.

We constantly hear criticism directed at us. We hear it and understand it. But people have to help each other,” the Pension Fund chairman says.

He also stresses that the number of people receiving additional domestic payments continues to grow:

“The number of people receiving supplementary payments is approaching 17,000 and will continue to grow. Many of our citizens no longer have enough Soviet-era work experience to qualify for a pension from Russia’s Social Fund, so they will receive only our payments. We will try to find the funds to increase these payments in the future.”

41,000 workers supporting 50,000 pensioners

The main obstacle to a significant increase in pensions is the imbalance between the number of officially employed residents and the number of people receiving pensions and benefits.

According to statistics, Abkhazia has a working-age population of 144,000. Of these, around 40,000–41,000 people officially work and pay social insurance contributions. Meanwhile, around 51,000 people receive supplementary payments or pensions.

“With this ratio, high pensions are simply impossible. The remaining part of the population, around 100,000 people, work but do not contribute to the Pension Fund,” Gularia explains.

Commercial businesses also create an additional problem by avoiding full payment of social insurance contributions:

“Unfortunately, not everyone declares their full salary. The minimum salary in commercial organisations here is 20,000 roubles [$215]**. But if someone earns more, employers and employees often agree to declare only the minimum.

People themselves should have an interest in ensuring that social insurance contributions are paid. Remember, the contributions made by the 40,000 people who work today support the entire older generation.”

Reforms, collection orders and individual records

To change the situation, the Pension Fund plans to introduce individual records for insurance contributions and tighten fiscal discipline.

“A flat-rate system is unfair to those who pay honestly. One person pays contributions based on their actual salary, while another declares the minimum, yet they both receive the same pension. That is unfair.

Once we introduce individual records for insurance contributions, it will benefit people who plan to remain economically active: in addition to the basic 6,000 roubles, they will receive substantial payments based on the contributions recorded in their personal account,” Gularia says.

At the same time, the fund is actively working with employers who fail to meet their obligations. According to the chairman, the agency can issue collection orders when contributions are overdue. A collection order allows a bank to debit money from a payer’s account without prior consent. In 2025, the fund recovered 49.9 million roubles [around $537,000] in this way.

Some businesses also voluntarily repay old debts.

“We need to adopt legislation that strengthens the responsibility of managers and accountants who fail to submit reports on time,” Gularia says.

Re-registration for oversight and transparency

The re-registration of pensioners, which runs from 1 September to 1 December 2026, is another necessary step towards putting the system in order.

“There are cases when relatives do not always register a pensioner’s death promptly or submit the death certificate to social welfare offices. The money saved as a result of these checks will go into a fund for future increases in supplementary payments to the most vulnerable groups,” the official explains.

Apparently, bringing businesses out of the shadow economy, introducing individual records and ensuring that people pay their contributions properly offer the only way to ensure that, in a few years, pensioners such as Marina Kachubeevna can retire without financial worries, feel secure and afford to buy gifts for their grandchildren without having to work at the age of 71.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Features of the pension system in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian authorities ‘suspect’ Tbilisi School of Political Studies of receiving grant without their consent
World.content:
The Georgian State Audit Office has launched an investigation into the financial activities of the Tbilisi School of Political Studies. The Audit Office’s Financial Transparency Department said the investigation concerns the possible receipt of a grant without the Georgian government’s consent.

“To examine the matter comprehensively, the State Audit Office will act within the powers granted to it by Georgian law, including the Law of Georgia on Grants,” the Audit Office told Interpressnews.

The Tbilisi School of Political Studies was founded in 1999 as a non-governmental organisation. The school operates under the auspices of the Council of Europe and is headed by politician Armaz Akhvlediani.

What happened

Government officials have repeatedly spoken about the Tbilisi School of Political Studies in recent weeks. Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said the school had held a seminar in the village of Bakhmaro with funding from the Council of Europe. He suggested that the funding for the event may have bypassed Georgian law.

According to Papuashvili, the school did not seek the government’s consent to receive the grant, while the Council of Europe’s media office said the event in Bakhmaro did not constitute a grant.

“So what was it, then?” Papuashvili asked.

He said the original version of the Law on Grants required government approval for all forms of foreign funding, including direct spending by organisations. The final version retained an exception for diplomatic activities. However, Papuashvili argued that organisations should not use this exception to circumvent the law.

ПPapuashvili suggests that, in the case of the seminar in Bakhmaro, the Council of Europe’s local office directly paid for hotel accommodation, transport and food, as well as fees for experts and speakers.

“If that is the case, we are dealing with an attempt to circumvent the law,” the speaker said.

According to Papuashvili, the law also covers cases where an agreement is described as a service contract but in substance amounts to a grant.

What the Law on Grants provides

The legislative package approved on 4 March 2026 significantly broadens the definition of a “grant”. It covers both financial and non-financial support if it can be used to influence the country’s domestic or foreign policy, including activities linked to the interests of a foreign state or political force.

The law also strengthens the State Audit Office’s oversight of the awarding and receipt of grants. If a foreign legal entity funds a branch operating in Georgia without government approval, it can face sanctions, including a fine equal to twice the value of the grant.

Violating the grants law can also result in criminal liability. Penalties include a fine, community service or up to six years in prison.

The changes also affect the political process. People who work for organisations that receive predominantly foreign funding will be barred from joining political parties for eight years. At the same time, restrictions imposed on political parties also apply to entities that are not formally parties but effectively engage in political activity.

The legislative package also tightens administrative liability for private companies if they become involved in public political activity.

Georgia’s Law on Grants

Frank Finger is an expert at turning a pup into a world-class working dog.

Australians know the central Queensland grazier as the season 1 winner of the Muster Dogs television series, taking out the top prize with kelpie Annie.

But away from the show ring, the working dog trainer is passionate about passing on the lessons and wisdom he's acquired throughout his 30-year career.

"Dogs can't make themselves," he said.

"The first 16 weeks of a pup's life is the most important time, that's where they learn the manners."

Several times a year, he opens his Clermont property to working dog trainees and their owners for weekend-long learning sessions.

"Sometimes there'll be a lot of young pups, sometimes there'll be a lot of old dogs, sometimes there'll be overeager dogs," he said.

"So, every school is slightly different because the people are different."

Since 2021, more than 1,000 eager trainees from across Australia and overseas have attended one of the working dog sessions.

"It's very humbling, very overwhelming," Mr Finger reflected

"One girl came from Liverpool in England … around Texas [in USA], a lot of people have made contact with us."

Training the next generation

While at the helm of the school for now, Mr Finger insists on educating the next generation of trainers.

His son Scott instructs most of the school's attendees.

Like his father, he finds the job rewarding.

"Even people coming you know for their fourth or fifth time to our schools and seeing … the progress they've made working their dogs on the livestock," he said.

But it's not just about teaching the dogs, he explained.

"People think they come here for a pup starting school, it's more so to get themselves right too.

"Whether it be their demeanour or … something like that, they can just … take it all on board and it'll all fall into place."

Trainer Jonty Beney has been learning from Mr Finger the last four years, including the agricultural show circuit.

He said the mentorship had empowered him to be a better trainer.

"He [Frank] always wants people to step up and have a go and not wait to be told to do something," Mr Beney said.

" He doesn't look down at anyone, he just wants everyone to go away with a win. "

Recognising a legacy

In his hometown, about four hours west of Rockhampton, the Clermont Tourism Board and Isaac Regional Council recently honoured Mr Finger's leadership in the community with a water tank mural.

Against the backdrop of a stunning Clermont sunset, the mural painting in the town centre depicts the revered local on his quad bike next to Annie.

Mr Finger's beloved dog, who he considers to be the best he's trained, passed away last year, in the same week as his wife Cathy.

A mural paying tribute to Frank Finger and Annie was painted on a water tank in Clermont. (ABC Capricornia: Jessica D'Souza)

A decade in the making, the artwork was spearheaded by Mr Finger's sister-in-law Marg Finger and her fellow members at the Clermont Tourism Committee.

"[It was] a no-brainer," Mrs Finger said.

"He's done a lot of work for our community and everybody's proud he's up there."

The recognition is adored by locals and visitors, according to committee chair Janine Williams.

"They're [the community] just amazed … Even people that live out of town and drive in every day say that they just absolutely love driving past and still glancing up and seeing it."

For Mr Finger, the mural captures what he believes to be the most important lesson when training working dogs.

"If you don't love dogs, it doesn't kind of work. You've got to like your dogs."

World.title: Fremantle and Brisbane AFL fans find 'homes away from home' in Melbourne
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Interstate footy fans descending on Melbourne for this weekend's AFL grand final are gravitating towards two pubs serving as unofficial embassies for travelling Fremantle and Brisbane fans.

This weekend is the fifth time two non-Victorian teams are competing in an AFL grand final and interstate fans are already streaming into the city.

An unassuming pub in Melbourne's inner north is gearing up to be a home away from home for Fremantle supporters.

Alistair Carragher bought the Great Northern Hotel in Carlton North in 2009.

The Perth expat said the pub was historically a home for Fremantle and West Coast supporters who moved to Melbourne.

"They'd go play a game of football at the park and then come to the pub after that," he said.

" West Australians in general were a bit neglected in sport and pubs. "

Alistair Carragher says Grand Final day at the Great Northern has been booked out since May. (ABC News: Ethan White)

Mr Carragher said since 2013, when Fremantle played its first grand final, the popularity of the hotel for local Dockers fans exploded.

"It's great to have somewhere to go, especially being the smaller group in Melbourne, there's not always a place that you can find people," Fremantle cheer squad member Jess Ritchie said.

Dockers fan Nacha Kirilak said it was "nice to have a safe ground to come to with like-minded people who aren't going to yell at you because you're wearing a different colour".

David Cowell, Nacha Kirilak and Jess Ritchie are all members of Fremantle's Melbourne cheer squad. (ABC News: Ethan White)

Along with local supporters, the hotel is expecting to host hundreds of Fremantle fans visiting Melbourne who were unable to get a ticket to the game at the MCG.

"It's a little bit of a community home, somewhere they can see their team," Mr Carragher said.

" Everyone's just super pumped. "

A different story for the Lions

While Dockers supporters in Melbourne needed to commandeer a suburban pub, just a few kilometres to the east, Lions fans had a very different story.

The suburb of Fitzroy is the spiritual home of the Lions, after the Victorian football club amalgamated with the Brisbane Bears 30 years ago, to form the Brisbane Lions.

Scott Villiers, a self-described Lions nuffy, said the team has always felt like the Fitzroy Lions to him.

"It's nostalgic, I actually feel proud to be part of a family, because that's what the Brisbane Lions is," he said.

"The club does an amazing job to preserve the history of both Fitzroy and the Bears."

Brisbane fan Scott Villiers says supporting the Lions is "genetic". (ABC News: Ethan White)

Mr Villiers acknowledged that a new generation of Brisbane fans have emerged since the amalgamation.

"I hope they feel welcome down here, we're an extended family by default," he said.

For the past three grand finals, the Royal Derby Hotel on Brunswick Street has served as the home of the Lions in Fitzroy.

"Thousands upon thousands of bowls of chips, 120 kegs of beer flowing, good vibes and lots of cheering," its venue manager Liam Huxley recalled.

The hotel staff are preparing to do it all again for a fourth consecutive year, while welcoming Queensland fans joining the Fitzroy fraternity.

"Last year, the amount of Bundy [rum] and Great Northern we went through — it's just unbelievable," Mr Huxley said.

Liam Huxley says he's nervous but ready for another premiership. (ABC News: Ethan White)

Victoria to reap the benefits

Both pubs completely booked out tables months ago, with staff expecting hundreds more walk-ins across the long weekend.

RMIT University finance professor Angel Zhong said the grand final weekend could generate up to $75 million in economic activity for the state.

"When interstate fans fly in, stay in hotels and eat in our restaurants, that is genuinely new money entering Victoria," she said.

Events such as the traditional grand final parade draw people into Melbourne's CBD ahead of the game. (ABC News: Richard Sydenham)

Dr Zhong also highlighted the economic strain placed on small business owners, who are required to pay penalty rates on Friday's public holiday in Victoria.

"How it balances out depends on the individual business, whether it opens, how busy it is and whether it can make up the lost day."

Melbourne Airport said more than 114,000 passengers are expected to travel through its terminals on Saturday.

Fans flying from Perth and Brisbane have faced surging flight fares, with return airfares reaching $6,000 ahead of Saturday's game.

While Melburnians may be used to living in the football capital of Australia, this weekend, it's the interstate fans who will be calling the city home.

World.title: Footballer who died after hitting goalpost remembered for cheeky smile
World.content:
A 25-year-old footballer who died after hitting a goalpost while being towed by a quad bike is being remembered as a fierce competitor and much-loved teammate.

Jed Griffin died at the Osborne Football Club's home ground south-west of Wagga Wagga on Sunday afternoon.

A 20-year-old man has been charged with dangerous driving occasioning death, driving in a dangerous manner and negligent driving occasioning death.

He was scheduled to face the Wagga Wagga Local Court today.

The incident happened one day after Mr Griffin took to the field for the Osborne senior side's game against Henty in the Hume Football Netball League grand final.

Osborne lost the grand final by six points.

Mr Griffin's coach of three years, Myles Aalbers, said Jed was a determined athlete with a cheeky demeanour and a quick-witted sense of humour.

"Every time I would see him, he would just have that cheeky smile … I'll never forget that about Jed," Mr Aalbers said.

" He loved his mates, he loved his outdoor fishing and hunting, and the people close to him. "

Mr Aalbers described Mr Griffin as one of the best footballers he had seen and an all-round great person.

"He was one of the fiercest competitors I've coached with in my time in football," he said.

"Just, with his stature, some of the contest he went into — I was amazed he came out the other end of it with no injuries."

The Osborne Recreation Ground in southern NSW. (ABC News: Jostina Basta )

Griffin committed to Osborne

Mr Aalbers said Mr Griffin's commitment to Osborne was evident in the literal journey he made to play and train, driving past several other clubs between his home and the ground.

"That speaks volumes itself. [It's the] same with his family, Terry, Nicole and Darby. They're a big part of our football club," he said.

He described the Osborne community as a "big family", and said the loss reverberated well beyond the playing group.

"This has obviously impacted a lot of people's lives, and we will aim to get through it together," Mr Aalbers said.

"It is obviously very difficult circumstances. As a playing group we are just trying to rally around each other and stick together as tight as we can.

"We don't know what the steps forward are, but we are just trying to keep the group together and be there for each other."

The club has received support from the wider community, with counselling services offered to players and others affected by Mr Griffin's death.

A floral tribute left at the Osborne Recreation Ground. (ABC News: Jostina Basta )

'Two teams, one league, one united community'

The Hume Football Netball League has been showing its support for the Osborne Football Netball Club, paying tribute to Mr Griffin in online posts.

The Henty Football Netball Club — the team Mr Griffin played his last match against — said it sent love, care and condolences to the 25-year-old's family and loved ones.

It described his death as a "tragic and heartbreaking loss".

"We further extend our arms to the entire Osborne Football Netball Club and all other families impacted by this sad moment in time," the club said.

" Two teams, one league, one united community of people. We are here for you all. "

The Henty Football Netball Club has paid tribute to the footballer online. (Supplied: Facebook.)

The Coreen Daysdale Hopefield Buraja Football Netball Club said it was "deeply saddened by the loss of a really great young man".

"There are simply no words big enough for what you are facing right now," the club said.

"Please know you are not facing it alone. We are right beside you, wrapping our arms around you and sending every bit of love, strength and support we possibly can."

The club said country sporting clubs were "so much more than football and netball".

"They are family. They are where we grow up, where lifelong friendships are formed, where families come together and where we stand beside one another through the very best and the very hardest of times."

The Corowa Rutherglen Football Netball Club, where Mr Griffin played some junior and senior matches, said his's death would leave an enormous hole in the hearts of those who knew him.

"Today, we want to acknowledge the life of Jed — a spirited young man who was loved by so many," the statement read.

"Vale Jed."

World.title: Boy, 9, drowns after entering drainpipe in Katherine
World.content:
A nine-year-old boy has drowned after entering a drainpipe in the Northern Territory town of Katherine, NT Police say.

About 5:15pm yesterday, it was reported a boy had "entered a drainpipe at Katherine Low Level and not resurfaced", police said in a statement,

"Police attended the scene and deployed divers who located the child at 1:45am," they said.

NT Police Commander Neil Hayes said the child's family was at the scene and they are now being provided with support.

"This is an incredibly tragic incident, and we are providing welfare to the attending members," he said.

Simulated drowning ad targets kids Cartoon frogs are replaced by a simulated drowning in a new ad campaign warning kids.

"Our thoughts are with the boy’s family."

He said a report on the death would be prepared for the coroner.

A long-running campaign across the NT has warned children of the dangers of playing in pipes and drains, particularly in the wet season.

In 2014, an eight-year-old boy in the Darwin satellite city of Palmerston drowned while playing in a drain, with a coronial inquest into the death recommending regular inspections of drains.

World.title: Neale's dad wants Lions to appeal grand final ban but says son is 'in two minds'
World.content:
Lachie Neale's father says he would like Brisbane to appeal the star Lion's AFL grand final ban, but believes his son will "be in two minds" over it.

Neale copped a one-game suspension for striking Jack Ginnivan during the Lions' stunning preliminary final victory at the MCG on Saturday night.

The club can take the AFL tribunal's decision to the appeals board in the hopes of overturning the ban and allowing Neale to face his former team as the Lions attempt to win a third straight premiership.

Neale's father, Robbie, told ABC Radio Adelaide that the former captain would not want to distract from the week leading up to Saturday afternoon's grand final.

"The club will be meeting this morning, I know that's happening," he said.

Why Neale's grand final ban was upheld The tribunal says it had reason not to overturn Lachie Neale's appeal. Now the AFL world waits to hear whether the Lions will launch an appeal.

"Lachie won't want the distraction for the team, so I think he'll be in two minds this morning as to the way forward. I'm sure he'll get the right advice.

"To me it's just plain wrong, so I hope they do appeal it."

"The last thing Lachie wanted this week was a headline. It's just so disappointing," he added.

The two-time Brownlow medallist has been in the headlines a lot this year, including giving up the captaincy before the season following a widely publicised marriage breakdown.

He was permitted to leave the team at the end of the season and went into Collingwood for a medical ahead of a reported move to the Magpies next year.

Robbie Neale (left) says he is worried about his son missing the grand final. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Robbie Neale said there had been "fabricated garbage" around Neale, particularly regarding the Collingwood visit during the season.

"He does even amaze me in terms of how he's been able to compartmentalise and just focus on his job and play footy, and he's had a pretty good year," he said.

Neale was also the centre of attention leading up to last year's grand final win over Geelong as he raced the clock to recover from a calf injury.

He ultimately played only the second half, kicking a crucial long-range goal in the third quarter.

"This one [the suspension], we're worried for him, because I know this means everything to him to play in this grand final," Robbie said.

"Easy to say that he's already played in a few, but they've got a chance to create history here."

The Lions are expected to reveal their appeals plans today, with a hearing potentially on Thursday evening.

World.title: Airport expansion a threat to character of beachside suburb, opponents say
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Community backlash is brewing over a $75 million plan that could transform part of the Sunshine Coast Airport into a resort, residential and retail precinct.

The airport recently submitted an application to state government entity Economic Development Queensland (EDQ) for the 34-hectare site between the runway and homes at Marcoola.

Airport North is listed as a Priority Development Area, which means development applications are accessed by EDQ, bypassing Sunshine Coast Council.

Several community groups and a councillor are urging residents to fight the plan.

Airport North is one of several precincts within the airport site. (Supplied)

Councillor Taylor Bunnag issued a personal statement on Tuesday morning, saying the development "risks destroying our local character".

"This proposal fundamentally risks undoing what makes this part of the Coast special, which generations have fought to protect," the statement said.

A town planning report included in the application seeks approval for a combination of potential uses of the site, including a resort, hotel, short-term accommodation, multiple dwellings, shops, bars, veterinary services, health services, indoor sports and a retirement facility.

Under existing approvals buildings up to 10 storeys high are permitted.

Sekisui development sent back to the drawing board Queensland's Supreme Court rules in favour of a community appeal against the development approval of a controversial beachside development.

Cr Bunnag told the ABC the airport proposal was reminiscent of the Sekisui development planned for Yaroomba, a few suburbs north, which was eventually thrown out by the Supreme Court.

"It is eerily similar in terms of a beachside location, hotels, accommodation," he said.

"I think that this has been the sleeping giant within the community in the sense that, from a council perspective, the airport is no longer under our planning authority."

'Very intense'

The Sunshine Coast Airport Master Plan 2040 states the Airport North precinct would have uses that "may include but are not limited to" logistics, cold storage, warehousing, food and beverage, freight facilities and commercial car parking.

An artist's impression of a hotel planned for the Gateway Precinct near the existing terminal. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Airport)

Marcoola Community Group president Susie Chapman was involved in consultations for the 2040 plan.

She said the new application was "very intense" for the "low-key" north shore area.

"All our conversations with the master plan was that it wasn't going to be accommodation and it was all going to be internal roadways," Ms Chapman said.

"But this current proposal is certainly nothing of the sort — it's going straight onto David Low Way."

A view of the airport site from David Low Way, which is the main arterial road on the north shore. (Supplied: Taylor Bunnag)

The planning report states the intersection of David Low Way and Green Turtle Place as a "potential site access" point.

"If something happens on the Sunshine Motorway, David Low Way is chock-a-block and held up for hours," she said.

" It really can't take too much more at this stage. "

Development Watch community group member Brian Anker said the plan was a significant "deviation" from the original intent of it being an aviation precinct.

"It's totally out of kilter with the current look and feel of the area," he said.

An artist's impression of the Sunshine Coast Airport's planned Gateway Precinct, located around the existing terminal. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Airport)

Studies 'still being finalised'

Airport chief executive Chris Mills declined to be interviewed but said in a statement that the airport had submitted the draft plan to EDQ for "initial feedback".

"Key supporting studies, including detailed traffic and flood modelling, are still being finalised in consultation with council and public notification will not commence until this information is complete and available to the community," the statement said.

"We believe it is important that the community has access to the full suite of relevant information when being asked to consider the proposal."

Ms Chapman argued that residents needed to be aware of the plans early so they had time to prepare for the public consultation period.

"People will only get 20 working days so we need to make sure that we're on the front foot," she said.

" This is certainly the greatest call to action that we've had yet. "

World.title: Prime minister defends social media reforms amid US backlash
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has pushed back against the Trump administration's "censorship" criticism of Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, as the US President rejected a push from Australia and other countries to impose AI safeguards.

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Mr Trump announced his government would officially rebrand artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" and underscored his strong opposition to regulating AI.

Late yesterday, the US embassy made a rare submission on Australia's draft domestic laws, saying the reforms would amount to an "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech" and calling on Australia to exempt US social media companies from the legislation.

In New York, Mr Albanese was asked if the Trump administration's comments undermined his fight against global tech giants on the world stage.

"Not at all," he said.

"I'll always stand up for Australia's national interests, and the digital duty of care is something that we've foreshadowed for some period of time," he said, referring to the US embassy's intervention.

" It's not about government control, it's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices. "

The draft legislation would require the tech giants to pre-emptively address harms and pave the way for giving users a choice to opt in to or out of the algorithm.

He stressed the government would "engage constructively" before finalising the legislation.

"I hope the whole of parliament supports it. This should not be a partisan issue," he said.

Anthony Albanese has hit back at criticism of his proposed social media reforms. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

But Coalition frontbencher Andrew Bragg has echoed the US's censorship concerns.

"I think there is a risk of censorship. There is a risk of bestowing too much power onto unelected bureaucrats," he told ABC Radio National today.

The opposition has previously said the proposed changes would give a "blank cheque for political censorship" and warned they posed a threat to free speech.

US slams Australian digital care bill In an extremely uncommon move, the US government has publicly criticised an Australian government policy proposal.

Earlier, Mr Albanese spoke on the sidelines of the United Nations about protecting children in the age of AI.

In his address, he defended the proposed changes, saying this was an "inevitable next stage" the government had to take to protect people online.

"With misinformation, disinformation, with the increased polarisation that we're seeing as well in the political system, people are moving away from the centre and more and more to the extremes, be they of the left or the right," he said.

"And that is why we think that this is a very positive move that we are [putting] forward."

Trump dismisses calls for AI guardrails

On the eve of the UN General Assembly, Australia was one of 22 countries to issue an urgent plea for global guardrails to keep AI "under human control".

They warned "the pace of development [of AI] could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks" and efforts to ring-fence it were failing.

The statement came in the weeks after a trio of tech leaders — Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk — all backed a slowdown in the pace of AI development.

Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will meet later this week to discuss AI. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Mr Trump has previously described dire warnings about the safety of AI as a "hoax". The US and China are jostling for supremacy in the AI race.

In an extraordinary speech at the UN, Mr Trump conceded there was a need to "be careful", but rejected a proposal to impose safety guardrails.

The US "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now," he said.

Australian AI 'early warning system' Australian Signals Directorate director-general Abigail Bradshaw says the nation needs an AI "early warning system" to help defend against the increasingly powerful technology.

Mr Albanese was asked if he was disappointed about Mr Trump's remarks, and he didn't directly respond to a question about whether Australia would be adopting the term "super intelligence".

"We listened, and we participate respectfully," Mr Albanese said.

"We have put forward a strong position. I'm proud of what we have done on social media."

He said he looked forward to meeting Mr Trump at a reception imminently and engaging with him there.

Mr Albanese later posted a selfie of the catch-up, writing on social media: "Always good to catch up with @POTUS."

Mr Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due to meet this week at the White House for a highly anticipated discussion about AI safety and governance.

"We'll wait and see what comes out of the meeting between President Trump and President Xi," Mr Albanese said.

"It's good that they're meeting and it's good that this is on the agenda."

World.title: CFMEU has record of 'ostentatiously' defying law, royal commission hears
World.content:
Powerful construction union the CFMEU has been accused of "ostentatiously" defying the law on the first day of Victoria's royal commission into corruption the construction sector.

A hearing opened in the Melbourne Magistrates' Court today to outline the commission's terms of reference, and is expected to detail the next steps before witnesses are called at later hearings.

Former South Australian Supreme Court chief justice Christopher Kourakis is heading up the commission, which has a budget of $50 million.

Today he said the royal commission's most important duty was to recommend "legal, structural, industrial and cultural reforms" for the construction industry.

He vowed the commission would not be "just one more in an endless series of investigations into the integrity of the industry — that requires much more than removing today's bad actors from the stage and ensuring that they never return".

The Victorian branch of the CFMEU will be at the centre of investigations by the royal commission. (ABC News)

"I assure the people of Victoria, and warn all people who have done wrong, that the commission will leave no stone unturned in search for whatever is hidden — or whomever lurks underneath it," Mr Kourakis said.

" Anyone who has an ambition to remain in the industry will be better served by early, voluntary disclosures to the commission than by waiting to be found out. "

The royal commission is being headed by former Chief Justice of South Australia Chris Kourakis. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Associate to the commissioner Peter Tantalos earlier kicked off proceedings by reading out a long letters patent that established the inquiry and its scope.

Since at least 1980 there had been "persistent allegations of consistent and criminal conduct in connection with major public and civil infrastructure construction projects across Australia", he said.

Mr Tantalos the terms of reference included investigating "blackmail, bribery and dishonest, bullying, intimidatory, menacing, harassing, discriminatory, misogynistic, threatened or violent behaviour" on major public infrastructure projects in Victoria including those of the government's signature Big Build initiative.

The royal commission will also investigate circumstances where there had been a lack of adherence to proper process, improper influence, favouritism or nepotism, he said.

Assisting counsel Chris Young KC told the commission that allegations "about what was done and was not done" reached from sheds at worksites to union offices, boardrooms, government departments and ministerial offices.

"Corruption is often described as a crime without victims. That is not what we have been told," he said.

Mr Young gave several examples of incidents alleged to have occurred, including a small Indigenous-owned labour hire business who he said wrote to the minister and the premier in April 2022.

"They said they'd been threatened with violence and banned from sites on a state project. They said they had recordings. They asked for help," he said.

"It is reported that they got a reply a year later, which referred them elsewhere."

In another incident, a woman working in traffic management on a new public hospital said she was locked in a storeman by a man recently released from prison for stalking and threatening children, Mr Young said.

"She says he smoked ice and blew the smoke in her face," he said.

"She reported it. She says that what happened next was she lost her job."

Other workers reported they no longer had jobs on a state tunnel project because they belonged to the wrong union, Mr Young said.

The other member of the commission's senior legal team, Chris Carr CS, said that the CFMEU had a track record of "ostentatiously" defying the law.

Mr Carr said the commission would explore the accuracy of allegations against union bosses.

Assisting counsel Chris Carr SC addresses the first day of the royal commission into Victoria's major construction sector. (ABC News)

These included the threat of industrial action to force employers to pay extravagant wages to "unqualified associates of union bosses, often bikies, who had no particular skill or indeed interest in doing the work that they were being paid to do".

"The scale of the rorting alleged is indicated by the allegation that one bikie associate of a CFMEU boss — a man with no particular skills and a reputation for being work-why — earned more than $15,000 in a week for doing little more than attending a worksite," he said.

The royal commission's purpose was to rebuild trust in the integrity of Victoria's major construction sector, Mr Carr said.

"It requires a full accounting of the criminal conduct, the corruption, and the serious misconduct that occurred in connection with the Big Build," he said.

"This commission cannot and will not shirk the duty of identifying the responsible parties."

Trust could only be rebuilt by identifying measures that would prevent criminal conduct, corruption and serious misconduct happening again, he said.

'Anyone and everyone can be called'

Ben Carroll called the royal commission in his first act as premier in July, promising an exhaustive inquiry into the corruption allegations "as soon as possible".

He committed to the royal commission after toppling his predecessor Jacinta Allan, who had long refused to call an inquiry despite internal pressure.

The Victorian opposition has persistently criticised the terms of reference, saying they allowed former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan to avoid being hauled before the commission.

However, Mr Carroll rejected the suggestion Ms Allan or Mr Andrews would not be called, having confirmed that ministers and former premiers would be fair game under the terms.

Former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan may be called to appear before the commission. (AAP Image: Daniel Pockett)

"Anyone and everyone can be called," he said in August.

The royal commission comes after an explosive report into the CFMEU released by the Queensland Commission of Inquiry in February.

In it, author Geoffrey Watson SC alleged the Victorian branch of the CFMEU descended into a "violent, hateful and greedy rabble" under former boss John Setka.

Mr Watson estimated that the actions of the CFMEU had cost the Victorian taxpayer around $15 billion — a figure that was strongly disputed by Ms Allan at the time.

An explosive report by Geoffrey Watson SC estimated the actions of the Victorian branch of the CFMEU cost taxpayers $15 billion.

Mr Watson said the terms of reference for the royal commission were "really excellently done" and he dismissed criticism by the Victorian opposition.

"I think they're very well designed, quite targeted, and sufficiently specific," he said.

The commission is expected to report to the state government by August next year.

World.title: Alleged victim of ex-cop was ‘petrified’ before his death, court told
World.content:
A Sydney man allegedly murdered by former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon was “petrified” of the accused and kept repeating that “he has a gun”, a court has heard. Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, his former casual romantic partner, and Luke Davies, 29, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. His NSW Supreme Court criminal trial started in Sydney on Monday. Beau Lamarre-Condon (left) is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. Baird’s former long-term boyfriend, Corey-Dean Thorpe, testified on Thursday that Baird was “petrified” of the accused in the months before his death. “I’d never heard him so scared in his voice before,” Thorpe said through tears. “And he just kept repeating: ‘He has a gun.’”



Thorpe agreed Baird had told him the accused would take videos and photos of him and post them on Instagram to give the impression they were in a relationship while hiding the posts from Baird. Baird told him he was scared to go to the police because Lamarre-Condon was a police officer, he said. Thorpe agreed Baird had also told him Lamarre-Condon had driven past a cafe when he was having a coffee with another man and texted him: “I hope you’re enjoying that coffee with that guy.” ‘Obsessive and jealous infatuation’ The prosecution case is that Lamarre-Condon killed Baird after developing an “an obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him after their casual relationship, which started in late 2022, was ended by Baird in November 2023.



Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Alleged double murderer Lamarre-Condon acted in self-defence, court told The alleged murder was premeditated and followed a series of preparatory steps and escalating obsessive conduct, the Crown alleges. It alleges Lamarre-Condon spontaneously killed Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime. The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon acted in self-defence after entering Baird’s Paddington home disguised as an Uber Eats rider, including a motorcycle helmet and high-visibility top, to retrieve some of his belongings. He had his police gun with him, the defence says, because “his training was that he was not allowed to leave a gun unminded in a car where it might be stolen”. The Crown case is that he was not rostered to work and should not have had his weapon with him. The defence says Lamarre-Condon was “surprised by” Baird inside the home and a struggle ensued because, “understandably, [Baird] did not recognise him because he was still wearing the motorcycle helmet”. His gun went off twice in the struggle and fatally wounded Baird, the defence says.



Davies died in a later struggle after he grabbed the weapon and accidentally shot himself, the defence claims. Lamarre-Condon had grabbed Davies by the arm and pushed the gun away from himself and towards Davies, according to the defence. The alleged break-in In a statement to police on August 17, 2023, Baird told police he woke up at about 11.47pm “because I sensed that somebody had entered my room”. He saw “a male standing over my bed” who “appeared to have my phone in his hand”, he said in the statement. Baird said he chased the man, clad in black clothing including a puffer jacket, but lost sight of him in the street. When he returned home he noticed his phone and wallet had been taken, he said. Baird had broken up with Lamarre-Condon in April, the court has heard, and they reunited only briefly late that year before Baird permanently ended the relationship in November.



A police officer who investigated the alleged break-in told the court he found a bobby pin in the lock of the front door of the home. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to aggravated break and enter over the alleged incident. His defence barrister, John Stratton, SC, said in his opening address to the court on Tuesday that the accused entered the home using a key that Baird had given him. ‘The real deal’ On Wednesday, Matthew Edwards, a close friend of Jesse Baird, said Baird had described the accused to him as “a friend and nothing more”. The court has heard Baird was on the cusp of moving out of his Paddington share house at the time of his death.



Edwards said that Baird told him on February 3, weeks before he died, that “once I move house this will be the last piece of me that Beau knows”. He agreed Baird had told him that in the past, he would wake up and find Lamarre-Condon going through his phone. In their last phone call on February 18, the day before Baird died, Edwards said Baird told him that he and Luke Davies were a confirmed couple. Edwards gave emotional evidence that he had “never seen Jesse as happy” as when he was with Davies, and he “just lit Jesse up”. “They were the real deal,” Edwards said, with tears in his eyes. The trial continues.

World.title: Warren Buffett just took a big risk with the $1.5 trillion giant he built
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesExecutive shake-up Opinion Warren Buffett just took a big risk with the $1.5 trillion giant he built Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 23, 2026 — 11:59am

September 23, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last week, Berkshire Hathaway announced that Warren Buffett’s son, Howard, would replace him as chairman of the sprawling conglomerate. There was no outcry. At face value, Howard, 71, has no obvious qualifications to be appointed chairman of a venerated $US1.08 trillion ($1.5 trillion) company, other than that he is the founder’s son. Warren Buffett with son Howard G. Buffett and grandson Howard W. Buffett. NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Howard is a farmer, on properties whose purchase was funded by his father. He is a philanthropist, deploying funds provided by his father. He’s not a college graduate and has little experience, if any, in operational management or asset management. He has been on the boards of a number of major public companies – including Coca-Cola and Conagra – but it is a reasonable question to pose whether he would have been appointed had Warren not been his father.



Related Article Updated

Warren Buffett Warren Buffett, 96, steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman Yet, there was no outcry in response to what would appear to be a clear case of nepotism. Even the proxy advisers, guardians of good corporate governance, seem to have fallen into line. That may be because Warren’s succession plan has been a long time in the making, having been flagged at least as far back as 2000, when Warren told the Wall Street Journal that Howard would eventually succeed him as chairman, citing his business acumen and Warren’s desire to maintain Berkshire’s culture. It didn’t come as a surprise. It might also, of course, because it is Warren’s plan and Berkshire shareholders, and the market-at-large, trust his judgement when it comes to the company that has always been built around Warren’s personal convictions and philosophies – and his success and folksy charisma – since he acquired an ailing textile company in 1965, built it into the world’s most revered investment conglomerate and became a cult figure to generations of investors and investment managers. Howard’s main qualification as the incoming chairman, apart from being Warren’s son, is that he has been on the Berkshire board for 33 years.



“This is a longer apprenticeship than I served before taking the reins at the age of 34,” Warren, 96, wrote in a letter to shareholders last Friday. Greg Abel, who succeeded Warren as chief executive in January last year, “runs the company,” Warren said. Buffett’s successor as Berkshire Hathaway CEO Greg Abel will be left to making the calls on acquisitions, investments or divestments. Getty “Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet. Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against.” The demarcation of responsibilities is clear. Howard won’t be making the calls on acquisitions, investments or divestments, those will be Abel’s responsibilities.



When Warren referred to culture and values, he was talking about something more than the way authority has historically been delegated to operational managers, or his focus on the long term, shareholder-first approach to investment and the deep personal engagement he developed with his shareholder base. He made it clear in an interview last year that his greatest fear for the future of the group he built was that the unusual mix of financial and industrial operations, its $US350 billion portfolio of listed investments and a similar level of cash holdings would lead to calls for it to be broken up. Related Article Opinion

Billionaires The end of a dynamic duo: How Charlie Munger shaped Warren Buffett’s success Elizabeth Knight Business columnist During Buffett’s era at the helm, Berkshire has had lengthy periods where it has done little but sit on its hoards of cash, underperforming the markets and increasing the apparent appeal of a break-up. It has been going through one of those periods in recent years, where Buffet sees little value, the cash piles up and Berkshire underperforms the market. Berkshire has underperformed the S&P 500 over the past decade, as the technology stocks that Warren historically avoided have increasingly driven the market.



“I care more about the future of Berkshire after I die than during the period I’m alive. It’s my creation,” he told the Wall Street Journal. “What I want is a company that’s successful and also embodies a company that belongs to shareholders. “That is something that takes a long time to build and could be torn apart quite easily if it fell into the hands of people who would want to break it up.” Buffett turned Berkshire Hathaway into an investing colossus. Bloomberg Berkshire’s new structure is not unique. Other large companies in the US have long had family members succeeding each other as chairs, overseeing the professional managers who actually run the companies. Ford, Walmart, Estée Lauder, Comcast and Fox and News Corps, where Lachlan Murdoch chairs both, spring to mind.



Howard, however – unlike some of those dynastic groups, including Fox and News, where Lachlan is executive chair – will be a non-executive chair. He will be the guardian of Berkshire’s structure and values, charged with protecting and preserving what his father created while Abel, as long as he doesn’t try to cross Warren’s no-go zones, will be left largely free to decide the future nature and shape of Berkshire’s asset base. So far, the market has absorbed the news of Howard’s elevation – and Warren’s to “chairman emeritus” – quite comfortably. Its shares are down about 0.1 per cent. There was no outcry in response to what would appear to be a clear case of nepotism. Even the proxy advisers, guardians of good corporate governance, seem to have fallen into line. There was a far bigger reaction when Warren announced he was stepping down as CEO in May last year, from which the shares have yet to recover. The A-class voting shares have fallen more than 6 per cent since that moment, while the S&P 500 has climbed more than 36 per cent.



Whether Howard can deliver on his father’s expectations of maintaining the group’s culture and structure will hinge on Abel’s ability to generate some share price momentum, which given Berkshire’s sheer size – there are few transactions that could move the dial for shareholder returns – won’t be easy. Related Article Updated

Billionaires ‘Distasteful’: Warren Buffett opens up on Bill Gates’ ties to Epstein The market won’t extend the same trust and tolerance for periods of under-performance to Abel and Howard that it has for Warren, with the spectre of pressure for a break-up likely to remain a continuing threat to his legacy. The family currently has an economic interest of about 13 per cent in Berkshire’s shares but, thanks to a capital base dominated by shares with reduced voting rights, has about 30 per cent of the votes. Over time, once Warren is no longer around, that could reduce as those shares are progressively distributed to the individual charitable trusts that Howard and other family members run.



Warren will remain a board member despite vacating the chair, but in future it will be Howard and, more particularly, Abel, as the drivers and faces of the company. They couldn’t have a more daunting act to follow. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ‘A thousand bucks for smear story’: Cash offered for negative Elliott coverage
World.content:
Follow our live coverage The former lawyer for disgraced developer Jean Nassif offered $1000 to a Liberal lobbyist to get a story into the media alleging then-police minister David Elliott breached COVID restrictions because he was having an affair. Sharangan Maheswaran, Nassif’s one-time lawyer and a former Labor councillor, offered the payment to lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood if he could convince a reporter to write a damaging story about Elliott having an affair. Sharangan Maheswaran is continuing his evidence at the ICAC on Wednesday. Sitthixay Ditthavong There is no suggestion the allegations are true, and Elliott has always denied any wrongdoing.



The Independent Commission Against Corruption is investigating whether Nassif wanted to damage the political career of Elliott, who was a long-time enemy of the disgraced developer. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Former Toplace lawyer, Strathfield councillor Sharangan Maheswaran to continue evidence The commission on Wednesday continued hearing evidence from Maheswaran, who is also a person of interest in the public inquiry codenamed Operation Rosny. Maheswaran is accused of blackmailing former Strathfield mayor Matthew Blackmore and illegally recording his fellow councillor. The corruption inquiry on Wednesday was told about a text exchange between Maheswaran and Greenwood after the Toplace lawyer sent a picture of a car, taken during surveillance of Elliott. Maheswaran told the commission he asked an investigator, known as Mr Nanetti, to do some basic surveillance on Elliott before personally paying Nanetti about $1000 to return to Elliott’s street to take photographs.



The lawyer then wanted to convince News Ltd journalists to write a story claiming Elliott was breaching COVID rules because he was in the company of a woman who was not his wife. Maheswaran told Greenwood: “A thousand bucks if you can get the yarn up”. Greenwood responded with “hahaha”. Maheswaran replied: “Not joking”. Maheswaran told the inquiry it was not a serious offer. Maheswaran also provided a brief to private investigator Shane De Kauwe naming Elliott as the principal target, and listed information about Elliott’s sons, wife and chief of staff, and a number of Hills Shire councillors. “It must have occurred to you that Mr Nassif was developing some conspiracy theories about why his developments were being blocked, rather than just actually looking at the genuine problems that were there with his developments,” counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, asked.



Maheswaran told the inquiry Nassif had considered launching defamation action against an individual who was making negative comments about his developments, and “he wished to see if there was some improper purpose or politically motivated purpose in the comments that were being made”. Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny Spy pens, eggs on toast and a side of alleged corruption: PI spills the beans to ICAC The commission has heard evidence Maheswaran and Jeremy Greenwood had ongoing discussions about getting a journalist to publish a negative story about Elliott supposedly breaching COVID restrictions but struggled to convince a reporter to run the unsubstantiated claims. “So you’re persistent about that story, weren’t you, because you knew that that was one of the outcomes that would please Jean Nassif, whether he was actively seeking it or not?” Dwyer asked. Maheswaran responded: “No, I have a decade of track record pitching stories that are adverse to Liberal National MPs, ministers, and, frankly, that’s something that I would do from time to time, if it came to my attention.”



Earlier, Dwyer told the commission former Wollondilly MP Nathaniel Smith had been called for a private examination after the inquiry had heard evidence Charles Perrottet possessed some audio recordings of Elliott. Those recordings had been referred to as “covert recordings”. However, after questioning Smith, Dwyer said the recordings were determined to be pocket dial voicemails, inadvertently left by Elliott on Smith’s phone. Smith then passed on those voicemails to Charles Perrottet. Dwyer told the commission that ICAC staff had amended previous transcripts to correct those references to covert recordings.
