World.title: Dylan Lucas on his miracle comeback and how he became an NRL star
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Dylan Lucas on his miracle comeback and how he became an NRL star Adrian Proszenko September 23, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Star Newcastle forward Dylan Lucas has paid tribute to his late coach Scott Dureau for helping to kickstart his career after he was unwanted at the Dragons. Lucas made a shock return in last weekend’s elimination final win over the Warriors in Auckland, from what was initially thought to be a season-ending fractured and dislocated ankle suffered in round 21 against the Roosters. Knights backrower Dylan Lucas in action against the Warriors, completing a remarkable return from a fractured ankle. Getty Images It caps a stunning season for Lucas, who will play in his side’s preliminary final against Penrith on Sunday. The 26-year-old also made his Origin debut for NSW this year. However, his footballing prospects weren’t always so bright. The Albion Park Eagles junior came through the Illawarra Steelers system, but as a five-eighth he wasn’t deemed a Dragons NRL prospect.



“When I was down there at the Steelers, they just weren’t that keen on me,” Lucas said. Undeterred, he shifted to Newcastle to chase his dream, where Dureau was one of his first coaches. Dureau was a former Knight, filling the famous No.7 jersey after the retirement of Andrew Johns. Dylan Lucas after suffering his ankle injury in July. Getty Images When his playing career finished - he made 42 first-grade appearances for Newcastle and 97 for the Catalans Dragons in the Super League - Dureau returned to the Hunter in coaching/development roles. For 13 years, Dureau struggled with cancer, succumbing in July at the age of 39. A respected member of the Newcastle community, Dureau first crossed paths with Lucas at Jersey Flegg level.



Scott Dureau during his playing days with Newcastle. Getty “Scotty was one of my first coaches when I got here in the under-20s,” Lucas said. “He had an impact on my time here, and then he was with the full-time squad when I first started training full-time as well. Scotty was a great man, and he had a fair bit to do with me when I first got here. Then I had a year at South Newcastle as well, which was a club that he was involved with.” Lucas began his career as a five-eighth, but Dureau felt his physique and skill-set would be better served elsewhere. “He sort of said ‘You’ve got a pretty good running game, I wouldn’t mind seeing you play in the centres’,” said Lucas, who then transitioned into a back-rower.



“He gave me that opportunity and then everything sort of flowed on from there. I’m very grateful for the impact that Scotty had on my career. “He’s probably right up there [with the biggest influence on my football]. He was here when I first got here, and I was just a young kid who took a chance coming up here. He had that belief in me and gave me my opportunity to give myself a chance. Scotty had a big impact on me.” Loading Asked what Dureau would make of Lucas’ and the Knights’ success, the forward said: “I’m sure he’d be up there smiling. I know how much the Knights meant to him, I’m sure he’d be very proud.” Lucas refused to give up on a shock comeback, despite the severity of his injury, and played 14 minutes off the bench against the Warriors.



“I just wanted to give myself every chance,” Lucas, who made his NRL debut for the Knights in 2023, said. “These opportunities don’t come around very often. So when they’re here, you want to be a part of it. “My injury just took a turn for the better around that six-week mark, and then I had my scan and it looked really good. So I just thought, ‘I’ll push the boundaries here and see where it gets me.’ … I worked really hard to get back, and it’s a credit to our medical staff and our physios.” It has been a rollercoaster season for Lucas, who also had to deal with the high of making his NSW debut for Origin II - and the low of being dropped for the decider. Knights backrower Dylan Lucas in Newcastle on Wednesday. Dean Sewell “I’m very grateful for that whole Origin opportunity and that campaign,” he said. “Obviously, the result didn’t go my way, but to get into that arena is not only an accomplishment for yourself, but it’s for your family as well. I know my family were very proud, and to be able to have my last name on my back there at the MCG is something that I’ll never forget.



“It definitely makes you hungrier being left out of the side. Obviously, no one likes being dropped, but that’s the way they wanted to go and they got the result done. I’m so happy that we won the series. So yeah, I took a lot of learnings out of it, and I’ll be better from it.”

World.title: ‘Too little, too late’: Data centre buffer carve-out leaves some residents vulnerable
World.content:
Buffer zones to keep data centres at least 150 metres from homes have arrived too late to stop three so-called hyper-scale projects in Melbourne’s west, exempting developers who lodged plans before Labor tightened the rules. Premier Ben Carroll revealed on Tuesday Labor’s policy to ban data centres near homes, while also introducing new power, water and community investment standards for developers. NextDC’s West Footscray data centre. New rules to stop data centres being built closer than 150 metres from homes won’t affect the project’s coming stages. Joe Armao But the changes will not be retrospective. Projects already under way or which have lodged planning applications will be unaffected by them – including a data centre about 60 metres from homes. Projects yet to be approved must still be approved under existing planning rules. At least three proposed data centre projects will breach the government’s 150-metre buffer, in communities which have protested against the AI infrastructure and raised concerns about noise, pollution and other impacts.



The Department of Planning and Transport is accepting public submissions over an application by Australian data centre giant NextDC to expand its West Footscray facility, with more computing infrastructure to be built adjacent to homes. The land the data centre sits on, zoned industrial and adjacent to a residential zone, once had small factories and warehouses on it. Developer GreenSquare has also lodged an application to build a data centre in Spotswood which would breach the government’s 150-metre buffer – even though it is proposed for badly contaminated land that once housed Mobil’s fuel storage tanks. The site of the proposed GreenSquare data centre in Spotswood was once Mobil’s main Melbourne fuel terminal. Joe Armao A planning report for the project notes that houses are “more than 60 metres away and separated by the [Werribee] railway corridor, ensuring that the development will not result in unacceptable amenity impacts”. Resident Jacqui Glover’s property boundary in West Footscray is just 15 metres from the edge of the sprawling NextDC data centre, which began construction in 2021 after initial approval by Maribyrnong City Council. The data centre will eventually fill almost the entire 10-hectare block.



Glover said while she welcomed the new rules, “it’s too little, too late for us in Tottenham and West Footscray”. Another planned data centre, on land owned by the Scalzo family that sits just 200 metres to the east of the NextDC campus, was approved by the state government last year. It too faces onto housing in the same street as Glover, but will also be unaffected by the new rules. Jacqui Glover, pictured in February, says the changes are too little, too late for people like her. Justin McManus “If Labor genuinely believes in these proposed guidelines they should be applied to every data centre development,” Glover said. She said the 150-metre rule would not help when data centres ran their back-up generators, which generally run off diesel fuel stored on site. “Diesel emissions aren’t going to just stop 150 metres away from homes.”



Related Article AI Buffer zones, drinking water bans: Carroll eyes new rules for data centres The premier said the changes would prevent suburban streets being transformed by multi-level data centres, while also allowing Victoria to capitalise on the economic benefits brought by AI’s rapid expansion. Asked if the changes were coming too late to protect neighbourhood character, Carroll said no. “I am a premier that gives certainty to industry. So applications that were made under the old rules will proceed.” The government intends to strengthen the regulations before it enters caretaker mode from November 3 in the lead-up to the state election, but Carroll could not offer certainty that the changes would be locked in by then.



The new requirements, outlined in Labor’s Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan, will also enforce guidelines for water and energy use and air and noise pollution. They come as global tensions over AI increase. Industry chiefs and world leaders have warned that the technology’s growth may outpace governments’ ability to regulate it, and that it could cause human extinction. At the United Nations this week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese signed a joint declaration calling for international oversight of AI models. On Wednesday, a federal inquiry into the technology will hold its first public hearings in Melbourne. CDC Data Centres welcomed on Tuesday the state government’s plan, and chief executive Greg Boorer said clear guidelines would help comfort investors considering making funding decisions. He said discussions about data centres were no longer just about planning but were “fundamentally a conversation about Australia’s digital future and the infrastructure required to support it”.



CDC Data Centres chief executive Greg Boorer. Alex Ellinghausen “As one of Australia’s most important data centre regions, the policy settings adopted by Victoria have an important role to play in supporting investment, innovation and Australia’s long-term digital capability,” Boorer said. “Communities want confidence that the organisations developing and operating critical infrastructure are responsible contributors to the places where they invest.” But Data Centres Australia, an advocacy group representing developers, technology companies and other related businesses, criticised the decision to include 150-metre buffer zones. Chief executive Belinda Dennett said operators already supported most aspects of the government’s rules, but the setback requirements would hurt projects where investments had already been committed.



“It is disappointing to see Victoria, the state that recognised the economic opportunity to attract data centre investment and proudly declared its ambition to be a global data centre leader, now move to impose requirements on data centres that apply to no comparable industrial use,” she said. Dennett said data centres were already restricted to industrial land, and individual projects had to go through environment and planning approvals. She said the 150-metre setback added a restriction that warehouses and logistics hubs did not have to meet, and that industrial land was already scarce. “It can render an otherwise suitable site unviable,” Dennett said. She also said the government’s faster approval process, the Development Facilitation Program, had recently not been making decisions on applications under the government’s old rules, leading to a “de facto freeze” that would force developers to spend elsewhere.



Artificial Intelligence Minister Anthony Carbines said setting clear regulations would give businesses certainty and Victoria a competitive edge over other states. Related Series

Data centres The cost of the cloud: Inside Australia’s data centre boom But Liberal frontbencher James Newbury said Carroll could not be trusted to regulate data centres, pointing to the suburban projects which ignited community protest. “Every Victorian can look on and see the track record of what they’ve allowed and the places they’ve allowed it to be built, and feel unfortunately certain that that would continue under a Labor government,” he said. The Greens said the government’s policy was a major retreat that had come after pressure from communities. But the party’s data centres spokeswoman, Sarah Mansfield, said noise could still be experienced from beyond 150 metres, and called on Labor to show the modelling for why that distance was chosen.



“There’s also a glaring hole in this announcement: what happens to the people already living next to these massive data centres?” she said. “Labor can’t admit these facilities need a buffer and then abandon the residents already living inside it. Big tech should pay to compensate those communities.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

In their last phone call on February 18, the day before Baird died, Edwards said Baird told him that he and Luke Davies were a confirmed couple. Edwards gave emotional evidence that he had “never seen Jesse as happy” as when he was with Davies, and he “just lit Jesse up”. “They were the real deal,” Edwards said, with tears in his eyes. The trial continues.

World.title: Warren Buffett just took a big risk with the $1.5 trillion giant he built
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesExecutive shake-up Opinion Warren Buffett just took a big risk with the $1.5 trillion giant he built Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 23, 2026 — 11:59am

September 23, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last week, Berkshire Hathaway announced that Warren Buffett’s son, Howard, would replace him as chairman of the sprawling conglomerate. There was no outcry. At face value, Howard, 71, has no obvious qualifications to be appointed chairman of a venerated $US1.08 trillion ($1.5 trillion) company, other than that he is the founder’s son. Warren Buffett with son Howard G. Buffett and grandson Howard W. Buffett. NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Howard is a farmer, on properties whose purchase was funded by his father. He is a philanthropist, deploying funds provided by his father. He’s not a college graduate and has little experience, if any, in operational management or asset management. He has been on the boards of a number of major public companies – including Coca-Cola and Conagra – but it is a reasonable question to pose whether he would have been appointed had Warren not been his father.



Related Article Updated

Warren Buffett Warren Buffett, 96, steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman Yet, there was no outcry in response to what would appear to be a clear case of nepotism. Even the proxy advisers, guardians of good corporate governance, seem to have fallen into line. That may be because Warren’s succession plan has been a long time in the making, having been flagged at least as far back as 2000, when Warren told the Wall Street Journal that Howard would eventually succeed him as chairman, citing his business acumen and Warren’s desire to maintain Berkshire’s culture. It didn’t come as a surprise. It might also, of course, because it is Warren’s plan and Berkshire shareholders, and the market-at-large, trust his judgement when it comes to the company that has always been built around Warren’s personal convictions and philosophies – and his success and folksy charisma – since he acquired an ailing textile company in 1965, built it into the world’s most revered investment conglomerate and became a cult figure to generations of investors and investment managers. Howard’s main qualification as the incoming chairman, apart from being Warren’s son, is that he has been on the Berkshire board for 33 years.



“This is a longer apprenticeship than I served before taking the reins at the age of 34,” Warren, 96, wrote in a letter to shareholders last Friday. Greg Abel, who succeeded Warren as chief executive in January last year, “runs the company,” Warren said. Buffett’s successor as Berkshire Hathaway CEO Greg Abel will be left to making the calls on acquisitions, investments or divestments. Getty “Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet. Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against.” The demarcation of responsibilities is clear. Howard won’t be making the calls on acquisitions, investments or divestments, those will be Abel’s responsibilities.



When Warren referred to culture and values, he was talking about something more than the way authority has historically been delegated to operational managers, or his focus on the long term, shareholder-first approach to investment and the deep personal engagement he developed with his shareholder base. He made it clear in an interview last year that his greatest fear for the future of the group he built was that the unusual mix of financial and industrial operations, its $US350 billion portfolio of listed investments and a similar level of cash holdings would lead to calls for it to be broken up. Related Article Opinion

Billionaires The end of a dynamic duo: How Charlie Munger shaped Warren Buffett’s success Elizabeth Knight Business columnist During Buffett’s era at the helm, Berkshire has had lengthy periods where it has done little but sit on its hoards of cash, underperforming the markets and increasing the apparent appeal of a break-up. It has been going through one of those periods in recent years, where Buffet sees little value, the cash piles up and Berkshire underperforms the market. Berkshire has underperformed the S&P 500 over the past decade, as the technology stocks that Warren historically avoided have increasingly driven the market.



“I care more about the future of Berkshire after I die than during the period I’m alive. It’s my creation,” he told the Wall Street Journal. “What I want is a company that’s successful and also embodies a company that belongs to shareholders. “That is something that takes a long time to build and could be torn apart quite easily if it fell into the hands of people who would want to break it up.” Buffett turned Berkshire Hathaway into an investing colossus. Bloomberg Berkshire’s new structure is not unique. Other large companies in the US have long had family members succeeding each other as chairs, overseeing the professional managers who actually run the companies. Ford, Walmart, Estée Lauder, Comcast and Fox and News Corps, where Lachlan Murdoch chairs both, spring to mind.



Howard, however – unlike some of those dynastic groups, including Fox and News, where Lachlan is executive chair – will be a non-executive chair. He will be the guardian of Berkshire’s structure and values, charged with protecting and preserving what his father created while Abel, as long as he doesn’t try to cross Warren’s no-go zones, will be left largely free to decide the future nature and shape of Berkshire’s asset base. So far, the market has absorbed the news of Howard’s elevation – and Warren’s to “chairman emeritus” – quite comfortably. Its shares are down about 0.1 per cent. There was no outcry in response to what would appear to be a clear case of nepotism. Even the proxy advisers, guardians of good corporate governance, seem to have fallen into line. There was a far bigger reaction when Warren announced he was stepping down as CEO in May last year, from which the shares have yet to recover. The A-class voting shares have fallen more than 6 per cent since that moment, while the S&P 500 has climbed more than 36 per cent.



Whether Howard can deliver on his father’s expectations of maintaining the group’s culture and structure will hinge on Abel’s ability to generate some share price momentum, which given Berkshire’s sheer size – there are few transactions that could move the dial for shareholder returns – won’t be easy. Related Article Updated

Billionaires ‘Distasteful’: Warren Buffett opens up on Bill Gates’ ties to Epstein The market won’t extend the same trust and tolerance for periods of under-performance to Abel and Howard that it has for Warren, with the spectre of pressure for a break-up likely to remain a continuing threat to his legacy. The family currently has an economic interest of about 13 per cent in Berkshire’s shares but, thanks to a capital base dominated by shares with reduced voting rights, has about 30 per cent of the votes. Over time, once Warren is no longer around, that could reduce as those shares are progressively distributed to the individual charitable trusts that Howard and other family members run.



Warren will remain a board member despite vacating the chair, but in future it will be Howard and, more particularly, Abel, as the drivers and faces of the company. They couldn’t have a more daunting act to follow. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ‘A thousand bucks for smear story’: Cash offered for negative Elliott coverage
World.content:
Follow our live coverage The former lawyer for disgraced developer Jean Nassif offered $1000 to a Liberal lobbyist to get a story into the media alleging then-police minister David Elliott breached COVID restrictions because he was having an affair. Sharangan Maheswaran, Nassif’s one-time lawyer and a former Labor councillor, offered the payment to lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood if he could convince a reporter to write a damaging story about Elliott having an affair. Sharangan Maheswaran is continuing his evidence at the ICAC on Wednesday. Sitthixay Ditthavong There is no suggestion the allegations are true, and Elliott has always denied any wrongdoing.



The Independent Commission Against Corruption is investigating whether Nassif wanted to damage the political career of Elliott, who was a long-time enemy of the disgraced developer. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Former Toplace lawyer, Strathfield councillor Sharangan Maheswaran to continue evidence The commission on Wednesday continued hearing evidence from Maheswaran, who is also a person of interest in the public inquiry codenamed Operation Rosny. Maheswaran is accused of blackmailing former Strathfield mayor Matthew Blackmore and illegally recording his fellow councillor. The corruption inquiry on Wednesday was told about a text exchange between Maheswaran and Greenwood after the Toplace lawyer sent a picture of a car, taken during surveillance of Elliott. Maheswaran told the commission he asked an investigator, known as Mr Nanetti, to do some basic surveillance on Elliott before personally paying Nanetti about $1000 to return to Elliott’s street to take photographs.



The lawyer then wanted to convince News Ltd journalists to write a story claiming Elliott was breaching COVID rules because he was in the company of a woman who was not his wife. Maheswaran told Greenwood: “A thousand bucks if you can get the yarn up”. Greenwood responded with “hahaha”. Maheswaran replied: “Not joking”. Maheswaran told the inquiry it was not a serious offer. Maheswaran also provided a brief to private investigator Shane De Kauwe naming Elliott as the principal target, and listed information about Elliott’s sons, wife and chief of staff, and a number of Hills Shire councillors. “It must have occurred to you that Mr Nassif was developing some conspiracy theories about why his developments were being blocked, rather than just actually looking at the genuine problems that were there with his developments,” counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, asked.



Maheswaran told the inquiry Nassif had considered launching defamation action against an individual who was making negative comments about his developments, and “he wished to see if there was some improper purpose or politically motivated purpose in the comments that were being made”. Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny Spy pens, eggs on toast and a side of alleged corruption: PI spills the beans to ICAC The commission has heard evidence Maheswaran and Jeremy Greenwood had ongoing discussions about getting a journalist to publish a negative story about Elliott supposedly breaching COVID restrictions but struggled to convince a reporter to run the unsubstantiated claims. “So you’re persistent about that story, weren’t you, because you knew that that was one of the outcomes that would please Jean Nassif, whether he was actively seeking it or not?” Dwyer asked. Maheswaran responded: “No, I have a decade of track record pitching stories that are adverse to Liberal National MPs, ministers, and, frankly, that’s something that I would do from time to time, if it came to my attention.”



Earlier, Dwyer told the commission former Wollondilly MP Nathaniel Smith had been called for a private examination after the inquiry had heard evidence Charles Perrottet possessed some audio recordings of Elliott. Those recordings had been referred to as “covert recordings”. However, after questioning Smith, Dwyer said the recordings were determined to be pocket dial voicemails, inadvertently left by Elliott on Smith’s phone. Smith then passed on those voicemails to Charles Perrottet. Dwyer told the commission that ICAC staff had amended previous transcripts to correct those references to covert recordings. World.title: Dylan Lucas on his miracle comeback and how he became an NRL star
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Dylan Lucas on his miracle comeback and how he became an NRL star Adrian Proszenko September 23, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Star Newcastle forward Dylan Lucas has paid tribute to his late coach Scott Dureau for helping to kickstart his career after he was unwanted at the Dragons. Lucas made a shock return in last weekend’s elimination final win over the Warriors in Auckland, from what was initially thought to be a season-ending fractured and dislocated ankle suffered in round 21 against the Roosters. Knights backrower Dylan Lucas in action against the Warriors, completing a remarkable return from a fractured ankle. Getty Images It caps a stunning season for Lucas, who will play in his side’s preliminary final against Penrith on Sunday. The 26-year-old also made his Origin debut for NSW this year. However, his footballing prospects weren’t always so bright. The Albion Park Eagles junior came through the Illawarra Steelers system, but as a five-eighth he wasn’t deemed a Dragons NRL prospect.



“When I was down there at the Steelers, they just weren’t that keen on me,” Lucas said. Undeterred, he shifted to Newcastle to chase his dream, where Dureau was one of his first coaches. Dureau was a former Knight, filling the famous No.7 jersey after the retirement of Andrew Johns. Dylan Lucas after suffering his ankle injury in July. Getty Images When his playing career finished - he made 42 first-grade appearances for Newcastle and 97 for the Catalans Dragons in the Super League - Dureau returned to the Hunter in coaching/development roles. For 13 years, Dureau struggled with cancer, succumbing in July at the age of 39. A respected member of the Newcastle community, Dureau first crossed paths with Lucas at Jersey Flegg level.



Scott Dureau during his playing days with Newcastle. Getty “Scotty was one of my first coaches when I got here in the under-20s,” Lucas said. “He had an impact on my time here, and then he was with the full-time squad when I first started training full-time as well. Scotty was a great man, and he had a fair bit to do with me when I first got here. Then I had a year at South Newcastle as well, which was a club that he was involved with.” Lucas began his career as a five-eighth, but Dureau felt his physique and skill-set would be better served elsewhere. “He sort of said ‘You’ve got a pretty good running game, I wouldn’t mind seeing you play in the centres’,” said Lucas, who then transitioned into a back-rower.



“He gave me that opportunity and then everything sort of flowed on from there. I’m very grateful for the impact that Scotty had on my career. “He’s probably right up there [with the biggest influence on my football]. He was here when I first got here, and I was just a young kid who took a chance coming up here. He had that belief in me and gave me my opportunity to give myself a chance. Scotty had a big impact on me.” Loading Asked what Dureau would make of Lucas’ and the Knights’ success, the forward said: “I’m sure he’d be up there smiling. I know how much the Knights meant to him, I’m sure he’d be very proud.” Lucas refused to give up on a shock comeback, despite the severity of his injury, and played 14 minutes off the bench against the Warriors.



“I just wanted to give myself every chance,” Lucas, who made his NRL debut for the Knights in 2023, said. “These opportunities don’t come around very often. So when they’re here, you want to be a part of it. “My injury just took a turn for the better around that six-week mark, and then I had my scan and it looked really good. So I just thought, ‘I’ll push the boundaries here and see where it gets me.’ … I worked really hard to get back, and it’s a credit to our medical staff and our physios.” It has been a rollercoaster season for Lucas, who also had to deal with the high of making his NSW debut for Origin II - and the low of being dropped for the decider. Knights backrower Dylan Lucas in Newcastle on Wednesday. Dean Sewell “I’m very grateful for that whole Origin opportunity and that campaign,” he said. “Obviously, the result didn’t go my way, but to get into that arena is not only an accomplishment for yourself, but it’s for your family as well. I know my family were very proud, and to be able to have my last name on my back there at the MCG is something that I’ll never forget.



“It definitely makes you hungrier being left out of the side. Obviously, no one likes being dropped, but that’s the way they wanted to go and they got the result done. I’m so happy that we won the series. So yeah, I took a lot of learnings out of it, and I’ll be better from it.”

World.title: ‘Too little, too late’: Data centre buffer carve-out leaves some residents vulnerable
World.content:
Buffer zones to keep data centres at least 150 metres from homes have arrived too late to stop three so-called hyper-scale projects in Melbourne’s west, exempting developers who lodged plans before Labor tightened the rules. Premier Ben Carroll revealed on Tuesday Labor’s policy to ban data centres near homes, while also introducing new power, water and community investment standards for developers. NextDC’s West Footscray data centre. New rules to stop data centres being built closer than 150 metres from homes won’t affect the project’s coming stages. Joe Armao But the changes will not be retrospective. Projects already under way or which have lodged planning applications will be unaffected by them – including a data centre about 60 metres from homes. Projects yet to be approved must still be approved under existing planning rules. At least three proposed data centre projects will breach the government’s 150-metre buffer, in communities which have protested against the AI infrastructure and raised concerns about noise, pollution and other impacts.



The Department of Planning and Transport is accepting public submissions over an application by Australian data centre giant NextDC to expand its West Footscray facility, with more computing infrastructure to be built adjacent to homes. The land the data centre sits on, zoned industrial and adjacent to a residential zone, once had small factories and warehouses on it. Developer GreenSquare has also lodged an application to build a data centre in Spotswood which would breach the government’s 150-metre buffer – even though it is proposed for badly contaminated land that once housed Mobil’s fuel storage tanks. The site of the proposed GreenSquare data centre in Spotswood was once Mobil’s main Melbourne fuel terminal. Joe Armao A planning report for the project notes that houses are “more than 60 metres away and separated by the [Werribee] railway corridor, ensuring that the development will not result in unacceptable amenity impacts”. Resident Jacqui Glover’s property boundary in West Footscray is just 15 metres from the edge of the sprawling NextDC data centre, which began construction in 2021 after initial approval by Maribyrnong City Council. The data centre will eventually fill almost the entire 10-hectare block.



Glover said while she welcomed the new rules, “it’s too little, too late for us in Tottenham and West Footscray”. Another planned data centre, on land owned by the Scalzo family that sits just 200 metres to the east of the NextDC campus, was approved by the state government last year. It too faces onto housing in the same street as Glover, but will also be unaffected by the new rules. Jacqui Glover, pictured in February, says the changes are too little, too late for people like her. Justin McManus “If Labor genuinely believes in these proposed guidelines they should be applied to every data centre development,” Glover said. She said the 150-metre rule would not help when data centres ran their back-up generators, which generally run off diesel fuel stored on site. “Diesel emissions aren’t going to just stop 150 metres away from homes.”



Related Article AI Buffer zones, drinking water bans: Carroll eyes new rules for data centres The premier said the changes would prevent suburban streets being transformed by multi-level data centres, while also allowing Victoria to capitalise on the economic benefits brought by AI’s rapid expansion. Asked if the changes were coming too late to protect neighbourhood character, Carroll said no. “I am a premier that gives certainty to industry. So applications that were made under the old rules will proceed.” The government intends to strengthen the regulations before it enters caretaker mode from November 3 in the lead-up to the state election, but Carroll could not offer certainty that the changes would be locked in by then.



The new requirements, outlined in Labor’s Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan, will also enforce guidelines for water and energy use and air and noise pollution. They come as global tensions over AI increase. Industry chiefs and world leaders have warned that the technology’s growth may outpace governments’ ability to regulate it, and that it could cause human extinction. At the United Nations this week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese signed a joint declaration calling for international oversight of AI models. On Wednesday, a federal inquiry into the technology will hold its first public hearings in Melbourne. CDC Data Centres welcomed on Tuesday the state government’s plan, and chief executive Greg Boorer said clear guidelines would help comfort investors considering making funding decisions. He said discussions about data centres were no longer just about planning but were “fundamentally a conversation about Australia’s digital future and the infrastructure required to support it”.



CDC Data Centres chief executive Greg Boorer. Alex Ellinghausen “As one of Australia’s most important data centre regions, the policy settings adopted by Victoria have an important role to play in supporting investment, innovation and Australia’s long-term digital capability,” Boorer said. “Communities want confidence that the organisations developing and operating critical infrastructure are responsible contributors to the places where they invest.” But Data Centres Australia, an advocacy group representing developers, technology companies and other related businesses, criticised the decision to include 150-metre buffer zones. Chief executive Belinda Dennett said operators already supported most aspects of the government’s rules, but the setback requirements would hurt projects where investments had already been committed.



“It is disappointing to see Victoria, the state that recognised the economic opportunity to attract data centre investment and proudly declared its ambition to be a global data centre leader, now move to impose requirements on data centres that apply to no comparable industrial use,” she said. Dennett said data centres were already restricted to industrial land, and individual projects had to go through environment and planning approvals. She said the 150-metre setback added a restriction that warehouses and logistics hubs did not have to meet, and that industrial land was already scarce. “It can render an otherwise suitable site unviable,” Dennett said. She also said the government’s faster approval process, the Development Facilitation Program, had recently not been making decisions on applications under the government’s old rules, leading to a “de facto freeze” that would force developers to spend elsewhere.



Artificial Intelligence Minister Anthony Carbines said setting clear regulations would give businesses certainty and Victoria a competitive edge over other states. Related Series

Data centres The cost of the cloud: Inside Australia’s data centre boom But Liberal frontbencher James Newbury said Carroll could not be trusted to regulate data centres, pointing to the suburban projects which ignited community protest. “Every Victorian can look on and see the track record of what they’ve allowed and the places they’ve allowed it to be built, and feel unfortunately certain that that would continue under a Labor government,” he said. The Greens said the government’s policy was a major retreat that had come after pressure from communities. But the party’s data centres spokeswoman, Sarah Mansfield, said noise could still be experienced from beyond 150 metres, and called on Labor to show the modelling for why that distance was chosen.



“There’s also a glaring hole in this announcement: what happens to the people already living next to these massive data centres?” she said. “Labor can’t admit these facilities need a buffer and then abandon the residents already living inside it. Big tech should pay to compensate those communities.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Why Iceland’s last whaler says the industry should not be banned
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentConservationWhales Why Iceland’s last whaler says the industry should not be banned Nick O'Malley September 23, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kristján Loftsson is the last Icelandic whaler, a businessman with a piratical air whose uncle died on a cargo ship torpedoed by a U-boat in the frigid oceans between Greenland and Canada during World War II and who, as a young man, served as a lookout on his father’s first whaling boat. Whaling magnate Kristján Loftsson in front of one of his two operational whaling vessels in 2015. Bloomberg via Getty Images Today at 83, he has made a fortune from the whaling outfit he inherited – and the sprawling investment and fishery businesses he built from it – yet is famous as the defiant face of an industry that refuses to die. This weekend, the International Whaling Commission will hold its biannual meeting in Hobart, while in Iceland there are political moves afoot to finally shut down Loftsson’s whaling operation, Hvalur. Loftsson normally attends IWC meetings and maintains a quiet presence as an observer, says Sharon Livermore, the marine program director with the International Fund for Nature, just as he normally avoids media attention. This year, Loftsson has pulled out of the meeting at the last moment, and is dispatching his son, Loftur Kristjánsson, in his place, but he seems happy enough to speak with this masthead as the meeting approaches.



The thought of his son turning up at the IWC clearly tickles him. According to Loftsson, opponents of whaling – whom he refers to collectively “the anti’s” – have taken to speculating that Icelandic whaling will end when he retires. His son’s appearance in Hobart, he says, will signal that it will not. At least not if he can help it. Kristján Loftsson at the cutting up of a fin whale at the seaside resort of Hvalfjordur. Alamy In conversation with Loftsson, it can be hard to tell if he is speaking with intent or for effect. At one point he says he is considering applying for carbon credits for all the whales he has killed over the years, given the extra carbon dioxide they would have exhaled had they been allowed to live full lives. As Loftsson sees it, there is no moral or ethical difference between killing, say, a cow, a kangaroo or a whale for human consumption, so long as their populations are healthy and the slaughter humane. Indeed, he seems baffled that Australia does not hunt its own whales.



“You have 40,000 humpback whales on the east coast, and you have 40,000 of different stock on the west coast. What are you going to do with these whales? Just let them swim there forever?” “What are you going to do with these whales? Just let them swim there forever?” Kristján Loftsson Loftsson speaks from some experience. He attended the 29th meeting of the IWC in Canberra in 1977, and afterwards flew to Western Australia to join a sperm whale hunt from Albany. He recalls being impressed by the Cheynes Beach Whaling Company’s use of aircraft to spot whales. A year later the business closed, marking the end of whaling in Australia. Since then, while humpback populations enjoyed a spectacular recovery, the bounce-back of southern right whales stalled at about 3500, and sperm whales have never recovered at all. Today, Hvalur – which means simply “whale” in Icelandic – still runs two whaling vessels after Sea Shepherd activists sank two others in a sabotage attack in port in 1986. This year, those vessels took 93 fin whales, out of a quota assigned by the Icelandic government of 150. Fin whales are the second-largest animals on earth after the blue whale, and it is estimated that since the international moratorium on whaling the North Atlantic population of the animal has recovered from about 15,000 before the global whaling moratorium to between 30,000 and 40,000.



Loftsson claims this year’s take was low due to poor weather. Captain Paul Watson, who founded the Sea Shepherd environmental direct action group in 1977 only to split with it in 2022, claims it was low due to his new foundation’s harassment efforts on the open ocean. Related Article Whales Do animals grieve? Rare footage of a mother and her calf may hold the answer Either way, Hvalur has so far been unable to sell the whale meat it harvested this season, which begins in July and ends in late September. According to Livermore, this is because beyond a tiny trade in selling whale meat to restaurants for tourists in Iceland, there is simply very little market for the product. Loftsson counters that he has been unable to sell the meat because Japan, to which he once exported, subsidises its own industry so heavily, a practice he describes as “discrimination”. Whatever the cause, it leaves him with about 1000 tonnes of whale meat sitting in cold storage. No matter, says Loftsson. He has a plan to turn the meat into iron supplement tablets for “pregnant women and women of childbearing age”, who he reckons would far prefer to eat tablets made of natural whale rather than synthetically produced ones. He says he can have machinery in place to make them by next season, though he can’t yet say how many he’d make with his 1000 tonnes of stored whale. Australia could secure its own supply by taking just 200 of its humpbacks a year, he has calculated.



As he keeps a weather eye on international efforts to end whaling, Loftsson is also facing increased pressure at home. His existing five-year licence to continue whaling was put in place by an outgoing conservative government in 2024. Iceland’s current centre/centre-left ruling coalition plans to introduce a bill to parliament in February that would end whaling, leaving Norway and Japan isolated as the only countries still conducting a commercial hunt in the face of the international moratorium. Kristján Loftsson holds a box of frozen whale meat destined for the Japan market. Bloomberg This comes after the same government commissioned a report that found the explosive-tipped harpoons used by Hvalur could leave whales fighting for their lives for up to two hours, and polls show support for the hunt falling. (Loftsson says the whales that Hvalur takes die in under three minutes.) Whether or not Loftsson – or his son – remain silent at the Hobart meeting, its practices will be central to parts of the conference. According to Livermore, the actions of Iceland at the meeting and over the coming months could mark a historical turning point, and she expects the meeting to highlight the growth of whale-watching tourism in Iceland. It will also consider a call to reduce shipping speeds in migration corridors to reduce the threat of ship strikes. As to why Loftsson is so determined to continue Hvalur’s whaling operations given its vast income from banking and fisheries, Livermore says she is baffled.



“I think with Kristján Loftsson it is a bit of a one-man mission. I think he wants to assert the rights of himself as an Icelander to access what he would refer to as marine resources, and what we would call sentient beings. Related Article Whales First drone footage of a humpback birth shows mum and bub thriving “He’s a billionaire, and he runs his whaling operations at an economic loss. There is no way that the whaling industry could stay afloat without either subsidies or, you know, the support of a billionaire.” Loftsson insists whaling is an important part of his business and laughs when asked if he is a billionaire. “It depends on how you are counting. Maybe in Icelandic krona,” he says. (There are about 80 krona to the Australian dollar.) As to why he is determined to keep whaling, he dismisses the question as absurd.



“It is like asking a fisherman why are you fishing? If you have a million Australian dollars in a bank and you have a fishing boat, why don’t you just scrap the fishing boat and spend the money? “Nobody talks like that, except these people.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.
