World.title: Locals voice concerns about Pahīatua Medical Centre at public meeting
World.content:
Audio player for " Pahiatua locals don't hold back at public meeting " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1533862%2Flocals-voice-concerns-about-pahiatua-medical-centre-at-public-meeting

Pahiatua locals don't hold back at public meeting Morning Report Download MP3 3m

In the first of three public meetings about the state of healthcare in Tararua, Pahīatua locals came out in a force to voice their concerns about an ownership model they no longer have faith in.

Almost 5000 patients depend on the Pahīatua Medical Centre in the Tararua district, where six staff resigned on Monday, amid concerns about extreme workload and patient safety.

Health New Zealand has since launched a review of the clinics owned by the Tararua Health Group, which is in turn owned by OmniHealth - a network of about 17 practices around the country.

OmniHealth has been contacted for comment.

Mark Emmerson, one of the six staff members who has resigned in response to continuing staffing and administrative challenges at the Pahīatua Medical Centre. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

On Tuesday night, Pahīatua locals who spoke to RNZ described long wait-times and fears about the future of doctor's visits.

A group of women, who did not want to share their names, said they had standing three-monthly appointments to ensure they got seen and just hoped they did not get sick between bookings.

"We still drive ... but there's a lot of people in Pahīatua that don't drive or even own a car, so what's going to happen to them?" one asked, worried about the clinic's sustainability.

A Pahīatua local speaking at the community meeting. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Deirdre Power said it was "just impossible" to get an appointment, which left her feeling "very afraid".

Another local said staff at Pahīatua Medical Centre were visibly under pressure and "strung out, tired, sick of it".

Nurse Mark Emmerson - who was among those who tendered their resignations - spoke at the meeting on Tuesday night and explained the decision.

"They [management] said we shouldn't have gone to the media ... we've damaged the relationship with the community, which obviously for a staff that deeply cares for the community was very hurtful and that's resulted in the six of us walking out and resigning on the spot."

He said they were all locals and didn't want to move.

"We're happy to engage with any interested party. But that interested party has to have the community at heart."

The Pahīatua Medical Centre where six staff have resigned amid concerns about extreme workload and patient safety. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Patient advocate Malcolm Mulholland said rural health care was in dire straits in some parts of Aotearoa, but that he had never seen a case like this.

"The level of dysfunction that has come out largely in the media now for the past few days has been quite staggering."

Emmerson, Mulholland, and Labour Party member Kieran McAnulty called for OmniHealth to go.

"We have an opportunity here to have a community-owned and run health centre," McAnulty said to applause.

"Get rid of OmniHealth, buy them out."

Pahīatua local Deirdre Power said it was "just impossible" to get an appointment at the centre. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Others in the audience followed suit, with one man proposing the community turn its back on OmniHealth.

"We look for a completely different group of people who can help us run our medical centre," he said.

"I'm going to move that we do this as soon as possible, that we use whoever is available to help us and we do it as publicly as we can."

Don Cameron, former Ruapehu mayor, said a community-owned health service in the central plateau could serve as a template for Pahīatua.

He said the practice was commercial but owned by both the community and local Māori health providers and had just received millions in government funding because "it was successful".

"Now if we can get our own health service going from our own community, you will attract the funding, that won't be the problem.

"The problem will be ... making sure you've got the right number of health experts here and keeping them."

A Pahīatua local speaking at the community meeting regarding challenges at Pahiatua Medical Centre. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Cameron said the community had to act quickly given the resignations.

"We do not want to lose Mark [Emmerson] and the staff, because once that happens you've got to start all over again."

Māori leader Hayden Hape of Ngāti Kahungunu finished the meeting by putting an offer on the table.

He said he had seen walkouts at medical practice's before and the iwi had moved to fill the gap.

World.title: Labour sums up its foreign policy approach as 'independent, principled and unafraid'
World.content:
Labour's foreign affairs spokesperson says there is a time for quiet diplomacy "and there is a time when quiet diplomacy must bend to moral clarity," as she responds to comments by Winston Peters.

Labour has outlined its focus to foreign policy, summing up its approach in three words, "independent, principled and unafraid".

Vanushi Walters was speaking alongside the Labour leader as part of Diplosphere's foreign policy election series at Parliament on Wednesday.

It comes after the foreign minister took aim at those insisting the country always use megaphone diplomacy, especially against the United States, as he states New Zealand's nuclear-free policy had a cost.

On Monday he called out those who focus on "national identity" rather than the national interest in his final speech as foreign affairs minister this term, making a case for quiet diplomacy.

On Wednesday morning, Walters responded specifically to Peters' comments.

She referenced Peters' argument that independence is about agency, suggesting agency is about New Zealand's interests over our identity.

But Walters said "our interests and our identity, or by another name, our values, are tethered together".

She then said New Zealand's silence on breaches of the UN Charter this term had been "noticed".

"We do not grow our agency if we stand for nothing, because that too is a choice that has consequences.

"We lost our reputation as an honest broker and a consistent champion of international law."

Walters said there was a time for quiet diplomacy, "and there is a time when quiet diplomacy must bend to moral clarity".

"That is undeniably the case when the scale of human rights abuses is so special that it amounts to genocide, to ethnic cleansing."

She said Labour would recognise Palestinian statehood and place economic sanctions on Israel, as well as "intervene in support of South Africa's case at the International Court of Justice in respect of a breach of the Genocide Convention."

Walters also specified that New Zealand's relationships with both the US and China are "equally important to us as major trading partners," as she called out Peters' comments to Lawrence Xu-Nan.

"Yet under this government, we have not seen a balanced foreign policy approach.

"To the contrary, what we've seen is outright racism directed at one partner and felt by the Chinese diaspora here in New Zealand, and silence when the US acted in breach of the UN Charter."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins also spoke, saying old assumptions were being tested in foreign policy, but New Zealand's response cannot be "fear".

He said New Zealand could not rely on old relationships, old institutions and old assumptions about trade, security and international cooperation, as power was being exercised more openly.

"While it is tempting to treat this as simply a phase that will pass to be waited out, that will be a mistake."

He specifically referenced the anti-nuclear movement, after saying independence didn't mean isolation, but the "confidence to make our own decisions in our own interests and to explain those to others".

He acknowledged the decisions about New Zealand's anti-nuclear stance came with a cost, "but each one also told the world something true about who we are as a country".

He said New Zealand's influence came from its willingness to "say what we think".

"In practice, that means we can trade with a country while disagreeing with them."

He said it was not in New Zealand's interests to have to choose between its partners, such as the United States and China.

Hipkins also said he wanted a Pacific that was "not militarised, and one whose future is not dictated by rising sea levels and worsening storms."

Later, speaking to reporters, Walters responded to questions about the recent missile test by China, and concerns by some Pacific nations that the United States conducts tests into the Marshall Islands, which is done with the country's consent.

Walters said neither were a breach of international law.

World.title: Future of Super Rugby and NPC among topics at crunch NZ Rugby summit
World.content:
Audio player for " Big changes could be on the way for rugby in NZ " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/sport/1531791%2Ffuture-of-super-rugby-and-npc-among-topics-at-crunch-nz-rugby-summit

Big changes could be on the way for rugby in NZ Morning Report Download MP3 6m

New Zealand Rugby will hold a critical summit this week as it weighs major decisions over the future of Super Rugby and the NPC, as it seeks to cut $20 million a year in costs.

NZ Rugby and its stakeholders, including provincial unions and the Players Association, will meet in Wellington on Thursday to discuss the governing body's financial position and options for reshaping the domestic game.

A confidential NZ Rugby document, seen by RNZ, outlines three proposals for the domestic game, including expanding Super Rugby with two additional teams; continuing with the current versions of Super Rugby and the NPC, but merging the Super Rugby clubs with the main provincial unions; or replacing both Super Rugby and the NPC with a new 8-10 team competition.

The proposals are still indicative and intended as starting points for discussion. The idea of scrapping Super Rugby and the NPC in favour of a new format has been put forward by the provincial unions.

The document states that rugby in New Zealand is unable to fund its own growth without changing course, with the current financial model, based on conservative revenue growth, described as unsustainable.

While revenue has doubled for NZR in over the past 10 years, the document noted costs are outpacing that growth causing recurring deficits.

It said NZR is forecast to make cumulative net losses of $68 million between 2022-26 and, based on "conservative revenue projection", a further $66m across 2027-31. Rugby in New Zealand is forecast to make net loss of $26m for 2026, according to figures in the document.

Current projections show NZR's cash reserves falling to $72m by the end of 2031 - a similar level to its closing reserves in 2021, before the Silver Lake capital raise.

The document said NZR needs to save about $20m a year to get back in the black.

That puts the structure and cost of the domestic competitions firmly in the spotlight, with the document stating that no domestic competition is currently profitable.

One proposal is to expand Super Rugby from 10 to 12 teams with a new entity "SPR Hold Co" set up to run the competition.

The new entity would hold pooled team commercial rights and run the logistics and marketing for the competition, with NZR and Rugby Australia keeping "broadcast control". Under this model, the five New Zealand Super Rugby clubs and their provincial unions - Auckland, Waikato, Wellington, Canterbury and Otago - would be merged to reduce the number of high-performance set-ups.

Another proposal would leave Super Rugby and the NPC unchanged, but costs would be cut by amalgamating the Super Rugby clubs with the provincial unions based in the same cities.

The third option is to create a new competition and cut ties with Australia. It is unclear how the New Zealand teams would be selected.

New Zealand Rugby Players Association boss Rob Nichol told RNZ's Morning Report that the domestic competitions were worth keeping.

"I cannot emphasise enough how well, in the men's game, NPC and Super Rugby, how well it's delivered over the last 25 years," Nichol said.

"Ironically, even though New Zealanders love to beat up on our comps, we're the envy of the world in that respect still."

He said his preference was to develop the current competitions.

"I think one of the things we need to do is make sure that we put a proper focus on those competitions and really drive them, whereas I think over recent years the focus has been more on the teams in black (All Blacks, Black Ferns etc) and how we commercialise those and set the game up that way."

Player payments across all entities is rugby's largest investment area and while they are not expected to be a major talking point at the summit, NZR is exploring ways they can save some money in that area.

The pre-summit document states NZR's desire to keep its best players and coaches in New Zealand. However, it is understood the governing body is willing to consider changes to the All Blacks eligibility rules to allow senior players to play overseas while still being eligible for national team selection.

Such a change is not currently in the works, but could help reduce NZR's costs.

The summit will also include the wider competitive pressures facing rugby in New Zealand, including the threat posed by the NRL.

"Rugby is up against a well organised, well-funded competitor - future success requires alignment against this challenge," the document states.

The NRL, which has 17 teams and 213 games a season (compared with Super Rugby's 10 teams and 86 games from 2027), now draws 28 million NZ viewing hours against Super Rugby's 19m and 14m for NPC, according to the document.

It also highlights the pressure the NRL is putting on rugby pathways in New Zealand, stating that 15 percent (61/434) players in NRL U21 competition in 2026 played 1st XV rugby in New Zealand.

World.title: Navy lieutenant facing rape charges scrutinised over memory of 'unremarkable' night
World.content:
Warning: This story contains sexual assault allegations.

A navy lieutenant facing three rape charges has been asked why his memory of the night is so clear if nothing remarkable happened.

The lieutenant is before the court martial at Auckland's Devonport Naval Base this week, after a woman he dated while deployed overseas alleged he tried three times to have unprotected sex with her against her wishes in September last year.

The lieutenant has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and argues the complainant made up the allegations out of jealousy after their brief relationship ended.

Cross examining the lieutenant, prosecutor Sam McMullan questioned his story, suggesting it had been rehearsed in the months leading up to the court martial.

"Have you done a bit of prep for the trial?" McMullan asked.

The lieutenant agreed.

"How many times did you read your evidence?" he continued.

"More than once, I haven't kept count," the lieutenant replied.

"Could be half a dozen, or a dozen?" McMullan pressed.

"Could be," the lieutenant said.

McMullan questioned whether the lieutenant's evidence was truly based on his memory, or just what was written down.

"The document is based on my memory," the lieutenant said.

"You seem to have an extremely clear memory of that night," McMullan continued.

"This was a night that was otherwise fairly unremarkable. But you remember the names of two of the bars you went to, the beach you went to the next day, is that really what a person remembers a year on?"

The lieutenant replied: "I've known about these allegations for nine months and I have had a lot of time to reflect on that night."

McMullan pressed him directly.

"If it was based on your recollection, wouldn't you remember putting your penis inside of her vagina three times without consent?" he asked.

"You'd recall at the point in time you put your penis in her vagina that she hadn't given her consent."

"I don't recall that because I never put my penis inside her vagina that night," the lieutenant said.

The next witness, the complainant's roommate during the hotel stay, was called to give evidence by the defence - surprising the prosecution.

"You said you were not available to be a witness for the prosecution," McMullan said.

"Is the reason why you decided not to appear for the prosecution because you've picked a side?"

"I didn't want to support a side I don't believe in," the roommate said.

The roommate did not know either the defendant or complainant before the events in September and hadn't kept up with them afterwards.

Defence lawyer Asta Gold asked her to describe the complainant's demeanour after the night in which she alleged she had been raped.

"[The mood between the complainant and defendant was] normal, as normal as it was the night before," she said.

Later that day, the complainant and defendant had consensual sex with a condom.

The roommate recalled the complainant being excited at the time.

"What was her mood like when she said she was going to see [the defendant]?" Gold asked her.

"Happy, like she was looking forward to hanging out with [him]."

During cross examination, McMullan questioned the roommate's memory.

"When you gave a statement to military police, could you remember the defendant's name?" he asked.

"I believe so," she replied.

"Paragraph 17: 'I can't recall his name'," McMullan read.

"I believe I just needed my memory jogged," the roommate said.

"So, it's all come flooding back after you've had another nine months to think about it?" McMullan asked.

"It was a trip, I had fun, I moved on with my life, so when I was called in January [to give a statement] I hadn't thought about it that much, but once I was called in, it was impactful, so I went through my memory," she said.

"You're just here to give evidence that is most favourable to [the defendant], aren't you?" he continued.

World.title: How Tokomanawa Queens lured WNBA star Hailey Van Lith to NZ women's basketball league
World.content:
The Tokomanawa Queens say luring WNBA player Hailey Van Lith to the Tauihi league will lead to other star imports choosing to play in the New Zealand women's basketball league.

The Connecticut Sun guard is the team-mate of New Zealander Charlisse Leger-Walker, who revealed in late August that she will be joining the Tokomanawa Queens, following her debut season in the American basketball league.

Leger-Walker is just the second New Zealand woman to reach the WNBA and getting her signature to play in Aotearoa for the first time in six years was already seen as a bold move by the Wellington-based franchise.

But Saturday's announcement that Van Lith, who was selected as the No. 11 overall pick in the 2025 WNBA Draft, will be playing in the 2026 Tauihi league would have been beyond the wildest dreams of bosses when they launched the competition four years ago.

Tokomanawa Queens general manager Walter Taulelei said no words could really describe it.

"It's not like we haven't had WNBA players here before but someone like Hailey, she's a little different because she's as big off the court as she is on the court," Taulelei said.

"She's got a very well curated portfolio of partnerships and endorsements that most athletes would dream of. And she's also had a very, very high profile American college career, that those who follow basketball will know exactly who she is."

Van Lith is the ninth most-followed WNBA player on Instagram, with 1.3m followers. Last week Van Lith had a busy New York Fashion Week between runway shows and speaking engagements.

"I think collectively across all social media platforms, she's sitting at about 2.6 million and in this country, we've never had that, ever."

Hailey Van Lith courtside. Michael Hirschuber

Taulelei, who handles the recruitment for the Queens, said Van Lith will draw attention to the league when other elite players consider their off-season options.

"It's going to open up conversations in the future and it's not something I hope for, I know it will happen. People will start to ask questions about what is it like playing in New Zealand and then these women will talk about their experiences like they have in the past, but you're talking about players who are at Hailey's level."

Taulelei said when planning started around what they wanted their roster to look like for 2026 , Australian Opals guard Kristy Wallace was central to that.

The Tokomanawa Queens held a spot for the 2025 Tauhi league MVP to return to the team but Wallace informed them in early September that she wouldn't be able to commit while juggling a new career as a firefighter.

"So we had to pivot and to pivot you've got to make contact with certain agents and Hailey's team were quite interested and intrigued by the New Zealand market."

Despite being WNBA team-mates, Taulelei said Leger-Walker didn't play a direct role in recruiting Van Lith, who won bronze with Team USA in women's 3x3 basketball at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

"I mean obviously athletes talk, they talk about where they're heading to. If that piqued an interest with Hailey, I don't know.

"But her management saw Charlisse's Instagram video when she revealed she was joining the league and wanted to talk more about it. So it was about three weeks worth of conversations leading up to her announcement."

Taulelei said Van Lith could play anywhere she wanted in the WNBA off-season in leagues in Europe and Asia.

"But what we were offering was something slightly different and her management team were quite keen to explore that."

Charlisse Leger-Walker at the 2026 WNBA draft. Angelina Katsanis/Getty Images

Van Lith had a challenging start to her professional career when she dealt with a serious ankle injury during her rookie season for Chicago Sky, and has been on short-term contracts at the Connecticut Sun.

"New Zealand is a bit of a bucket list destination to a lot of people, including athletes. But it was a bit more than that because the women's game in America is changing and it's adopting a style that appeals to a global market of players.

"So you have to appeal to FIBA [International Basketball Federation] style of play and those types of athletes from Europe and Asia and this part of the world have become more appealing to WNBA teams.

"But that also means that local players, those Americans have to adjust their way of playing and sometimes it takes a bit longer. For some, especially the younger ones are looking for opportunities where they can continue to advance their knowledge of how the game is played in other markets and Hailey is one of those players.

"She is known as one of the hardest working players in the gym so for a player like that she's jumping into the challenge of trying to adapt the way that she plays to fit the new direction of a league."

Walter and his wife Rachel Taulelei are also co-owners of the franchise.

Rachel Taulelei said Tauihi was building a reputation as a league that would enhance the careers of import players.

"It's obviously a curiosity for people to come to New Zealand but equally they can improve their game. They can perfect elements of their game in what would ordinarily be their off-season and then take that back and put it into practice in other leagues.

"For example we had Korean national player Ji-Hoon Park the last two years. It was the first time she stepped out of Korea to come and play in the Queens - she's now playing for the LA Sparks in the WNBA," Rachel said.

Guard Hailey Van Lith of the Connecticut Sun. ALI GRADISCHER

Walter Taulelei said players like Van Lith did not come to New Zealand for the money.

"Our market unfortunately is not attractive in terms of it's low-end money with a very unfavourable exchange rate and for Americans, when they do the conversion, it's not as appealing.

"But players tend to weigh up what else are they looking for and what we offered to try and help Hailey, it was more important than worrying about what she was going to be earning."

The Queens have also recruited WNBA-experienced player Taylor Mikesell, who played for the Mainland Pouākai last season and Mimi Collins, who comes from a highly successful American college basketball career.

Walter Taulelei said there was a huge sense of excitement in the team when they secured Leger-Walker, who will be joining her older sister Krystal.

The 25-year-old was selected 18th overall in the 2026 WNBA Draft by Connecticut, where she has enjoyed a solid rookie campaign.

"The opportunity to play with Charlisse will be a highlight for all those girls' careers. They are really excited that Charlisse is going to lead the team in the point guard role so she will control the tempo and the offense."

Taulelei said he enjoyed sharing the news that Van Lith was also joining the team.

"We've got lots of amateurs that sit as role players on our bench. If you'd seen what it meant to them to have the opportunity to play with Hailey, you could see it written all over their faces.

"Taylor and Mimi have both played against Hailey and said that she is just relentless, that's how they describe her, like that girl just doesn't stop."

Rachel Taulelei hopes the star power will appeal to sports fan, outside of the basketball faithful.

She said their home court in Porirua allowed people to get up close with the players and the game and they were trying to enhance the game-day experience for fans.

"We've got an exercise this year where we're rolling out a big royal carpet between the Rapid League game and the Tauihi game at Te Rauparaha stadium where people can jump on and be right next to the players as they're warming up. So we try to make it as immersive as possible.

"We gave ourselves one KPI [Key Performance Indicator] this year and that was bums on seats because one of the challenges that women's sports has is getting people to come and see it live. It's just a matter of lifting people out of their lounges and once they're there, they become pretty converted," Rachel said.

Leger-Walker and Van Lith will arrive in Wellington later this month when their WNBA commitments end and the pair will be ready to play the Queens' second round game against Mainland Pouākai on 4 October.

World.title: Call for greater protection for journalists at Pacific media summit
World.content:
The president of the Pacific Islands News Association (PINA) says journalists need greater protection when reporting on organised crime networks.

Speaking at a panel discussion on organized crime in Savusavu, Kalafi Moala said journalists investigating drug trafficking face increasing threats to their personal safety.

Moala, who is also RNZ Pacific correspondent in Tonga, recalled an incident involving a journalist from Tongas Kele'a newspaper who reported on Tongan gangs.

A gang member went to the newspaper's office the following day and threatened the journalist.

Moala pointed out that in Tonga alone, organized crime has become more sophisticated.

He said as crime grows, continued reporting and scrutiny are needed, but journalists must be protected from threats and violence while doing their job.

Participants of the 8th Pacific Islands News Association Media Summit with the Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka in Savusavu. 23 September 2026 Fijian Media Association

Pacific media professionals from across the region are in Fiji for this year's PINA Media Summit. The summit, which officially begins on Wednesday, will shine a spotlight on issues facing many Pacific newsroom across the region.

Moala told RNZ Pacific he hoped the summit will address some of the fundamental issues facing journalism in the region.

"In terms of storytelling, in terms of engagement with government and other powers, how do we do research to be able to do stories? How do we fact-check our stories?

"Those are fundamental things that I think it needs to be brought back and re-emphasized in our training. And the reason for that is there are a lot of young people that are coming in."

More than 200 people are taking part in the PINA summit. Moala said this is its biggest gathering yet.

He told RNZ Pacific that PINA still needs to exist.

"It is an association where it allows us to be able to stand together on the key principles of our profession, of our faith. It is always better to stand together than to stand alone."

Women in media

A Fijian media leader says Pacific women in media continue to face challenges in the industry, including accessing information from government agencies.

Audio player for " Fiji media leader calls for stronger support for women journos " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/pacific/1533034%2Fcall-for-greater-protection-for-journalists-at-pacific-media-summit

Fiji media leader calls for stronger support for women journos Pacific Waves Download MP3 5m

Rosi Doviverata from the Women in Media Fiji organisation said delays in responses can hold up reporting on issues affecting communities.

She told Pacific Waves reporters can sometimes wait two or three months for answers.

"That can be really frustrating, and we have people in the community asking why have not you reported this, and that is mainly because we are waiting on ministries to respond to those issues."

Speaking prior to the launch of the PINA media summit in Savusavu, Doviverata said support from colleagues and editors can help Pacific female reporters advance in their careers.

"For us in Fiji, we have seen we are where we are because of that male allyship," she said.

World.title: Decision on moving Woolworths contact centre to Australia due next week
World.content:
Workers are expecting to hear next week whether Woolworths is going ahead with a decision to close its New Zealand-based contact centre and move about 130 jobs to Australia.

The supermarket operator is looking at whether it can combine its customer care operations in Sydney.

It said that would use the group's scale, systems and expertise to provide customer service for New Zealand customers.

Workers First union submitted feedback on behalf of its members, which said offshoring was already going wrong for the company. It said 13 Australian-based staff had been answering New Zealand calls in recent weeks and there had been a spike in complaints about service quality.

Audio player for " Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1532747%2Fdecision-on-moving-woolworths-contact-centre-to-australia-due-next-week

It said the closure would also happen just before Christmas and New Year, the busiest time of the year for the company, which added business risk as well as human cost.

The union said most customer care centre roles were held by working mothers who took the jobs specifically because they were secure and allowed them to work from home.

Many had relocated out of expensive city centres because they had that work and would find it very hard to replace it in their local areas.

The union also said staff had knowledge that would be hard to replace overseas. Local staff could be redeployed into the customer hub rather than full offshoring which would cut costs without job losses, it suggested.

Workers First deputy secretary Rudd Hughes said: "Woolworths is a profitable company moving good jobs out of New Zealand while it posts record earnings.

"These are 130 local workers who know Woolworths' stores, systems and customers better than anyone in Australia hired to replace them.

"There are ways to save money here that don't involve sending the work overseas, and we've outlined them clearly to Woolworths. It's on the company to take them up."

Woolworths said proposals like this allowed it to explore what was possible so it could invest in what mattered most to customers. It said there had been 500 new retail roles introduced in the 2026 financial year and 500 new front-line roles forecasted for the 2027 year.

"Our future demands a Woolies that is simpler and more competitive, with increasing investment in value and experiences for Kiwi customers. We understand that this proposal, if implemented, represents a significant change for our team.

"We are deeply mindful of the personal impact this transition may have. We are committed to transparency with our team and will provide support with care and respect as we work through consultation. We are also working one on one with each individual team member to get their feedback and are actively working on redeployment opportunities across the business."

World.title: Grey Lynn and Ponsonby: From working class roots to Auckland's most sought after suburbs
World.content:
Audio player for " The evolution of Auckland’s inner suburbs " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/regions_auckland/1525954%2Fgrey-lynn-and-ponsonby-from-working-class-roots-to-auckland-s-most-sought-after-suburbs

The evolution of Auckland’s inner suburbs Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Auckland's villa-lined and leafy central suburbs are some of the city's most sought after and expensive, with the trendiest cafes and bars.

But Grey Lynn and Ponsonby were once working class areas, home to Pasifika communities and a social justice movement.

RNZ spoke to some of the people who have hung on through all of the changes.

One of them is Josephina Faiva - she has been living in her family home on Richmond Road for nearly 50 years - her family bought the house when they moved from Tonga when she was 17.

"A lot of a different Island people were in the area and now they all moved out and White man moved in. They've got the money and they move in."

As living nearer to the city became more desirable, house prices and rents shot up through the 1980s and 1990s and much of the Pasifika community was pushed to South Auckland.

Richmond Road in Ponsonby, Auckland. RNZ / Luka Forman

But, Josephina's family stayed put, and she said despite having to travel to South Auckland to visit extended family, she still loved living in the area.

"We're sitting in the cafe, mostly with my White friends for coffee, and we get on very well."

Tigilau Ness was a member of the Polynesian Panthers, a social justice movement which was an important part of Ponsonby's history in the 1970s.

They were formed to fight against racism across society - including the infamous dawn raids, Ness said.

"It was a scary time for us. For Polynesians, and as Polynesian Panthers we stood up against it. We were dead set against any policy like that. It was state sanctioned terrorism to us."

Tigilau Ness. RNZ / Luka Forman

Ness said there were illegal speakeasies run by gangs in Ponsonby at the time, which many young people frequented.

The Polynesian Panthers aimed to offer a more positive community, he said, offering homework centres and legal aid.

Ness had lived in the area for most of his life - but he found out this year his home on Ivanhoe Road would be forcibly bought out by the Transport Agency as part of the Northwestern busway project.

He was "hoping to" buy again in the area, but was unsure if he and his wife would be able to afford it.

"We've had a look around already. It's all in the $1 million + area, and we don't want to move in to apartments."

Local artist John Reynolds had lived in his house Richmond Road since the 1980s. He remembered a dairy owned by an "old communist" named George across the road.

John Reynolds Starkwhite

"George was a wonderful character, and he'd go out the back if I mentioned communism, and bring out old Soviet magazines, like propaganda."

Reynolds said the building where George's dairy used to be was now a French wine bar.

World.title: 'Flying mullet' Browning announces athletics retirement
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Two-time Olympian Rohan Browning has reflected on the moment that changed his life, as he announced his retirement from athletics.

Browning finishes his career as the fourth-fastest Australian over 100 metres, having run a personal best of 10.01 seconds at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021.

Sporting a distinctive hairstyle which earned the nickname 'Flying mullet', Browning recorded the time in the heats to qualify for the semifinals in his Olympic debut.

"That was a moment that changed my life," Browning said in an Australian Athletics statement.

"It gave me a really healthy dose of self-belief because it had been a quiet period for Australian men's sprinting.

Bizarre end to Australia's athletics campaign A hilariously understated celebration marked the end of an enthralling athletics campaign in Glasgow, and the beginning of Australian track and field being taken seriously around the world.

"There weren't many role models on the scene, and I feel like I had to forge that path myself."

A four-time national champion, Browning was content to call time on his career following Australia's shock victory in the men's 4x100m relay at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

The 28-year-old joined Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi and Calab Law in winning Australia's first gold medal in the event since 1974.

"I really wanted to go out on a high note, and after winning the gold medal at the Commonwealth Games in the relay, it was only going to go downhill from there," Browning said.

"The athlete in me still thinks that I could get back, run personal bests and compete at the highest level, but no athlete is ever going to be truly satisfied.

Rohan Browning (left) helped Australia win a drought-breaking relay gold at the Commonwealth Games. (Getty images: Ian MacNicol)

"The thing that I'm actually proudest of is that I made every team from my debut in 2017 to my retirement in 2026."

Australian Athletics chief executive Simon Hollingsworth said Browning did himself proud during his career.

"Rohan has been a fantastic athlete and ambassador for our sport," Hollingsworth said.

"His 2021 Tokyo performance inspired Australians and the generation of sprinters who followed.

"To go out with a superb relay run for gold in Glasgow is a fitting finale."

Although Browning was unable to dip under 10 seconds legally, he did run a wind-assisted PB of 9.89 in Austria earlier this year.

Browning also competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

He ran at five World Athletics Championships, with his best finish in the 100m being a semifinal appearance at the 2023 edition in Budapest.

World.title: Mary Fowler's Man City score controversial goal with flare burning on pitch
World.content:
Mary Fowler's Manchester City have started their Women's Champions League campaign with a controversial draw against Bayern Munich, scoring a crucial goal with a flare burning among the players.

The reigning English champions came back from 2-0 down to equalise after Fowler's injection in the 63rd minute.

But it was City's first goal from Beth Mead that had Bayern players fuming.

In the final seconds of the first half, Kerstin Casparij broke down the right wing and was pursued by Franziska Kett towards the edge of the 18-yard box, where a flare was sending purple smoke billowing.

Bayern goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic waved her arms in an apparent attempt to get the attention of officials as the play unfolded, but Casparij seemed unfazed by the nearby flare as she outpaced Kett and whipped a cross into the box, where Bunny Shaw's shot was blocked, and Mead cleaned up the scraps to make it 2-1 heading into the break.

As City celebrated, Mahmutovic and Kett started to complain before their teammates joined in, with referee Olatz Rivera Olmedo immediately removing the projectile from the pitch.

Discussions continued as the ball returned to halfway for the kick-off before VAR confirmed the goal would stand, giving City crucial momentum heading into half-time, leading to an improved second-half performance and ultimately an 86th-minute equaliser by Carlotta Wamser.

Elsewhere on the first matchday of the tournament, Arsenal's trio of Australians — Steph Catley, Kyra Cooney-Cross and Caitlin Foord — all started as the 2025 winners began the quest to regain their continental crown against Danish part-timers HB Køge.

The Gunners won 1-0, but needed an injury-time penalty from Mariona Caldentay that bank worker Alberte Vingum almost saved.

"It was a pretty crazy last five minutes, but that's football," Catley said.

"They defended great; we tried so many avenues to goal.

"Credit to the girls, they kept trying, and Mariona was very calm in that moment."

And in Monza, veteran Matildas defender Aiva Luik played the 90 minutes as Hacken went down 1-0 to Internazionale, becoming the oldest group stage/league phase player at 41, according to UEFA.

Capped 45 times by Australia, Luik is at her 16th club in her 10th country during her 26-year career.

"I still feel young. The secret is coffee and chocolate," she said.

Inter, making its competition debut, scored in the fifth minute through Haley Bugej from a corner but couldn't find a second, with the Swedes more dangerous on the break.

World.title: Banned Swans to make first public appearance since Pullman Hotel scandal
World.content:
Sydney's five suspended players will make their return to the club this week and will address the Swans' playing group "at some point".

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are expected to return to club this week for their exit meetings.

Exit meetings are carried out with all players on a senior list at the end of each season to discuss their future with the club.

Swans coach Dean Cox arrived at the club's Moore Park base early today, before Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich briefly spoke to media.

"Look, it's a natural thing that the players will come into the club over the next period," Pavlich said.

"Don't know exactly when that'll be, given that the season's now finished and player exit meetings are occurring.

"And the players at some point will have a chat to the broader group and the club, but yeah, there's no timeline."

Swans coach Dean Cox arrives at the club's headquarters ahead of player exit meetings. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

The five have not been at the club since August after they were stood down for breaching club standards following a post-match party at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.

Those suspensions are separate from a police investigation into sexual assault allegations, with Victoria Police flagging an update is not expected until late October.

No charges have been laid, and there is no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Pavlich would not be drawn on the specifics surrounding the five's return.

Asked what he would want the five to say in their address, Pavlich said: "I want them to be themselves.

"I want them to come in and do what we'd normally do at the end of a season, which is, yeah, player exit meetings.

"If they've got something to say to their player group, if they've got something to say to the club, then we'll hear them out then."

World.title: Tones And I breaks silence on NRL grand final pre-match fiasco
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

On Tuesday, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys told ABC Sport the NRL's plans to have Tones And I perform before next month's showpiece event would be cancelled.

The NRL will use the money set aside for pre-match entertainment to contribute to children playing rugby league.

But Tones And I's management said no deal had been signed or confirmed in writing.

Via a statement sent to ABC Sport, her management representative Regan Lethbridge said "prior commitments" were a sticking point.

"Tones was recently approached to perform the pre-show at the NRL grand final," the statement read.

"An offer was presented to Tones via management on September 5.

NRL grand final loses pre-match act The NRL grand final is set to go ahead without pre-match entertainment after negotiations with Australian artist Tones and I collapsed.

"Tones had a prior commitment with Macklemore in America and explored all avenues to make it work.

"Nothing was signed or confirmed in writing.

"Due to the last-minute nature and prior commitments by Tones, we were unable to accept the offer.

"We wish the NRL nothing but the very best for their event."

The Sydney Morning Herald reported the issue centred the NRL's insistence Tones And I perform the song Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

But neither Tones And I nor V'Landys has cited the set list as the issue at play.

Tones And I has previously said she loathed the hit song, which enjoyed significant commercial success when released in 2019.

Macklemore found himself at the centre of his own live upheaval after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's The Loop Tour, over pro-Palestinian comments.

'A different direction'

V'landys said he wished Tones And I well.

"I'm a fan of Tones And I," he told ABC Sport on Tuesday.

"She is a great performer, no doubt about that, and she's got some great songs, but as I said, we both decided to go to a different direction."

V'landys said the cost of putting on any artist for a grand final performance was about a million dollars.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend a million dollars on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

Peter V’landys said money set aside for pre-match entertainment would be invested in junior rugby league. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

To have no pre-game show would be a stunning break from tradition.

The grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop star Teddy Swims last year.

Billy Idol and Tina Turner are among other acts to have taken the stage for the event.

V'landys was unconcerned as to whether the event could be underwhelming without pre-match entertainment.

"Our game sells itself," he said.

"People come to watch rugby league. They don't come to watch a pop concert."

V'landys did not provide details on the record of why or how the negotiations with Tones And I broke down.

"You spend money to get outcomes, and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to … play rugby league," he said.

" We consider a lot of artists over a period of time, but as I said, I've been toying with this idea for a couple of years now, about giving the money to kids to play rugby league rather than a musical act. "

State governments across the country are bidding for the grand final hosting rights.

New South Wales holds the rights, but it is unclear whether the state minister for sport, Steve Kamper, or Premier Chris Minns were consulted.

Neither provided comment in response to questions.

New South Wales Rugby League chief executive David Trodden said he had "a short conversation" with V'landys about the prospect of funds being directed towards grassroots footy.

"I applaud his decision to use the funds to support grassroots rugby league, and particularly those children who may have financial constraints on their ability to participate in such a wonderful community sport," Trodden said.

"Rugby league has a unique ability to provide community support to those who need it the most."

World.title: Why the AFL tribunal upheld Neale's grand final ban
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Finding Lachie Neale guilty was the easy bit for the AFL tribunal.

The hard part was deciding whether to apply the "exceptional and compelling clause".

Neale to miss AFL grand final Brisbane's Lachie Neale has failed in his attempt to overturn a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan at the AFL tribunal and will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle.

As tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC noted at the end of a sensational four-and-a-half-hour hearing last night: "There are matters trending both ways on this issue."

Gleeson and his fellow tribunal members, former AFL players Darren Gaspar and Scott Stevens, decided not to enact the clause.

Neale remains banned from the grand final against Fremantle, although the Lions have until midday today to submit a notice of appeal, which would likely be heard tomorrow.

Why was the suspension upheld?

For many reasons, according to Gleeson.

Neale's evidence was rejected by Gleeson as "inconsistent".

Neale insisted he did not strike Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan during last Saturday night's preliminary final.

"It was more a bump or body-check," the dual Brownlow medallist said.

Neale said Ginnivan "might have taken a bit of a dive to get a free kick".

The tribunal did not buy the argument.

"We have listened carefully to Mr Neale's evidence, but we find it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video," Gleeson said.

"And to that extent we do not accept it."

Lachie Neale was suspended for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in Saturday's preliminary final. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

Neale maintained his shoulder and chest made contact with Ginnivan, but the tribunal found it was "a forceful blow delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand".

The only video footage of the incident was long-range and, even when enhanced, remained grainy, no matter how many times it was played frame by painstaking frame.

"It is the case that there is no single frame in the vision that shows Neale's hand or lower arm making contact with Ginnivan's abdomen," Gleeson said.

"When played at normal speed, it appears clear to us that this was, to use the common vernacular, a strike to the guts.

"We are mindful of the significant consequences for Neale of this finding of intentional strike. But we find the evidence to be cogent."

'He knew the consequences'

That was the guilty part.

Now, for what Gleeson said was "the more difficult issue".

Was using the exceptional and compelling circumstances clause justified to downgrade Neale's penalty from a ban to a fine?

Introduced this year, the clause had been deployed once: to downgrade a one-match ban for Collingwood legend and AFL games record-holder Scott Pendlebury to a fine.

Neale wanted it applied to him.

But, as Gleeson noted, Pendlebury was charged with rough conduct. Specifically, it was graded as careless conduct, medium impact, and high contact.

Neale was charged with striking. Specifically, it was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

Gleeson narrowed in on the difference between conduct gradings: Pendlebury was careless, but Neale was intentional.

Lachie Neale (left) has helped the Lions win the past two flags. (AFL Photos via Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

There was also Neale's record, which his barrister — the AFL's former football operations boss Adrian Anderson — compared to Pendlebury's.

Until March, Pendlebury had never fronted the tribunal or been suspended in his 21-year career.

Neale has not previously been banned in a 15-year career that has included two Brownlow Medals, six club champion awards, and co-captaining the Lions to two premierships.

But as AFL counsel Andrew Woods KC pointed out, Neale had previously been found guilty of offences eight times: three of them for striking the body of opponents.

But he had never been suspended.

"This is not the first occasion on which Neale has been found to have struck his opponent," Gleeson said.

The tribunal chair also noted the purpose of the AFL's so-called gut-punch law, also introduced this year. Nine other players have been banned for the offence this season.

"The purpose of the guideline is to stamp out this very sort of conduct. Neale ignored it, and he knew the consequences," Gleeson said.

"Being of Neale's outstanding record does not render a one-match suspension for that act inappropriate or unreasonable."

AAP

World.title: NRL's hardest job a family affair for Rob Toia
World.content:
Marking Herbie Farnworth is just about the hardest job any centre can have in rugby league, but Roosters flyer Robert Toia will not have to do it alone.

Friday night's preliminary final will be a family affair for the 22-year-old in more ways than one.

As a Redcliffe junior and one of 10 siblings, Toia cannot even begin to count how many friends and family he will have in the stands at a sold-out Lang Park, but he is sure to have some kin close at hand for his battle with Farnworth.

"Me, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong, we're all related," Toia said.

"We're cousins through our grandparents. Me and Salesi have always known since we were young, but Siua we only found out last year.

"[Redcliffe] is home. It's always felt like home, and every time I play at Lang Park, it's the stadium with the best atmosphere."

Toia and Wong discovered they were related last year. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Wong will line up at second row alongside Toia on the Tricolours right edge, against Farnworth and Toia's State of Origin teammate Max Plath, and both know what to expect from the fires of "The Cauldron".

Toia made his Queensland debut there after just 10 NRL games last year, while Wong is in the midst of his fourth finals campaign in as many years.

Foketi has been a later starter, only securing a place in the run-on side in recent weeks, but the three have been close ever since they lived together in the Roosters academy house as boys.

Around that same time, the trio played in a junior grand final against a Penrith side containing future Dolphins kingpin Isaiya Katoa, who will be a target for Foketi on Friday night.

The miracle wins that made Isaiya Katoa Isaiya Katoa prepares for his NRL semifinal debut as the prince of the game's playmakers and four years ago it was a series of brilliant finals performances that birthed his budding legend.

A bustling run from the 20-year-old knocked Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes out of last week's semifinal after just 75 seconds and proved why he is a danger man even among a team with as much strike as the Roosters.

"I'm so proud of him. Everything is God's timing, because he was battling and playing Cup in the beginning of the year, but he got an opportunity and took it with both hands," Toia said.

"He's one of the best backrowers in the comp."

But as big a job as the Dolphins face with containing Foketi, Toia has an even more difficult one on his hands as he tries to put a saddle on Farnworth.

The Englishman has proven he is the best centre in the world several times over, if not one of the best players overall.

Farnworth leads the NRL in tackle breaks with 161, a full 44 ahead of the next best centre, and is first among all players for offloads with 75.

Farnworth is the best centre in the world and enters the prelim in terrific form. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

He is first among centres for runs, run metres and post-contact metres and is fresh off a magnificent showing in the Dolphins' 26-16 win over the Warriors that has them one win away from their first-ever grand final.

Toia has the size and athleticism to hold his own in any battle — in that star-making Origin debut last year, he held his own against no less than Latrell Mitchell — but Farnworth still shapes as a challenge that will go a long way towards deciding whether the Roosters can progress to their first grand final since 2019.

"You see the tackle-busting ability he has, but his work rate is underrated. He's always involved, on the offensive side and the defensive side," Toia said.

"I think pressuring him, shutting him down, getting my D movements right and hopefully, I can stop him from doing what he does best."

Toia comes into the match in imperious form of his own. He has scored in both the Roosters' finals matches and, along with Mark Nawaqanitawase, was the club's chief destroyer in last week's win over Cronulla.

The highlight was a massive fend on KL Iro that sent the rugged Sharks centre, who normally defends like someone taught a bicep muscle how to tackle, fully airborne.

It is a measure of how much Toia has continued to improve this season after claiming rookie of the year honours last year and a reminder that the best is yet to come, something the Tongan international believes is just as true for his team.

"I got a bit lucky there," Toia said.

"The boys just put me in the right spots and I was just moving for them.

"It's the best feeling [winning]. It's been frustrating for a lot of the year, we haven't been able to produce our brand of game, so it was good to show a glimpse of that.

"I feel like we still haven't played 80 minutes of Roosters footy."

World.title: Chimney colours unveiled for Norwood SANFL victors amid TV ratings boost
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Norwood Football Club's colours have been unveiled atop the Brickworks chimney to celebrate its SANFL Grand Final win in what was the most-viewed game since a modern rating system began.

The total national television audience on Sunday was up 16 per cent on 2025 numbers to 109,700, which included 93,500 broadcast TV viewers.

It also included 16,100 viewers from broadcaster video on demand (BVOD), which was up 52 per cent.

The VOZ ratings, which started in 2022 and combine both broadcast TV and BVOD, found that 87,500 viewers of broadcast TV viewers were from Adelaide, along with 12,800 of those streaming online.

The Norwood and Sturt colours will stay atop the Hoffman Kiln until the end of season 2027. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"The broadcast ratings were exceptional, broke every record for the last five years," SANFL executive Darren Chandler said.

"And when you compare those to what's happening in Western Australia and Victoria, we've absolutely blown it off the charts."

SANFL kicking TV goals SANFL crowds are continuing to climb each year after COVID-19 restrictions put a dent in numbers

Football commentator Mark Soderstrom said 71 per cent of South Australian televisions switched on were tuned into the decider between Sturt and Norwood, which drew 38,250 spectators to Adelaide Oval.

The WAFL Grand Final, on the other hand, drew 19,210 people to Perth Stadium, continuing a four-year decline in crowds, while the VFL Grand Final drew just 12,941, the first time the league had attracted more than 8,000 fans in seven years.

A time-honoured tradition

The annual winners and runners-up of the SANFL grand final have been displaying their colours atop the 1913 Hoffman-designed kiln at Thebarton since the start of the decade.

The much-loved ceremony of nearly 70 years had to be moved from its previous home chimney at the West End Brewery after the facility was closed by its owners, Lion, in 2021.

Redlegs supporters came out to celebrate their team's 2026 premiership win. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Redlegs coach Jade Sheedy, who was a premiership player for Sturt in 2002 when he won the Magarey Medal with teammate Tim Weatherald, also coached Woodville-West Torrens in back-to-back premierships in 2020-21.

He told the crowd of Redleg supporters at Thebarton that when the siren blew on Sunday and Norwood beat Sturt 87 points to 73 after a final-quarter comeback, he thought he was "still in a dream for 15 minutes".

"I guess it was two years of building something pretty special, and to come together in the last 30 minutes and to believe in that, and to kick five goals three to one point in the last quarter showed how much the group had grown and that's what I'm most proud of," Sheedy said.

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and coach Jade Sheedy were still celebrating on Tuesday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said the team had not changed "too much structurally" since they lost the preliminary final by two points in 2025 but had "increased the belief in how we play".

"We just fell short in 2025, but we took a lot of learnings from that and a lot of confidence reviewing how we were playing our footy," he said.

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle payed tribute to the Redlegs at the chimney ceremony. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle attended the ceremony on behalf of the runners-up.

"I think we can all agree that Sunday was a great spectacle, and it was a great  for the competition and the league across the country," he said.

He said Norwood were "deserved winners" as the "most consistent team all year".

World.content:

Teddy Swims performed at last year's NRL grand final. (Supplied: NRL)

V'Landys was unconcerned as to whether the event could be underwhelming without pre-match entertainment.
